Personal data needed to ensure interoperability can be separated in the following three major categories: a. the message content themselves that would be exchanged between servers of the gatekeeper and those of the other providers. b. the personal data that is needed to ensure technical aspects of interoperability between the NIICS of the gatekeeper and of the provider requesting interoperability, including to ensure that end users of the different NIICS can address each other and communicate. c. personal data that gatekeepers may process to ensure that the level of security they provide to their own end users is preserved across the interoperable services, in line with Article 7(3) DMA. 202. In relation to point b. in paragraph 201, gatekeepers need to decide how to resolve identities across the different NIICS. Users of a NIICS may obtain the identity of a user of another NIICS “out of band” (i.e. via a separate, independent communication channel, such as by email or verbally). Gatekeepers should then ensure that their end users have requested to use interoperable features from specific alternative NIICS before enabling end users of those NIICS to communicate with their end users. Furthermore, in light of Article 7(7) DMA, it is important that gatekeepers raise their end users’ awareness by informing them about the possibility to communicate across NIICS, including whenever a third party NIICS becomes interoperable with the gatekeeper’s NIICS. 203. In line with Article 7(7) DMA, end users of the gatekeepers’ NIICS and of the third party NIICS need to remain free to decide whether to make use of the interoperable basic functionalities that may be provided by the gatekeeper pursuant to Article 7(1) DMA. This means that end users should be free to decide whether to engage in conversations and be discoverable by users of third-party NIICS, including through automated discovery mechanisms that might entail the sharing of data that is not strictly required to ensure interoperability between the gatekeeper and the alternative NIICS provider where applicable. End users should remain free to opt-in to those mechanisms. 204. It is also relevant that the interoperability requests displayed to users specify the NIICS providers (i.e., the new controllers) that would gain access to some necessary end users’ personal data. If the number of providers of NIICS achieving interoperability becomes very significant, gatekeepers may want to avoid ‘choice fatigue’ by requesting end users to make their choices in parallel to “moments of discontinuity” in their relationship with end users (e.g. the moment of subscription, of a software update or during a communication campaign), or when the end user of an interoperable NIICS tries to initiate a communication. They may also implement simple interoperability management systems where end users can give, review, or modify their interoperability choices across multiple providers at once (while keeping the possibility to go granular if the user wishes to), thereby reducing repetitive requests. If end users accept the exchange of identity data between the gatekeepers and providers of other NIICS requesting interoperability, and the gatekeeper and the provider requesting interoperability establish a common naming convention, exchanging only the information defined in the convention (including the end user’s identifier in each of the NIICS) might be considered “strictly necessary” in accordance with Article 5(1), point (c) GDPR. 7.2 Personal data processing to preserve the level of security across interoperable services 205. Under Article 7(3) DMA, gatekeepers are required to preserve the level of security across interoperable services. In cases where the gatekeeper offers end-to-end- encryption to its end users of its NIICS, such encryption should be preserved across the interoperable services. End-to-end-encryption (“E2EE”) is generally understood as a technology that encrypts the content data on the end device of the sending party and decrypts it on the end device of the addressed recipient in such a way that only the sender and the recipient, at the exclusion of any third party, including the carrier or the chain of involved carriers, can access and control the content data of the communication.161 Maintaining trustworthy E2EE through the process of interoperability is key to ensure that the standard of security remains the same for end users in all services. 206. Ensuring E2EE across interoperable NIICS is a task that requires both the gatekeeper and the NIICS provider requesting interoperability to actively cooperate. In that context, the implemented libraries and software solution should be well defined. 207. From a data protection point of view, implementing a well-defined protocol for managing the exchange and certification of cryptographic keys between gatekeepers and providers of NIICS requesting interoperability would greatly contribute to a secure foundation for a reliable implementation of E2EE. From the perspective of the purpose limitation principle under Article 5(1), point (b) GDPR, gatekeepers should also consider appropriate measures to ensure that the different service providers can only use the keys as well as any other corresponding content exchanged for key agreement received from the gatekeeper for the intended purpose of enabling interoperability of the NIICS. 208. Another example of measures that gatekeepers should implement to maintain the level of security under Article 7(3) DMA having data protection implications are measures to protect the metadata of the communication between end users and use the minimum amount of metadata for effective encryption key management. Another possible measure is to cryptographically verify the authenticity of the communication"

result.reason: The activity 'Organize ambulance service' involves arranging patient transport, which inherently requires processing personal data. In a hospital/clinic context, organizing an ambulance for a patient necessitates accessing and transmitting the patient’s identifiable health information (e.g., name, medical condition, location, urgency level, and potentially health records from the *Kardex*—a patient data store referenced in the diagram). This qualifies as processing of health data (a special category under GDPR Article 9) and transmission of personal data to the ambulance service or emergency responders. The *Kardex* data object (linked as input) further confirms the activity’s reliance on patient-specific records, which are explicitly classified as personal data under GDPR (Recital 35, Article 4(15)). The activity thus enables the collection, consultation, and disclosure of personal data to third parties (e.g., ambulance providers), triggering GDPR relevance.

The activity 'Prepare patient for examination' directly involves handling a patient’s personal and health data. Preparing a patient for a medical examination requires accessing and potentially updating their health records (e.g., allergies, current medications, prior diagnoses) stored in the *Kardex* (a patient data store linked as both input and output). This constitutes processing of health data (GDPR Article 9) and may include recording or updating personal information (e.g., vital signs, symptoms reported by the patient). The context of a hospital/clinic and the explicit link to the *Kardex* (a repository of patient-specific data) confirm that this activity processes identifiable personal data, as it relies on the patient’s unique medical history to ensure safe and accurate examination preparation.

The activity 'Fill in transport document' explicitly processes personal data by creating a transport document (a data object output) for patient transfer. This document would necessarily include identifiable patient information such as: name, date of birth, or patient ID (to ensure correct identification); medical condition or urgency level (health data under GDPR Article 9); destination (e.g., specific department or external facility), which may reveal sensitive details about the patient’s treatment; and timing/logistics (linked to the *Time of departure* data object), which could be tied to the patient’s identity. Even if the document does not include all health details, the combination of identifiable logistical and medical information qualifies as processing personal data, as it enables the patient to be singled out and their health status to be inferred. The activity thus involves recording, structuring, and transmitting personal data to enable safe transport, fulfilling the GDPR definition of processing (Article 4(2)).

Data Protection Officers (‘DPO’s) will be at the heart of this new legal framework for many organisations, facilitating compliance with the provisions of the GDPR. Under the GDPR, it is mandatory for certain controllers and processors to designate a DPO.2 This will be the case for all public authorities and bodies (irrespective of what data they process), and for other organisations that - as a core activity - monitor individuals systematically and on a large scale, or that process special categories of personal data on a large scale. Even when the GDPR does not specifically require the appointment of a DPO, organisations may sometimes find it useful to designate a DPO on a voluntary basis. The Article 29 Data Protection Working Party (‘WP29’) encourages these voluntary efforts. The concept of DPO is not new. Although Directive 95/46/EC3 did not require any organisation to appoint a DPO, the practice of appointing a DPO has nevertheless developed in several Member States over the years. Before the adoption of the GDPR, the WP29 argued that the DPO is a cornerstone of accountability and that appointing a DPO can facilitate compliance and furthermore, become a competitive advantage for businesses.4 In addition to facilitating compliance through the implementation of accountability tools (such as facilitating data protection impact assessments and carrying out or facilitating audits), DPOs act as intermediaries between relevant stakeholders (e.g. supervisory authorities, data subjects, and business units within an organisation). DPOs are not personally responsible in case of non-compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR makes it clear that it is the controller or the processor who is required to ensure and to be able to demonstrate that the processing is performed in accordance with its provisions (Article 24(1)). Data protection compliance is a responsibility of the controller or the processor. 1Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016). Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Organize ambulance service (sid-804E11C9-5A21-4CED-AC60-387CAD4945DE)**: The activity 'Organize ambulance service' involves arranging patient transport, which inherently requires processing personal data. In a hospital/clinic context, organizing an ambulance for a patient necessitates accessing and transmitting the patient’s identifiable health information (e.g., name, medical condition, location, urgency level, and potentially health records from the *Kardex*—a patient data store referenced in the diagram). This qualifies as processing of health data (a special category under GDPR Article 9) and transmission of personal data to the ambulance service or emergency responders. The *Kardex* data object (linked as input) further confirms the activity’s reliance on patient-specific records, which are explicitly classified as personal data under GDPR (Recital 35, Article 4(15)). The activity thus enables the collection, consultation, and disclosure of personal data to third parties (e.g., ambulance providers), triggering GDPR relevance. - **Prepare patient for examination (sid-24E41551-0FD9-438B-B46C-CC2F70C77891)**: The activity 'Prepare patient for examination' directly involves handling a patient’s personal and health data. Preparing a patient for a medical examination requires accessing and potentially updating their health records (e.g., allergies, current medications, prior diagnoses) stored in the *Kardex* (a patient data store linked as both input and output). This constitutes processing of health data (GDPR Article 9) and may include recording or updating personal information (e.g., vital signs, symptoms reported by the patient). The context of a hospital/clinic and the explicit link to the *Kardex* (a repository of patient-specific data) confirm that this activity processes identifiable personal data, as it relies on the patient’s unique medical history to ensure safe and accurate examination preparation. - **Fill in transport document (sid-E1C0CEBD-E12E-4DF4-B123-25F61C00532B)**: The activity 'Fill in transport document' explicitly processes personal data by creating a transport document (a data object output) for patient transfer. Even if the document does not include all health details, the combination of identifiable logistical and medical information qualifies as processing personal data, as it enables the patient to be singled out and their health status to be inferred. [organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[concept] Consent — Consent, as defined by Regulations 2016/679 (GDPR), particularly under Articles 4(11), 6(1)(a), and 7, is a fundamental legal basis for the processing of personal data. It signifies a freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's or end user's wishes, demonstrated by a clear, affirmative action, agreeing to the processing of their personal data for specified purposes. This applies to various data handling scenarios, including direct information retrieval, targeted advertising, processing of location data, or the storing/accessing of information on their devices. It is also an alternative legal basis for direct marketing activities when legitimate interest is not applicable and a legal ground for processing sensitive data, such as health or biometric data, under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. For consent to be valid, it must adhere to strict conditions: it must be given freely, without coercion, intimidation, deception, or negative consequences for withholding it. [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

Under GDPR, **consent** is a lawful basis for processing personal data (Article 6(1)(a)), and **health data** (a special category) requires **explicit consent** (Article 9(2)(a)). Even if the form itself does not explicitly list personal data fields, the purpose of the form (requesting medical procedures) and its position in the process (following health-data-processing tasks) confirm that it handles personal data. Key indicators include: health data context (the form pertains to diagnostic examinations, which are special category data), patient identifiability (requests must be tied to specific patients), process flow (the activity is embedded in a clinical pathway where adjacent tasks explicitly process health data), and the hospital core activity (filling clinical request forms is essential to healthcare provision).

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. Recital 97 specifies that the core activities of a controller relate to ‘primary activities and do not relate to the processing of personal data as ancillary activities’. ‘Core activities’ can be considered as the key operations necessary to achieve the controller’s or processor’s goals. However, ‘core activities’ should not be interpreted as excluding activities where the processing of data forms an inextricable part of the controller’s or processor’s activity. For example, the core activity of a hospital is to provide health care. However, a hospital could not provide healthcare safely and effectively without processing health data, such as patients’ health records. Therefore, processing these data should be considered to be one of any hospital’s core activities and hospitals must therefore designate DPOs. As another example, a private security company carries out the surveillance of a number of private shopping centres and public spaces. Surveillance is the core activity of the company, which in turn is inextricably linked to the processing of personal data. Therefore, this company must also designate a DPO. On the other hand, all organisations carry out certain activities, for example, paying their employees or having standard IT support activities. These are examples of necessary support functions for the organisation’s core activity or main business. Even though these activities are necessary or essential, they are usually considered ancillary functions rather than the core activity. 2.1.3 ‘LARGE SCALE’ Article 37(1)(b) and (c) requires that the processing of personal data be carried out on a large scale in order for the designation of a DPO to be triggered. The GDPR does not define what constitutes large- scale processing, though recital 91 provides some guidance.14 Indeed, it is not possible to give a precise number either with regard to the amount of data processed or the number of individuals concerned, which would be applicable in all situations. This does not exclude the possibility, however, that over time, a standard practice may develop for identifying in more specific and/or quantitative terms what constitutes ‘large scale’ in respect of certain types of common processing activities. The WP29 also plans to contribute to this development, by way of sharing and publicising examples of the relevant thresholds for the designation of a DPO. In any event, the WP29 recommends that the following factors, in particular, be considered when 14 According to the recital, ‘large-scale processing operations which aim to process a considerable amount of personal data at regional, national or supranational level and which could affect a large number of data subjects and which are likely to result in a high risk’ would be included, in particular. On the other hand, the recital specifically provides that ‘the processing of personal data should not be considered to be on a large scale if the processing concerns personal data from patients or clients by an individual physician, other health care professional or lawyer’. It is important to consider that while the recital provides examples at the extremes of the scale (processing by an individual physician versus processing of data of a whole country or across Europe); there is a large grey zone in between these extremes. In addition, it should be borne in mind that this recital refers to data protection impact assessments. This implies that some elements might be specific to that context and do not necessarily apply to the designation of DPOs in the exact same way. 8 determining whether the processing is carried out on a large scale:  The number of data subjects concerned - either as a specific number or as a proportion of the relevant population  The volume of data and/or the range of different data items being processed  The duration, or permanence, of the data processing activity  The geographical extent of the processing activity Examples of large-scale processing include:  processing of patient data in the regular course of business by a hospital  processing of travel data of individuals using a city’s public transport system (e.g. tracking via travel cards)  processing of real time geo-location data of customers of an international fast food chain for statistical purposes by a processor specialised in providing these services  processing of customer data in the regular course of business by an insurance company or a bank  processing of personal data for behavioural advertising by a search engine  processing of data (content, traffic, location) by telephone or internet service providers Examples that do not constitute large-scale processing include:  processing of patient data by an individual physician  processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences by an individual lawyer 2.1.4 ‘REGULAR AND SYSTEMATIC MONITORING’ The notion of regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects is not defined in the GDPR, but the concept of ‘monitoring of the behaviour of data subjects’ is mentioned in recital 2415 and clearly includes all forms of tracking and profiling on the internet, including for the purposes of behavioural advertising. [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Source: Article 37(1) of the GDPR 2 What does ‘core activities’ mean? ‘Core activities’ can be considered as the key operations to achieve the controller’s or processor’s objectives. These also include all activities where the processing of data forms as inextricable part of the controller’s or processor’s activity. For example, processing health data, such as patient’s health records, should be considered as one of any hospital’s core activities and hospitals must therefore designate DPOs. On the other hand, all organisations carry out certain supporting activities, for example, paying their employees or having standard IT support activities. These are examples of necessary support functions for the organisation’s core activity or main business. Even though these activities are necessary or essential, they are usually considered ancillary functions rather than the core activity. Source: Article 37(1)(b) and (c) of the GDPR 21 3 What does ‘large scale’ mean? The GDPR does not define what constitutes large-scale processing. The WP29 recommends that the following factors, in particular, be considered when determining whether the processing is carried out on a large scale:  the number of data subjects concerned - either as a specific number or as a proportion of the relevant population  the volume of data and/or the range of different data items being processed  the duration, or permanence, of the data processing activity  the geographical extent of the processing activity Examples of large scale processing include:  processing of patient data in the regular course of business by a hospital  processing of travel data of individuals using a city’s public transport"

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Recital 97 specifies that the core activities of a controller relate to ‘primary activities and do not relate to the processing of personal data as ancillary activities’. ‘Core activities’ can be considered as the key operations necessary to achieve the controller’s or processor’s goals. However, ‘core activities’ should not be interpreted as excluding activities where the processing of data forms an inextricable part of the controller’s or processor’s activity. For example, the core activity of a hospital is to provide health care. However, a hospital could not provide healthcare safely and effectively without processing health data, such as patients’ health records. Therefore, processing these data should be considered to be one of any hospital’s core activities and hospitals must therefore designate DPOs. As another example, a private security company carries out the surveillance of a number of private shopping centres and public spaces. Surveillance is the core activity of the company, which in turn is inextricably linked to the processing of personal data. Therefore, this company must also designate a DPO. On the other hand, all organisations carry out certain activities, for example, paying their employees or having standard IT support activities. These are examples of necessary support functions for the organisation’s core activity or main business. Even though these activities are necessary or essential, they are usually considered ancillary functions rather than the core activity. 2.1.3 ‘LARGE SCALE’ Article 37(1)(b) and (c) requires that the processing of personal data be carried out on a large scale in order for the designation of a DPO to be triggered. The GDPR does not define what constitutes large- scale processing, though recital 91 provides some guidance.14 Indeed, it is not possible to give a precise number either with regard to the amount of data processed or the number of individuals concerned, which would be applicable in all situations. This does not exclude the possibility, however, that over time, a standard practice may develop for identifying in more specific and/or quantitative terms what constitutes ‘large scale’ in respect of certain types of common processing activities. The WP29 also plans to contribute to this development, by way of sharing and publicising examples of the relevant thresholds for the designation of a DPO. In any event, the WP29 recommends that the following factors, in particular, be considered when 14 According to the recital, ‘large-scale processing operations which aim to process a considerable amount of personal data at regional, national or supranational level and which could affect a large number of data subjects and which are likely to result in a high risk’ would be included, in particular. On the other hand, the recital specifically provides that ‘the processing of personal data should not be considered to be on a large scale if the processing concerns personal data from patients or clients by an individual physician, other health care professional or lawyer’. It is important to consider that while the recital provides examples at the extremes of the scale (processing by an individual physician versus processing of data of a whole country or across Europe); there is a large grey zone in between these extremes. In addition, it should be borne in mind that this recital refers to data protection impact assessments. ## Test Case 16 - Order blood bottles - Amount of Correct Activities: 3 - Amount of False Positives: 0 - Amount of False Negatives: 0 - **Expected:** Fill in the order form (sid-D8309D0D-4482-428E-A648-46AE8CB7144E), Send order form (sid-525EA4D4-3E64-473A-A143-CF609068A875), Receive delivery of blood bottles from blood donor center (sid-43330E63-E36F-4FFB-A853-944AB5A202A7) - **Actual:** Fill in the order form (sid-D8309D0D-4482-428E-A648-46AE8CB7144E), Send order form (sid-525EA4D4-3E64-473A-A143-CF609068A875), Receive delivery of blood bottles from blood donor center (sid-43330E63-E36F-4FFB-A853-944AB5A202A7) - **Result:** ✅ Passed - **False Positives:** None - **False Negatives:** None - **Amount of Retries:** 1 ### RAG Metrics (Ragas) - **Faithfulness:** 0.643 - **Context Utilization:** 0.616 - **Samples:** 3 (failed: 0)

Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Fill in the order form (sid-D8309D0D-4482-428E-A648-46AE8CB7144E)**: **Fill in the order form** involves the collection and entry of patient-specific data required for a blood order prior to surgery. In a hospital context, such an order form inherently includes **personal data**—most critically, the **patient’s identity** (e.g., name, medical record number, date of birth) and **health-related information** (e.g., blood type, surgical procedure details, clinical notes). These details qualify as **health data** under GDPR Article 4(15) and Recital 35, which explicitly includes 'information related to the physiological or biomedical state of the data subject' obtained in a healthcare setting. The activity thus constitutes **processing of personal data** through the **collection, recording, and structuring** of identifiable patient information, which is necessary for the provision of health or social care (GDPR Article 9(2)(h)). The hospital’s core activity of healthcare delivery inextricably involves such data processing, as confirmed by the EDPB’s guidance on health data in scientific research (e.g., 'processing of patient data in the regular course of business by a hospital' is deemed large-scale and core). - **Send order form (sid-525EA4D4-3E64-473A-A143-CF609068A875)**: **Send order form** transmits the previously collected **patient-specific order form** (containing personal and health data) to the blood donor center. This activity constitutes **disclosure by transmission** of personal data under GDPR Article 4(2), as it involves sharing identifiable patient information (e.g., name, medical record number, blood type, surgical details) with a third party (the donor center). The transmission of health data for healthcare purposes (e.g., ensuring blood availability for surgery) is explicitly covered under GDPR Article 9(2)(h) as necessary for 'health or social care' provision. The activity also aligns with the **recipient** concept in GDPR (Article 4(9)), where the donor center acts as a recipient of the disclosed data. Given the sensitive nature of health data, this transmission triggers GDPR obligations, including ensuring lawful basis (e.g., patient consent or contractual necessity for treatment) and safeguarding the data during transfer. - **Receive delivery of blood bottles from blood donor center (sid-43330E63-E36F-4FFB-A853-944AB5A202A7)**: **Receive delivery of blood bottles from blood donor center** involves handling the **associated order form data** (linked via the data object reference) upon physical delivery of the blood products. While the primary action is logistic (receiving bottles), the activity implicitly includes **retrieval and consultation** of the patient-specific order form to verify the delivery matches the request (e.g., blood type, quantity, patient identifier). This constitutes **processing of personal data** under GDPR Article 4(2), as the ward doctor must cross-reference the delivered blood with the patient’s identity and clinical needs—both of which are personal data. The activity is thus GDPR-relevant because it **uses** and **consults** health data (the order form) to ensure correct allocation to the patient, which is integral to the **provision of health care** (GDPR Article 9(2)(h)). The hospital’s obligation to process such data safely is further underscored by the EDPB’s emphasis on health data protection in clinical contexts.

A physical examination involves the collection, recording, and assessment of a patient’s **physiological or biomedical state** (e.g., vital signs, symptoms, medical history, or diagnostic observations). This aligns with GDPR’s definition of **health data** (Article 4(15)), which is a **special category of personal data** (Article 9) requiring heightened protection. The activity is performed by a **Senior Physician**, a **Health Professional** as referenced in the legal context, who directly obtains and documents information about the patient’s health status. The supporting legal excerpts explicitly state that **medical history, clinical treatment, or physiological state**—regardless of source (e.g., physician, hospital, or diagnostic test)—constitute personal data. Thus, this task involves **processing** (collection, recording, and structuring) of **personal data** for the purpose of **medical diagnosis**, which is explicitly GDPR-relevant.

**Explain further procedure to patient** involves **direct communication with the data subject (patient)** about their **medical treatment plan**, which inherently requires the use of their **personal data**. The task likely includes discussing the patient’s **diagnosis, proposed diagnostic tests (e.g., ultrasound, CT scans), and next steps in their care**—all of which are tied to their **health data** (a special category under GDPR). Even if no new data is collected, the activity **consults and uses** the patient’s existing personal data (e.g., from the **Kardex** data store, which is linked to this task) to provide tailored explanations. Under GDPR, **any use of personal data**, including verbal communication about a patient’s health status or treatment, qualifies as **processing**. The legal context emphasizes that **health professionals** (here, the Senior Physician) routinely handle **physiological or biomedical state** data, making this activity GDPR-relevant.

**Arrange further examinations** involves **organizing and structuring** diagnostic procedures (e.g., ultrasound, CT scans, NMR) that directly relate to the patient’s **health data**. This task requires accessing and using the patient’s **existing medical records** (linked via the **Kardex** data store) to determine which tests are clinically necessary. The activity also **generates new personal data** by scheduling and documenting these examinations, which will later be associated with the patient’s identity and health status. Under GDPR, **health data** (including diagnostic test results) is a **special category of personal data**, and any operation—such as **structuring, storing, or preparing for further processing**—qualifies as **processing**. The legal context explicitly highlights that **hospitals** and **health professionals** process such data as part of their core activities, and that **further processing** (e.g., using initial data to schedule additional tests) is subject to GDPR requirements.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

In order to ensure that the DPO is accessible, whether internal or external, it is important to make sure that their contact details are available. The DPO, with the help of a team if necessary, must be in a position to efficiently communicate with data subjects and cooperate with the supervisory authorities concerned. This means that this communication must take place in the language or languages used by the supervisory authorities and the data subjects concerned. The availability of a DPO (whether physically on the same premises as employees, via a hotline or other secure means of communication) is essential to ensure that data subjects will be able to contact the DPO. The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Furthermore, a Hospital can also be an organization involved in scientific research, as exemplified by "Project X," which necessitates the use of real patient dental records. The Hospital has also been identified as a victim of ransomware attacks (e.g., Case No. 03), where its information systems were compromised, leading to data encryption and subsequent delays in patient care. Consequently, a Hospital is an organization legally obliged to notify relevant authorities and affected individuals in cases of cyber-attacks impacting medical records.
A hospital's core activity is providing healthcare, which inextricably involves processing health data like patient health records.
An example of an organization whose core activities involve processing health data, thus requiring the designation of a DPO.
A hospital is an organization that processes patient data in the regular course of business.
An example context where unavailability of critical medical data can pose a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.
A hospital is an organization that holds medical records and is obliged to notify in case of a data breach, especially if it poses a high risk to patients.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[person] Children — Children are consistently identified as a vulnerable category of data subjects and individuals who require specific and enhanced protection regarding their personal data, especially under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This heightened protection is due to their susceptibility to influence from targeted campaigns, their potential lack of awareness regarding risks and their rights concerning personal data processing, and their possible inability to knowingly and thoughtfully oppose or consent to such processing. The GDPR mandates particular consideration for Children's capacity to provide informed consent for data processing. Their personal data receives heightened protection, particularly in relation to information society services, with the age for valid consent varying between 13 and 16 years under Article 8 of the GDPR. Compliance with national laws concerning contractual capacity is also essential when engaging with Children. They also require comprehensible information about personal data processing due to their vulnerability. As individuals who may be disproportionately affected by legislative measures, Children merit specific protection, particularly concerning profiling for marketing and automated decision-making with significant effects. Article 12.1 of the GDPR specifies that clear and plain language is especially important when providing information to Children, an audience segment that benefits from child-centred language and transparency. Recital 38 GDPR additionally highlights the particular attention required for Children regarding data processing. These principles are further reinforced through codes of conduct that address their personal data protection and consent mechanisms. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child recognizes individuals under the age of 18 years as Children.

[concept] Preventive or Occupational Medicine — Medical practices related to preventing illness or managing health in the workplace, for which personal data processing may be necessary.

[person] Chair — The Chair, along with the LSA, is responsible for deciding whether the file is complete according to Article 11(2) RoP.
The Chair refers subject-matter to the EDPB and makes decisions with the competent supervisory authority regarding file completeness.
