Personal data needed to ensure interoperability can be separated in the following three major categories: a. the message content themselves that would be exchanged between servers of the gatekeeper and those of the other providers. b. the personal data that is needed to ensure technical aspects of interoperability between the NIICS of the gatekeeper and of the provider requesting interoperability, including to ensure that end users of the different NIICS can address each other and communicate. c. personal data that gatekeepers may process to ensure that the level of security they provide to their own end users is preserved across the interoperable services, in line with Article 7(3) DMA. 202. In relation to point b. in paragraph 201, gatekeepers need to decide how to resolve identities across the different NIICS. Users of a NIICS may obtain the identity of a user of another NIICS “out of band” (i.e. via a separate, independent communication channel, such as by email or verbally). Gatekeepers should then ensure that their end users have requested to use interoperable features from specific alternative NIICS before enabling end users of those NIICS to communicate with their end users. Furthermore, in light of Article 7(7) DMA, it is important that gatekeepers raise their end users’ awareness by informing them about the possibility to communicate across NIICS, including whenever a third party NIICS becomes interoperable with the gatekeeper’s NIICS. 203. In line with Article 7(7) DMA, end users of the gatekeepers’ NIICS and of the third party NIICS need to remain free to decide whether to make use of the interoperable basic functionalities that may be provided by the gatekeeper pursuant to Article 7(1) DMA. This means that end users should be free to decide whether to engage in conversations and be discoverable by users of third-party NIICS, including through automated discovery mechanisms that might entail the sharing of data that is not strictly required to ensure interoperability between the gatekeeper and the alternative NIICS provider where applicable. End users should remain free to opt-in to those mechanisms. 204. It is also relevant that the interoperability requests displayed to users specify the NIICS providers (i.e., the new controllers) that would gain access to some necessary end users’ personal data. If the number of providers of NIICS achieving interoperability becomes very significant, gatekeepers may want to avoid ‘choice fatigue’ by requesting end users to make their choices in parallel to “moments of discontinuity” in their relationship with end users (e.g. the moment of subscription, of a software update or during a communication campaign), or when the end user of an interoperable NIICS tries to initiate a communication. They may also implement simple interoperability management systems where end users can give, review, or modify their interoperability choices across multiple providers at once (while keeping the possibility to go granular if the user wishes to), thereby reducing repetitive requests. If end users accept the exchange of identity data between the gatekeepers and providers of other NIICS requesting interoperability, and the gatekeeper and the provider requesting interoperability establish a common naming convention, exchanging only the information defined in the convention (including the end user’s identifier in each of the NIICS) might be considered “strictly necessary” in accordance with Article 5(1), point (c) GDPR. 7.2 Personal data processing to preserve the level of security across interoperable services 205. Under Article 7(3) DMA, gatekeepers are required to preserve the level of security across interoperable services. In cases where the gatekeeper offers end-to-end- encryption to its end users of its NIICS, such encryption should be preserved across the interoperable services. End-to-end-encryption (“E2EE”) is generally understood as a technology that encrypts the content data on the end device of the sending party and decrypts it on the end device of the addressed recipient in such a way that only the sender and the recipient, at the exclusion of any third party, including the carrier or the chain of involved carriers, can access and control the content data of the communication.161 Maintaining trustworthy E2EE through the process of interoperability is key to ensure that the standard of security remains the same for end users in all services. 206. Ensuring E2EE across interoperable NIICS is a task that requires both the gatekeeper and the NIICS provider requesting interoperability to actively cooperate. In that context, the implemented libraries and software solution should be well defined. 207. From a data protection point of view, implementing a well-defined protocol for managing the exchange and certification of cryptographic keys between gatekeepers and providers of NIICS requesting interoperability would greatly contribute to a secure foundation for a reliable implementation of E2EE. This principle states that the controller is responsible for and must be able to demonstrate compliance with the principles of personal data processing.
Accountability is a principle enshrined in Article 5 of the GDPR, requiring the controller to be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, the other principles of data protection.
[data] End User Account Settings — End user account settings are used by gatekeepers to record and honor preferences for signed-in end users across various devices.
[organization] Independent Body — An entity entrusted with the appointment of supervisory authority members under Member State law.
[method] Fraud Monitoring and Prevention — Techniques and activities aimed at detecting and preventing fraudulent activities, which can be a basis for automated processing.
[method] Electronic Means of Information Exchange — This method describes the formats and procedures for exchanging information between various entities electronically.

[concept] Data Transfers — Data transfers involve the movement of data from one location or entity to another.
Data Transfers refer to the movement of data to third countries or international organizations, which can be based on appropriate safeguards and legal remedies for data subjects.
Data transfers involve the movement of personal data, and possible risks due to absence of adequacy decisions or safeguards (Article 46) must be informed.
Data Transfers involve the movement of personal data from one entity or location to another, especially across borders.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

Therefore, a security incident resulting in personal data being made unavailable for a period of time is also a type of breach, as the lack of access to the data can have a significant impact on the rights and freedoms of natural persons. To be clear, where personal data is unavailable due to planned system maintenance being carried out this is not a ‘breach of security’ as defined in Article 4(12). As with a permanent loss or destruction of personal data (or indeed any other type of breach), a breach involving the temporary loss of availability should be documented in accordance with Article 33(5). This assists the controller in demonstrating accountability to the supervisory authority, which may ask to see those records16.However, depending on the circumstances of the breach, it may or may not require notification to the supervisory authority and communication to affected individuals. The controller will need to assess the likelihood and severity of the impact on the rights and freedoms of natural persons as a result of the lack of availability of personal data. In accordance with Article 33, the controller will need to notify unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Of course, this will need to be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Examples available at http://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r4.pdf. CNSSI-4009 also refers to: " Timely, reliable access to data and information services for authorized users." See https://rmf.org/wp- content/uploads/2017/10/CNSSI-4009.pdf. ISO/IEC 27000:2016 also defines “availability” as “Property of being accessible and usable upon demand by an authorized entity”: https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/#iso:std:iso- iec:27000:ed-4:v1:en 16 See Article 33(5) 9 In the context of a hospital, if critical medical data about patients are unavailable, even temporarily, this could present a risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms; for example, operations may be cancelled and lives put at risk. Conversely, in the case of a media company’s systems being unavailable for several hours (e.g. due to a power outage), if that company is then prevented from sending newsletters to its subscribers, this is unlikely to present a risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. It should be noted that although a loss of availability of a controller’s systems might be only temporary and may not have an impact on individuals, it is important for the controller to consider all possible consequences of a breach, as it may still require notification for other reasons. Example Infection by ransomware (malicious software which encrypts the controller’s data until a ransom is paid) could lead to a temporary loss of availability if the data can be restored from backup. However, a network intrusion still occurred, and notification could be required if the incident is qualified as confidentiality breach (i.e. personal data is accessed by the attacker) and this presents a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. 3. The possible consequences of a personal data breach A breach can potentially have a range of significant adverse effects on individuals, which can result in physical, material, or non-material damage. The GDPR explains that this can include loss of control over their personal data, limitation of their rights, discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss, unauthorised reversal of pseudonymisation, damage to reputation, and loss of confidentiality of personal data protected by professional secrecy. It can also include any other significant economic or social disadvantage to those individuals17. Accordingly, the GDPR requires the controller to notify a breach to the competent supervisory authority, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk of such adverse effects taking place. Where there is a likely high risk of these adverse effects occurring, the GDPR requires the controller to communicate the breach to the affected individuals as soon as is reasonably feasible18. The importance of being able to identify a breach, to assess the risk to individuals, and then notify if required, is emphasised in Recital 87 of the GDPR: “It should be ascertained whether all appropriate technological protection and organisational measures have been implemented to establish immediately whether a personal data breach has taken place and to inform promptly the supervisory authority and the data subject. The fact that the notification was made without undue delay should be established taking into account in particular the nature and gravity of the personal data breach and its consequences and adverse effects for the data subject. Such notification may result in an intervention of the supervisory authority in accordance with its tasks and powers laid down in this Regulation.” Further guidelines on assessing the risk of adverse effects to individuals are considered in section IV. Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Send invoice by email (sid-3B0EDBCF-BE0F-418E-A24E-215628C04F84)**: The activity **Send invoice by email** processes personal data because it involves transmitting an invoice to a customer via email. Invoices inherently contain personal data such as the customer's name, address, contact details (email), and potentially financial information (e.g., bank account details, payment history, or service usage tied to an identifiable individual). Under GDPR, any operation involving the transmission of such identifiable information qualifies as 'processing' (Article 4(2) GDPR), and email communication is explicitly an electronic means of exchanging personal data. The act of sending an invoice directly links the data to a natural person, making this activity GDPR-relevant. - **Suspend internet (sid-6405B6D9-193A-47DD-B53F-5A88532EC807)**: The activity **Suspend internet** is GDPR-relevant because suspending an individual’s internet service inherently involves processing their personal data. To perform this action, the ISP must identify the specific customer (a natural person) whose service is being suspended, which requires accessing and using their account information (e.g., name, address, contract details, or IP address). The suspension itself may also log or record the action in the customer’s account history, constituting further processing. Under GDPR, any operation tied to an identified or identifiable person—including restricting or altering their service based on their account—qualifies as processing personal data (Article 4(1) and 4(2) GDPR). - **Close account (sid-C77F7087-5BB2-434F-B771-2520EE9DECEE)**: The activity **Close account** processes personal data because closing a customer account requires accessing, updating, and potentially archiving the individual’s personal information. This includes identifying the account holder (a natural person) via their name, contact details, contract history, payment records, or online identifiers (e.g., customer ID). The GDPR defines such operations—including erasure, restriction, or structural changes to personal data—as 'processing' (Article 4(2)). Additionally, the activity may involve notifying the customer or retaining records for legal or billing purposes, both of which further process personal data. - **Send payment (sid-810FB071-74CD-4663-A9BB-9B5250944404)**: The activity **Send payment** is GDPR-relevant because it involves transmitting financial data (e.g., bank account details, payment amounts) linked to an identifiable natural person (the customer). Even if the payment itself is a transactional act, the underlying data—such as the payer’s name, account number, or reference to an invoice—constitutes personal data under GDPR (Article 4(1)). The transmission of this data to a bank or payment processor qualifies as 'disclosure by transmission' (Article 4(2)), making this activity subject to GDPR compliance requirements. - **Send payment (sid-561300F0-B48F-4BC0-B67F-4B118F1D1714)**: The activity **Send payment** (second instance) is GDPR-relevant for the same reasons as the first instance: it involves transmitting personal financial data (e.g., payment details, customer identifiers) to a bank or recipient. The act of sending a payment inherently links the transaction to an identifiable individual (the customer), and the GDPR classifies such transmissions as processing (Article 4(2)). Even routine financial transactions are covered if they involve personal data, as they enable the recipient to associate the payment with a specific person. - **Debit money (sid-C0C3F9F6-471C-475A-9AD8-528C78DE08DF)**: The activity **Debit money** processes personal data because debiting a customer’s bank account requires accessing and using their financial information (e.g., account number, name, transaction history). This data is explicitly personal under GDPR (Article 4(1)), as it relates to an identified or identifiable natural person. The bank, acting as a controller or processor, performs operations (retrieval, alteration, and transmission of account data) that qualify as processing (Article 4(2)). Additionally, the activity may involve logging the transaction, which further processes personal data. - **Debit money (sid-BCB72B81-B9AB-497A-BA9F-7CE550FD9A88)**: The activity **Debit money** (second instance) is GDPR-relevant for identical reasons to the first instance: it involves processing the customer’s personal financial data (e.g., account details, transaction records) to execute a debit. The GDPR defines such operations as processing (Article 4(2)), and financial data linked to an individual is explicitly protected. The bank’s role in initiating the debit requires handling this personal data, making the activity subject to GDPR compliance. - **Charge late fee (sid-2EBB860C-A2E8-4FE5-BDD3-7AC743E46EF7)**: The activity **Charge late fee** processes personal data because it involves updating a customer’s account with a financial penalty. This requires accessing and modifying their personal information, such as their name, account number, payment history, and contact details (to notify them of the fee). The GDPR classifies such updates and financial transactions as processing (Article 4(2)), especially when linked to an identifiable individual. result.reason: The activity "issue death certificate" processes personal data because it involves the creation and formal recording of a legal document tied to a deceased individual’s identity. A death certificate inherently contains personal data as defined by GDPR Article 4, including the name of the deceased (a direct identifier), biographical details (e.g., date of birth, date of death, place of residence), potentially health-related information (e.g., cause of death, which may reflect physiological or biomedical state), and family relationships (e.g., next of kin, which can indirectly identify living relatives). Under GDPR Recital 36 and Article 9, health data (including cause of death) is classified as a special category of personal data, requiring heightened protection. The act of issuing the certificate involves collecting, recording, and structuring this data, all of which constitute 'processing' under GDPR Article 4(2). Additionally, the certificate may be disclosed to recipients (e.g., family members, registries, or authorities), further triggering GDPR obligations around data transmission (Article 4(9)). The Clinic (as the controller) is responsible for ensuring lawful processing, accuracy, and secure handling of this data, including compliance with retention periods and access rights for bereaved families. The activity’s placement in the Physician lane reinforces its link to health data processing, as physicians are health professionals who routinely handle sensitive personal data (GDPR Recital 36).

The activity "inform relatives and family physician" processes personal data because it involves the transmission of sensitive information about a deceased individual to identified third parties. Key GDPR-relevant aspects include: 1) Disclosure of Personal Data: The activity explicitly communicates details about the death (e.g., name, date, cause) to relatives (who are identifiable natural persons) and the family physician (a health professional). Under GDPR Article 4(9), relatives and the physician are recipients of personal data, and their receipt of this information constitutes a data transfer. The cause of death and associated medical context qualify as health data (GDPR Article 9), a special category of personal data requiring explicit safeguards. 2) Processing Operations: The act of informing involves consulting the patient’s record (retrieving data), structuring the information for communication, and transmitting it to external parties. All these actions are forms of 'processing' under GDPR Article 4(2). The family physician, as a health professional, may further process this data for their own records (e.g., updating the patient’s medical history), extending the GDPR scope. 3) Contextual Indicators: The activity occurs in a Clinic setting, where the Physician (as controller) is responsible for ensuring lawful disclosure. The absence of explicit consent from the deceased or relatives does not negate GDPR applicability; instead, it shifts focus to alternative lawful bases (e.g., public health obligations or legitimate interest, per GDPR Article 6). The sensitivity of the data (death and health information) heightens the risk to individuals’ rights (e.g., emotional distress, reputational harm), as noted in GDPR Recital 75. 4) Accountability Requirements: The Clinic must document this disclosure (GDPR Article 30) and ensure recipients handle the data appropriately (e.g., family physicians must treat it confidentially under professional ethics and GDPR). If the information is transmitted electronically or via unsecured channels, additional risks (e.g., interception) arise, necessitating safeguards like encryption (GDPR Article 32). In summary, this activity is GDPR-relevant due to the transmission of health-related personal data to identifiable recipients, triggering obligations around lawful basis, transparency, and data security.

The activity "complete and archive patient record" processes personal data because it involves finalizing, storing, and retaining a deceased patient’s medical records, which are explicitly classified as special categories of personal data under GDPR. Key GDPR-relevant aspects include: 1) Nature of the Data: Medical records contain highly sensitive information such as health data (diagnoses, treatment histories, examination results, and cause of death (GDPR Article 9)), identifiers (name, date of birth, patient ID, and contact details (GDPR Article 4(1))), and biographical data (family medical history or next-of-kin information, which may indirectly identify living relatives). GDPR Recital 36 and Article 9(1) emphasize that health data—regardless of source (e.g., physician, hospital, or diagnostic tests)—requires specific protection. 2) Processing Operations: Completing the record involves updating the file with final entries (e.g., death confirmation, cause of death), which constitutes altering or structuring personal data (GDPR Article 4(2)). Archiving, the long-term storage of the record for legal, historical, or research purposes, falls under archiving in the public interest (GDPR Article 89 and Recital 158). While archiving may exempt certain rights (e.g., erasure), it does not eliminate GDPR’s core requirements for security, purpose limitation, and retention periods. The Hospital/Clinic (as controller) must ensure the archived data remains confidential, accurate, and accessible only to authorized personnel (GDPR Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32). 3) Risks and Safeguards: Unauthorized access to medical records is a frequent target of breaches (e.g., ransomware attacks on hospitals). GDPR mandates technical/organizational measures (e.g., encryption, access controls) to mitigate risks (Article 32). The controller must define and justify how long the record is stored, balancing legal obligations (e.g., national health laws) with GDPR’s storage limitation principle (Article 5(1)(e)). Data subject rights may still apply post-mortem, allowing relatives to exercise rights (e.g., access to the record) under national laws or GDPR’s posthumous data protection provisions (where applicable). 4) Contextual Indicators: The activity is performed by a Physician in a Clinic, both of which are controllers routinely processing health data. The Hospital context highlights the high risk associated with medical record breaches, including delays in patient care or reputational harm. Archiving for public health or research purposes (e.g., mortality statistics) must comply with GDPR’s scientific research exemptions (Article 89), requiring safeguards like pseudonymization. In summary, this activity is GDPR-relevant due to the handling of special-category health data in a high-risk context, requiring compliance with Article 9 (special categories), Article 5 (principles), and Article 32 (security).

[concept] Certification — Certification is a formal mechanism that provides reliable evidence of compliance with specified standards, particularly in the context of data protection regulations such as GDPR. It involves an impartial, third-party assessment where entities, processes, or services are evaluated against specific criteria established by a Certification Body. This process results in a status being issued, attesting that the fulfillment of these criteria has been demonstrated. Under GDPR, certification is a crucial tool for demonstrating adherence to the regulation, and the bodies performing these assessments often require accreditation. This entire certification activity is designed to ensure transparency in the evaluation process and officially verify that processing operations comply with data protection requirements, thereby offering added value and competitive advantage to certified entities.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

Under various data protection frameworks, such as GDPR Article 17.3.d, Archiving Purposes can serve as a specific ground for processing personal data. This designation may allow for exceptions to certain individual rights, including the right to erasure (delisting) or exemptions from specific information provision obligations for data controllers. Such exceptions are generally foreseen under certain conditions and are often subject to appropriate safeguards to protect the rights and freedoms of data subjects.

The sensitive nature of the data processed means that data breaches at a Hospital are highly impactful, and the unavailability of critical medical data can pose a substantial risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[organization] Supervisory Authorities — Supervisory Authorities (SAs) are independent national public bodies primarily tasked with overseeing the application and enforcement of data protection law, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), within their respective countries. Their foundational mission involves protecting the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects while also facilitating the free flow of personal data within the European Union. These authorities play a crucial role in monitoring adherence to data protection principles, advising on and documenting proportionality and necessity tests, and ensuring the consistent application of data protection principles and individual rights. They evaluate data processing features and assess compliance, including with Article 25 of the GDPR. They are also responsible for establishing and publicizing lists of processing operations that require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). SAs are also responsible for monitoring and ensuring compliance with data protection rules, possessing equivalent powers and sanctions across the Union. Supervisory Authorities are endowed with significant enforcement powers under GDPR Article 58, allowing them to issue corrective measures and impose administrative fines for infringements. These fines are expected to be effective, dissuasive, and proportionate, adjusted based on aggravating and mitigating factors. Both data controllers and processors are directly accountable to these authorities for GDPR compliance. Past decisions based on Directive 95/46/EC remain in force until amended or repealed. Beyond enforcement, SAs handle and investigate complaints from data subjects, including those related to search engine providers' refusal to erase search results under Article 17 GDPR, and are responsible for assessing delisting requests. They also encourage the development of codes of conduct and foster certification mechanisms, potentially acting as certification bodies themselves, and approving criteria and issuing certifications, as well as receiving reasons for granting or withdrawing certification from certification bodies and making requirements and criteria for certification public. SAs have powers to obtain access to personal data and premises from data controllers or processors. Their competence does not extend to courts acting in their judicial capacity. Supervisory Authorities have a legal obligation to cooperate, exchange information, and endeavor to reach consensus, especially within the "One Stop Shop" (OSS) model and obligations under Article 60 of the GDPR. This involves coordinating through draft decisions, where other Supervisory Authorities (CSAs) receive relevant information and draft decisions from the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and provide feedback. They are considered fully acquainted with notified decisions and take decisions on issues handled in the consistency mechanism, which are registered by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). Instances of conflicting views among Supervisory Authorities can lead to EDPB decisions, demonstrating their cooperative yet authoritative role in ensuring GDPR compliance and consistency across the EU. Supervisory Authorities are stakeholders with whom Data Protection Officers (DPOs) act as intermediaries, and data subjects and DPOs can contact them for data protection matters, with DPO contact details and name communicated to them. They are also involved in the exchange of information with controllers, processors, and the Board regarding binding corporate rules and mutual assistance, and cooperate to ensure the consistent application of the Regulation and communicate with the Board, promoting cooperation, information exchange, and training. They are regulatory bodies responsible for interpreting and enforcing data protection regulations, including assessing "substantial effect" on a case-by-case basis.
Supervisory authorities are responsible for overseeing data protection and cooperate with the Commission and EDPB.

(36) The main establishment of a controller in the Union should be the place of its central administration in the Union, unless the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing of personal data are taken in another establishment of the controller in the Union, in which case that other establishment should be considered to be 4.5.2016 L 119/6 Official Journal of the European Union EN (1) Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients' rights in cross‑border healthcare (OJ L 88, 4.4.2011, p. 45). the main establishment. The main establishment of a controller in the Union should be determined according to objective criteria and should imply the effective and real exercise of management activities determining the main decisions as to the purposes and means of processing through stable arrangements. That criterion should not depend on whether the processing of personal data is carried out at that location. The presence and use of technical means and technologies for processing personal data or processing activities do not, in themselves, constitute a main establishment and are therefore not determining criteria for a main establishment. The main establishment of the processor should be the place of its central administration in the Union or, if it has no central administration in the Union, the place where the main processing activities take place in the Union. In cases involving both the controller and the processor, the competent lead supervisory authority should remain the supervisory authority of the Member State where the controller has its main establishment, but the supervisory authority of the processor should be considered to be a supervisory authority concerned and that supervisory authority should participate in the cooperation procedure provided for by this Regulation. In any case, the supervisory authorities of the Member State or Member States where the processor has one or more establishments should not be considered to be supervisory authorities concerned where the draft decision concerns only the controller. Where the processing is carried out by a group of undertakings, the main establishment of the controlling undertaking should be considered to be the main establishment of the group of undertakings, except where the purposes and means of processing are determined by another undertaking. (37) A group of undertakings should cover a controlling undertaking and its controlled undertakings, whereby the controlling undertaking should be the undertaking which can exert a dominant influence over the other undertakings by virtue, for example, of ownership, financial participation or the rules which govern it or the power to have personal data protection rules implemented. An undertaking which controls the processing of personal data in undertakings affiliated to it should be regarded, together with those undertakings, as a group of undertakings. (38) Children merit specific protection with regard to their personal data, as they may be less aware of the risks, consequences and safeguards concerned and their rights in relation to the processing of personal data. Such specific protection should, in particular, apply to the use of personal data of children for the purposes of marketing or creating personality or user profiles and the collection of personal data with regard to children when using services offered directly to a child. The consent of the holder of parental responsibility should not be necessary in the context of preventive or counselling services offered directly to a child. (39) Any processing of personal data should be lawful and fair. It should be transparent to natural persons that personal data concerning them are collected, used, consulted or otherwise processed and to what extent the personal data are or will be processed. The principle of transparency requires that any information and communi cation relating to the processing of those personal data be easily accessible and easy to understand, and that clear and plain language be used. In relation to point b. in paragraph 201, gatekeepers need to decide how to resolve identities across the different NIICS. Users of a NIICS may obtain the identity of a user of another NIICS “out of band” (i.e. via a separate, independent communication channel, such as by email or verbally). End users should remain free to opt-in to those mechanisms. 204. It is also relevant that the interoperability requests displayed to users specify the NIICS providers (i.e., the new controllers) that would gain access to some necessary end users’ personal data. If the number of providers of NIICS achieving interoperability becomes very significant, gatekeepers may want to avoid ‘choice fatigue’ by requesting end users to make their choices in parallel to “moments of discontinuity” in their relationship with end users (e.g. the moment of subscription, of a software update or during a communication campaign), or when the end user of an interoperable NIICS tries to initiate a communication. They may also implement simple interoperability management systems where end users can give, review, or modify their interoperability choices across multiple providers at once (while keeping the possibility to go granular if the user wishes to), thereby reducing repetitive requests. End-to-end-encryption (“E2EE”) is generally understood as a technology that encrypts the content data on the end device of the sending party and decrypts it on the end device of the addressed recipient in such a way that only the sender and the recipient, at the exclusion of any third party, including the carrier or the chain of involved carriers, can access and control the content data of the communication.161 Maintaining trustworthy E2EE through the process of interoperability is key to ensure that the standard of security remains the same for end users in all services. 206. In that context, the implemented libraries and software solution should be well defined. 207. Depending on the nature of the personal data involved in a breach, for example, special categories of data, the potential damage to individuals that could result can be especially severe, in particular where the breach could result in identity theft or fraud, physical harm, psychological distress, humiliation or damage to reputation. If the breach concerns personal data about vulnerable individuals, they could be placed at greater risk of harm. Whether the controller is aware that personal data is in the hands of people whose intentions are unknown or possibly malicious can have a bearing on the level of potential risk. This may occur, for example, where personal data is sent accidentally to the wrong department of an organisation, or to a commonly used supplier organisation. The controller may request the recipient to either return or securely destroy the data it has received. In both cases, given that the controller has an ongoing relationship with them, and it may be aware of their procedures, history and other relevant details, the recipient may be considered “trusted”. In other words, the controller may have a level of assurance with the recipient so that it can reasonably expect that party not to read or access the data sent in error, and to comply with its instructions to return it. Even if the data has been accessed, the controller could still possibly trust the recipient not to take any further action with it and to return the data to the controller promptly and to co-operate with its recovery. In such cases, this may be factored into the risk assessment the controller carries out following the breach – the fact that the recipient is trusted may eradicate the severity of the consequences of the breach but does not mean that a breach has not occurred. However, this in turn may remove the likelihood of risk to individuals, thus no longer requiring notification to the supervisory authority, or to the affected individuals. Again, this will depend on case-by-case basis. Nevertheless, the controller still has to keep information concerning the breach as part of the general duty to maintain records of breaches (see section V, below). For example, a medical organisation will process special categories of personal 26 data, meaning that there is a greater threat to individuals if their personal data is breached, compared with a mailing list of a newspaper.  The number of affected individuals A breach may affect only one or a few individuals or several thousand, if not many more. Generally, the higher the number of individuals affected, the greater the impact of a breach can have. However, a breach can have a severe impact on even one individual, depending on the nature of the personal data and the context in which it has been compromised. Again, the key is to consider the likelihood and severity of the impact on those affected.  General points Therefore, when assessing the risk that is likely to result from a breach, the controller should consider a combination of the severity of the potential impact on the rights and freedoms of individuals and the likelihood of these occurring. Clearly, where the consequences of a breach are more severe, the risk is higher and similarly where the likelihood of these occurring is greater, the risk is also heightened. ## Test Case 51 - Patient dies - Amount of Correct Activities: 3 - Amount of False Positives: 0 - Amount of False Negatives: 0 - **Expected:** issue death certificate (sid-BF17F79E-2728-4C4E-A8F4-B95C0036CE4B), inform relatives and familiy physician (sid-14183816-D7CD-4AF7-A2E9-208E151796AE), complete and archive patient record (sid-54418E5F-348A-474E-A214-F556D67EE515) - **Actual:** issue death certificate (sid-BF17F79E-2728-4C4E-A8F4-B95C0036CE4B), inform relatives and familiy physician (sid-14183816-D7CD-4AF7-A2E9-208E151796AE), complete and archive patient record (sid-54418E5F-348A-474E-A214-F556D67EE515) - **Result:** ✅ Passed - **False Positives:** None - **False Negatives:** None - **Amount of Retries:** 1 ### RAG Metrics (Ragas) - **Faithfulness:** 1.000 - **Context Utilization:** 0.583 - **Samples:** 3 (failed: 0)

Reasoning of the LLM

 - **issue death certificate (sid-BF17F79E-2728-4C4E-A8F4-B95C0036CE4B)**: The activity "issue death certificate" processes personal data because it involves the creation and formal recording of a legal document tied to a deceased individual’s identity. A death certificate inherently contains personal data as defined by GDPR Article 4, including the name of the deceased (a direct identifier), biographical details (e.g., date of birth, date of death, place of residence), potentially health-related information (e.g., cause of death, which may reflect physiological or biomedical state), and family relationships (e.g., next of kin, which can indirectly identify living relatives). Under GDPR Recital 36 and Article 9, health data (including cause of death) is classified as a special category of personal data, requiring heightened protection. The act of issuing the certificate involves collecting, recording, and structuring this data, all of which constitute 'processing' under GDPR Article 4(2). Additionally, the certificate may be disclosed to recipients (e.g., family members, registries, or authorities), further triggering GDPR obligations around data transmission (Article 4(9)). The Clinic (as the controller) is responsible for ensuring lawful processing, accuracy, and secure handling of this data, including compliance with retention periods and access rights for bereaved families. The activity’s placement in the Physician lane reinforces its link to health data processing, as physicians are health professionals who routinely handle sensitive personal data (GDPR Recital 36). - **inform relatives and familiy physician (sid-14183816-D7CD-4AF7-A2E9-208E151796AE)**: The activity "inform relatives and family physician" processes personal data because it involves the transmission of sensitive information about a deceased individual to identified third parties. Key GDPR-relevant aspects include: 1) Disclosure of Personal Data: The activity explicitly communicates details about the death (e.g., name, date, cause) to relatives (who are identifiable natural persons) and the family physician (a health professional). Under GDPR Article 4(9), relatives and the physician are recipients of personal data, and their receipt of this information constitutes a data transfer. The cause of death and associated medical context qualify as health data (GDPR Article 9), a special category of personal data requiring explicit safeguards. 2) Processing Operations: The act of informing involves consulting the patient’s record (retrieving data), structuring the information for communication, and transmitting it to external parties. All these actions are forms of 'processing' under GDPR Article 4(2). The family physician, as a health professional, may further process this data for their own records (e.g., updating the patient’s medical history), extending the GDPR scope. 3) Contextual Indicators: The activity occurs in a Clinic setting, where the Physician (as controller) is responsible for ensuring lawful disclosure. The absence of explicit consent from the deceased or relatives does not negate GDPR applicability; instead, it shifts focus to alternative lawful bases (e.g., public health obligations or legitimate interest, per GDPR Article 6). The sensitivity of the data (death and health information) heightens the risk to individuals’ rights (e.g., emotional distress, reputational harm), as noted in GDPR Recital 75. 4) Accountability Requirements: The Clinic must document this disclosure (GDPR Article 30) and ensure recipients handle the data appropriately (e.g., family physicians must treat it confidentially under professional ethics and GDPR). If the information is transmitted electronically or via unsecured channels, additional risks (e.g., interception) arise, necessitating safeguards like encryption (GDPR Article 32). In summary, this activity is GDPR-relevant due to the transmission of health-related personal data to identifiable recipients, triggering obligations around lawful basis, transparency, and data security. - **complete and archive patient record (sid-54418E5F-348A-474E-A214-F556D67EE515)**: The activity "complete and archive patient record" processes personal data because it involves finalizing, storing, and retaining a deceased patient’s medical records, which are explicitly classified as special categories of personal data under GDPR. Key GDPR-relevant aspects include: 1) Nature of the Data: Medical records contain highly sensitive information such as health data (diagnoses, treatment histories, examination results, and cause of death (GDPR Article 9)), identifiers (name, date of birth, patient ID, and contact details (GDPR Article 4(1))), and biographical data (family medical history or next-of-kin information, which may indirectly identify living relatives). GDPR Recital 36 and Article 9(1) emphasize that health data—regardless of source (e.g., physician, hospital, or diagnostic tests)—requires specific protection. 2) Processing Operations: Completing the record involves updating the file with final entries (e.g., death confirmation, cause of death), which constitutes altering or structuring personal data (GDPR Article 4(2)). Archiving, the long-term storage of the record for legal, historical, or research purposes, falls under archiving in the public interest (GDPR Article 89 and Recital 158). While archiving may exempt certain rights (e.g., erasure), it does not eliminate GDPR’s core requirements for security, purpose limitation, and retention periods. The Hospital/Clinic (as controller) must ensure the archived data remains confidential, accurate, and accessible only to authorized personnel (GDPR Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32). 3) Risks and Safeguards: Unauthorized access to medical records is a frequent target of breaches (e.g., ransomware attacks on hospitals). GDPR mandates technical/organizational measures (e.g., encryption, access controls) to mitigate risks (Article 32). The controller must define and justify how long the record is stored, balancing legal obligations (e.g., national health laws) with GDPR’s storage limitation principle (Article 5(1)(e)). Data subject rights may still apply post-mortem, allowing relatives to exercise rights (e.g., access to the record) under national laws or GDPR’s posthumous data protection provisions (where applicable). 4) Contextual Indicators: The activity is performed by a Physician in a Clinic, both of which are controllers routinely processing health data. The Hospital context highlights the high risk associated with medical record breaches, including delays in patient care or reputational harm. Archiving for public health or research purposes (e.g., mortality statistics) must comply with GDPR’s scientific research exemptions (Article 89), requiring safeguards like pseudonymization. In summary, this activity is GDPR-relevant due to the handling of special-category health data in a high-risk context, requiring compliance with Article 9 (special categories), Article 5 (principles), and Article 32 (security).

result.reason: The activity "An Terminal ein- und ausstempeln" (Clocking in/out at a terminal) processes personal data because it involves recording an employee’s working hours, which is inherently linked to their identity as a natural person. Under GDPR Article 88(1), personal data may be processed in the employment context for purposes such as management, planning, and organisation of work, including timekeeping and attendance tracking. The terminal equipment used for clocking in/out stores or accesses information tied to the employee’s identity (e.g., employee ID, timestamp, or location data if the terminal is geolocated). This constitutes processing of personal data as defined in Article 4(1) GDPR, since the data relates to an identified or identifiable employee. Additionally, the EDPB Guidelines on controllers/processors clarify that employment-related processing—such as recording working hours—falls under the performance of the employment contract (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR) and requires compliance with Article 88 GDPR (processing in the employment context). The activity is thus GDPR-relevant because it directly handles data tied to an employee’s professional identity and work patterns.

The activity "An Web-Terminal ein- und ausstempeln" (Clocking in/out via a web terminal) processes personal data for the same reasons as the physical terminal activity. This task involves recording an employee’s working hours through a digital interface, which inherently links the data to the employee’s identity (e.g., via login credentials, employee ID, or IP address). Under GDPR Article 4(1), this qualifies as processing of personal data because the information (timestamps, user account, or device identifiers) relates to an identified or identifiable natural person (the employee). The EDPB Guidelines emphasize that employment-related processing—such as time tracking—is subject to Article 88 GDPR, which governs the processing of employees' personal data for workforce management. Additionally, the joint EDPB-DMA guidelines highlight that terminal equipment (including web terminals) stores or accesses information tied to end users (employees), which may include online identifiers (e.g., session cookies, IP addresses) that qualify as personal data under GDPR Recital 30. The annotation "Manuell Ein- und Ausbuchen" (manual clocking) further confirms that the activity involves intentional recording of personal work data, reinforcing its GDPR relevance.

The activity "Arbeitszeit in der Zeiterfassungsübersicht erfassen" (Recording working hours in the time-tracking overview) processes personal data because it involves documenting and structuring an employee’s working hours, which is inherently linked to their identity. Under GDPR Article 4(1), this constitutes processing of personal data since the recorded information (e.g., employee name/ID, dates, hours worked) relates to an identified or identifiable natural person. The annotation "Zeiterfassung" (time tracking) and "für den aktuellen Tag" (for the current day) clarify that the activity focuses on individual-level data collection, not anonymized or aggregated statistics. Article 88 GDPR explicitly permits processing employees' personal data for workforce management, including timekeeping and attendance records, but requires compliance with principles like purpose limitation and data minimization. The EDPB Guidelines further confirm that such processing falls under the performance of the employment contract (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR) and must adhere to employment-specific safeguards. Thus, this activity is GDPR-relevant.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

[equipment] Terminal Equipment — Terminal equipment broadly refers to a user's device from which digital information can be accessed, processed, sent, or received. This category includes a wide range of devices such as computers, smartphones, smart TVs, and connected vehicles, often encompassing telematics devices. According to Directive 2008/63/CE, terminal equipment is specifically defined as any device directly or indirectly connected to a public telecommunications network interface for the purpose of transmitting, processing, or receiving information. This equipment serves as the point where individuals access data, potentially leading to the processing of personal data. These devices are generally owned by end-users and serve as the location where information, including sensitive data like location data, can be collected and stored. For example, collected information from contact tracing applications typically resides on the user's terminal equipment. The storage and access of information on terminal equipment are subject to stringent security measures and user-centric conditions to protect privacy and data integrity.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[person] End Users — End Users are defined as natural or legal persons who engage with core platform services (CPS), distinct from business users. They are also considered "data subjects" under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), signifying that their personal data is processed, often by gatekeepers and other providers of numerically independent interpersonal communication services (NIICS). These individuals benefit from fair market conditions promoted by regulatory frameworks like the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The autonomy and decision-making of End Users are protected, requiring gatekeepers to seek their consent for data access, including the processing of personal data for online advertising services or combining personal data. They should be able to freely choose to opt-in to data processing and sign-in practices, with alternative services potentially being offered. Their reasonable expectations regarding personal data processing must be considered, and they have the right to set third-party apps or app stores as their default. End Users' consent is also required for certain processing operations and for the storage of information on their terminal equipment. End Users interact with online interfaces, generating various forms of data such as ranking, query, click, and view data through their use of gatekeepers' services. When their data is shared under Article 6(11) DMA, anonymization is required to protect their identity. They are presented with choices and consent requests from gatekeepers, and their rights are safeguarded by various regulations, ultimately encouraging increased choice and includes the right to data portability under Article 6(9) DMA. End Users use services provided by gatekeepers and other NIICS providers, with their personal data managed for interoperability and security.

Their personal data may be processed by employers, but consent for this processing is often not freely given due to an inherent imbalance of power between employer and employee. This group includes individuals authorized to process personal data, who require access to such data to perform their job tasks for which the processor was hired.
