Identifying a lead supervisory authority: the key concepts. 1.1 ‘Cross-border processing of personal data’. Identifying a lead supervisory authority is only relevant where a controller or processor is carrying out the cross-border processing of personal data. Article 4(23) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) defines ‘cross-border processing’ as either the: - processing of personal data which takes place in the context of the activities of establishments in more than one Member State of a controller or processor in the Union where the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State; or the - processing of personal data which takes place in the context of the activities of a single establishment of a controller or processor in the Union but which substantially affects or is likely to substantially affect data subjects in more than one Member State. This means that where an organisation has establishments in France and Romania, for example, and the processing of personal data takes place in the context of their activities, then this will constitute cross-border processing. Alternatively, the organisation may only carry out processing activity in the context of its establishment in France. However, if the activity substantially affects – or is likely to substantially affect - data subjects in France and Romania then this will also constitute cross- border processing. 1.1.1 ‘Substantially affects’. The GDPR does not define ‘substantially’ or ‘affects’. The intention of the wording was to ensure that not all processing activity, with any effect and that takes place within the context of a single establishment, falls within the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. The most relevant ordinary English meanings of ‘substantial’ include; ‘of ample or considerable amount or size; sizeable, fairly large’, or ‘having solid worth or value, of real significance; solid; weighty, important’ (Oxford English Dictionary). The most relevant meaning of the verb ‘affect’ is ‘to influence’ or ‘to make a material impression on’. The related noun -‘effect’- means, amongst other things, ‘a result’ or ‘a consequence’ (Oxford English Dictionary). This suggests that for data processing to affect someone it must have some form of impact on them. Processing that does not have a substantial effect on individuals does not fall within the second part of the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. However, it would fall within the first part of the definition where the processing of personal data takes place in the context of the activities of establishments in more than one Member State of a controller or processor in the Union, where the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State. Processing can be brought within the second part of the definition if there is the likelihood of a substantial effect, not just an actual substantial effect. Note that ‘likely to’ does not mean that there is a remote possibility of a substantial effect. The substantial effect must be more likely than not. On the other hand, it also means that individuals do not have to be actually 4 affected: the likelihood of a substantial effect is sufficient to bring the processing within the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

 - **Überweisung tätigen (sid-F3F50770-5691-45D3-883A-FC877E27DD5F)**: The activity "Überweisung tätigen" (performed by a *Studierender*, i.e., a student) involves executing a payment transaction linked to a matriculation number (Mtknr). Since the Mtknr is a unique student identifier, this activity processes personal data by associating a financial transaction (e.g., tuition fees, contributions) with an identifiable natural person. The GDPR explicitly classifies payment data (e.g., bank transfers tied to an individual’s account or student ID) as personal data under Article 4(1), as it enables the identification of the data subject (the student). Additionally, the activity’s context—refunds of fees/dues—implies handling of financial records, which are subject to GDPR when linked to an individual. - **Zahlung auf Mtknr verbuchen (sid-E89A7F49-9F81-4250-902D-23792F62D8C2)**: The activity "Zahlung auf Mtknr verbuchen" (posting a payment to a matriculation number) directly processes personal data by linking a financial transaction (payment) to a student’s unique identifier (Mtknr). The Mtknr serves as a pseudonymised but re-identifiable reference to the student, making this a GDPR-relevant operation. The annotation clarifies that the target amount (Soll-Stellung) is calculated automatically, with possible adjustments (e.g., exemptions, reductions) by the Studiensekretariat—further confirming that the activity involves individualised financial records tied to students. Financial data (e.g., tuition payments) are explicitly covered under GDPR as personal data when associated with an identifiable person. - **Bankdaten-sätze importieren und prüfen, ob Mtrnr zuordenbar ist (sid-194AAA1D-E826-46D4-9C81-CE3E330D3939)**: The activity "Bankdaten-sätze importieren und prüfen, ob Mtrnr zuordenbar ist" (importing bank transaction records and checking if they can be assigned to a matriculation number) processes personal data in two ways: 1) Bank data records inherently contain personal data (e.g., account holder names, IBANs, transaction references). 2) The activity explicitly matches bank transactions to matriculation numbers (Mtrnr), which are unique student identifiers. This linking operation constitutes processing of personal data under GDPR, as it involves structuring and aligning data to identify or profile individuals (students). Even if the bank data are partially anonymised, the attempt to re-associate them with Mtknrs qualifies as processing under Article 4(2). - **Mtknr anhand Bankdaten eruieren (sid-6F13CD11-AE8E-48B9-BAD5-C795B6879946)**: The activity "Mtknr anhand Bankdaten eruieren" (determining a matriculation number from bank data) involves analysing bank transaction records to extract or infer a student’s unique identifier (Mtknr). Bank data (e.g., payer names, reference fields) are personal data under GDPR, and the activity’s purpose—identifying or re-identifying a student—constitutes processing. This aligns with GDPR’s definition of processing as any operation performed on personal data, including retrieval, alignment, or combination to link information to an individual. - **Zahlung ins Verwahrbuch buchen (sid-E5E03447-B337-46D7-8F03-238F00B3F11C)**: The activity "Zahlung ins Verwahrbuch buchen" (posting a payment to a trust account) processes personal data because it records a financial transaction linked to a student’s payment (e.g., tuition fees). While the activity itself does not explicitly mention student identifiers, the context of the process (refunds of fees/dues) and the preceding steps (e.g., verification of Mtknr) imply that the payment is traceable to an individual via the matriculation number or bank details. Financial transactions tied to identifiable persons are personal data under GDPR, and storing or recording such data qualifies as processing. - **Datei mit Bankdaten-sätzen erstellen und exportieren (sid-9CEAD8DE-8FD2-4261-9246-2E0CFF741387)**: The activity "Datei mit Bankdaten-sätzen erstellen und exportieren" (creating and exporting a file with bank transaction records) processes personal data because bank transaction files inherently contain personally identifiable information (e.g., account numbers, payer names, transaction references). Exporting such data—even for internal use—constitutes transmission under GDPR, and the activity enables further processing (e.g., matching to Mtknrs). The GDPR explicitly covers structured sets of personal data (e.g., bank statement files) as personal data when they relate to identifiable individuals. - **Mtknr eruieren (sid-CCF3E63A-FD90-4A73-BDD9-70C715E16550)**: The activity "Mtknr eruieren" (determining a matriculation number) involves retrieving or inferring a student’s unique identifier (Mtknr) from available data (e.g., bank records, payment references). Since the Mtknr is a pseudonymised identifier that can be linked back to an individual student, this activity constitutes processing of personal data under GDPR. The operation falls under the GDPR’s broad definition of processing, which includes retrieval, consultation, or alignment of data to identify a natural person. - **Überweisung tätigen (sid-A43741FF-A223-499C-997D-9CCC02485896)**: The activity "Überweisung tätigen" (performed by a *Bewerber*, i.e., applicant) involves an external individual initiating a payment (e.g., application fee, tuition deposit) to the university. While the applicant’s action occurs outside the university’s direct control, the payment itself is personal data when linked to the applicant’s identity (e.g., via application reference numbers, bank details, or subsequent communication). The GDPR applies because the university, as the recipient/controller, will process the payment data (e.g., for reconciliation or refunds), and the activity is a prerequisite for such processing. Payments tied to identifiable individuals (applicants/students) are explicitly covered under GDPR.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[organization] Lead Supervisory Authority — The Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) is a central concept within data protection under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), specifically designed for cross-border processing activities. Also recognized as the "one-stop-shop" mechanism, the LSA is the supervisory authority situated in the Member State of a controller's or processor's main establishment. Its primary role is to lead GDPR enforcement for cases that span multiple Member States, acting as the sole point of contact for the controller or processor in such multi-jurisdictional data protection scenarios. The LSA has a leading function in cooperation procedures, explicitly mandated to collaborate with other Concerned Supervisory Authorities (CSAs). Its responsibilities include overseeing data protection operations, conducting investigations, and sharing relevant information with other CSAs. The LSA is also tasked with preparing and submitting draft decisions under Articles 60 and 62, striving for consensus. It plays a crucial role in the Article 60 procedure. Furthermore, the LSA is responsible for handling objections raised by other CSAs. Should a dispute arise where the LSA does not follow a relevant and reasoned objection, or if it deems an objection not relevant or reasoned, it refers the matter to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) for resolution. The LSA also conducts joint operations, facilitates information exchange, and serves as the primary authority a controller must notify in the event of a cross-border processing breach. As specified in GDPR Article 56, the LSA is a specific supervisory authority for transnational code members, underscoring its integral role in managing cross-border data protection and ensuring compliance, including taking measures intended to produce legal effects like administrative fines.
The Lead Supervisory Authority is the primary interlocutor for the Commission in cases where a gatekeeper has a "main establishment" under the GDPR, responsible for cooperating with concerned supervisory authorities.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[person] Data Protection Officer — A Data Protection Officer (DPO) is an individual, organization, or team responsible for overseeing, advising on, and monitoring an entity's data protection strategy and its implementation to ensure compliance with relevant data protection laws and regulations, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), as detailed in Articles 37 to 39. This role requires expert knowledge of data protection law and practices. The DPO's responsibilities include providing guidance on appropriate measures and demonstrating compliance regarding personal data processing, assisting the controller or processor in monitoring internal compliance with regulations, and advising on Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), including their performance, monitoring, and documenting related advice and decisions. DPOs also play a crucial role in assessing the applicability of GDPR Article 6(1)(f). They act as a key contact point for information regarding personal data breaches, cooperating with supervisory authorities, and their contact details may need to be communicated as part of GDPR information duties. They are involved in all issues related to personal data protection, supported by controllers and processors with necessary resources, and report directly to the highest management level. Appointment of a DPO may be mandatory under GDPR Article 37, especially when an organization's core activities involve processing special categories of data or regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects, though organizations can also voluntarily appoint one. Whether an employee or an external contractor, the DPO must perform duties independently, without fear of dismissal or penalization, and avoid conflicts of interest, meaning they cannot represent a controller or processor in court for data protection matters. While responsible for monitoring compliance of data processing operations, the DPO's role cannot be certified under GDPR Article 42.7. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) encourages DPO involvement in integrating data protection by design and by default principles, highlighting their essential role in accountability and record-keeping in personal data protection.
[concept] Extraterritorial Application of Laws — Extraterritorial Application of Laws refers to the enforcement of a country's laws outside its own borders.

[concept] Personal Data Transfer — Personal Data Transfer refers to the processing operation where personal data is made available by an exporter (controller or processor subject to GDPR) to an importer (another controller, joint controller, or processor in a third country or international organization).

Online search engines are services provided by gatekeepers and third-party undertakings, subject to data access obligations under Article 6(11) DMA.
Online search engines are services provided by requesting third-party undertakings that receive and reuse data shared by gatekeepers.

[location] Third Country — A "Third Country" is a nation or geographical region situated outside the jurisdiction of both the European Union (EU) and the European Economic Area (EEA), or more broadly, any country outside the territorial scope of specific data protection regulations. This designation is particularly relevant in the context of international transfers of personal data, especially under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Personal data originating from the EU/EEA may be transferred to and processed within a Third Country. However, such transfers are subject to stringent conditions and safeguards as outlined in Chapter V of the GDPR. This is due to the potential for different, and possibly inadequate, legal frameworks for data protection in these jurisdictions compared to GDPR standards. The European Commission assesses the level of personal data protection in Third Countries to determine if they offer an adequate level of protection. Entities, including public bodies, involved in data transfers to a Third Country must adhere to GDPR regulations, implement appropriate safeguards, and sometimes provide specific information to data subjects before data is transferred. The potential risks associated with data processing in a Third Country can be elevated, including concerns about disproportionate government access to data. Supervisory Authorities may have jurisdiction over these transfers and, in some cases, may even suspend data flows to a Third Country.
A third country is a nation outside the EEA to which personal data may be transferred, subject to adequacy decisions or consent.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Lead Supervisory Authority is central to the oversight of cross-border data processing, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Lead Supervisory Authority is identified for a Controller primarily based on its central administration or the location where decisions concerning processing are made. In situations involving both a Controller and a Processor, the Lead Supervisory Authority for the Controller typically assumes the role for both, as outlined in Recital 36. Furthermore, the supervisory authority of a Member State where a Controller's main establishment is located often acts as the competent Lead Supervisory Authority. This authority is competent to supervise cross-border processing activities conducted by a Controller. A key responsibility of the Controller in this relationship is to notify the Lead Supervisory Authority in the event of breaches involving cross-border processing. Beyond notification, the Lead Supervisory Authority serves as the sole interlocutor for the Controller regarding cross-border processing, meaning the Controller interacts exclusively with this authority. The Lead Supervisory Authority is responsible for adopting and notifying decisions to the Controller, who, in turn, is obligated to take measures to ensure compliance with these decisions. Note that ‘likely to’ does not mean that there is a remote possibility of a substantial effect. The substantial effect must be more likely than not. On the other hand, it also means that individuals do not have to be actually 4 affected: the likelihood of a substantial effect is sufficient to bring the processing within the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. The fact that a data processing operation may involve the processing of a number – even a large number – of individuals’ personal data, in a number of Member States, does not necessarily mean that the processing has, or is likely to have, a substantial effect. Processing that does not have a substantial effect does not constitute cross-border processing for the purposes of the second part of the definition, regardless of how many individuals it affects. Supervisory Authorities will interpret ‘substantially affects’ on a case by case basis. We will take into account the context of the processing, the type of data, the purpose of the processing and factors such as whether the processing: o causes, or is likely to cause, damage, loss or distress to individuals; o has, or is likely to have, an actual effect in terms of limiting rights or denying an opportunity; o affects, or is likely to affect individuals’ health, well-being or peace of mind; o affects, or is likely to affect, individuals’ financial or economic status or circumstances; o leaves individuals open to discrimination or unfair treatment; o involves the analysis of the special categories of personal or other intrusive data, particularly the personal data of children; o causes, or is likely to cause individuals to change their behaviour in a significant way; o has unlikely, unanticipated or unwanted consequences for individuals; o creates embarrassment or other negative outcomes, including reputational damage; or o involves the processing of a wide range of personal data. Ultimately, the test of ‘substantial effect’ is intended to ensure that supervisory authorities are only required to co-operate formally through the GDPR’s consistency mechanism "where a supervisory authority intends to adopt a measure intended to produce legal effects as regards processing operations which substantially affect a significant number of data subjects in several Member States”. (Recital 135) 1.2 Lead supervisory authority. Put simply, a ‘lead supervisory authority’ is the authority with the primary responsibility for dealing with a cross-border data processing activity, for example when a data subject makes a complaint about the processing of his or her personal data. The lead supervisory authority will coordinate any investigation, involving other ‘concerned’ supervisory authorities. Identifying the lead supervisory authority depends on determining the location of the controller’s ‘main establishment’ or ‘single establishment’ in the EU. Article 56 of the GDPR says that: - the supervisory authority of the main establishment or of the single establishment of the controller or processor shall be competent to act as lead supervisory authority for the cross-border processing carried out by that controller or processor in accordance with the [cooperation] procedure provided in Article 60. 5 1.3 Main establishment. Article 4(16) of the GDPR states that ‘main establishment’ means: - as regards a controller with establishments in more than one Member State, the place of its central administration in the Union, unless the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing of personal data are taken in another establishment of the controller in the Union and the latter establishment has the power to have such decisions implemented, in which case the establishment having taken such decisions is to be considered to be the main establishment; - as regards a processor with establishments in more than one Member State, the place of its central administration in the Union, or, if the processor has no central administration in the Union, the establishment of the processor in the Union where the main processing activities in the context of the activities of an establishment of the processor take place to the extent that the processor is subject to specific obligations under this Regulation; 2. The essence of the lead authority principle in the GDPR is that the supervision of cross- border processing should be led by only one supervisory authority in the EU. In cases where decisions relating to different cross-border processing activities are taken within the EU central administration, there will be a single lead supervisory authority for the various data processing activities carried out by the multinational company. First, the gatekeeper needs to evaluate the extent to which the initial dataset (i.e. the ranking, query, click and view data generated by end users) contains personal data of end users. Recital 61 DMA, referring to Article 6(11) DMA, clarifies that what needs to be anonymised is the personal data of the end user generating the data, and not the personal data of other individuals that might be identifiable via ranking, query, click and view data (e.g., a person mentioned in a query). However, the GDPR remains applicable to the sharing of personal data of other individuals that might be identifiable via ranking, query, click and view data by gatekeepers pursuant to their legal obligation under Article 6(11) DMA and the re-use of the data by the requesting third- party undertakings providing online search engines. 184. When complying with Article 6(11) DMA, gatekeepers should consider both possibilities of direct and indirect identification to determine whether the dataset contains personal data before sharing the dataset with a requesting third party to determine whether appropriate measures should be put in place to anonymise the data of the end user. 185. Particular attention should be given to the means that the requesting third-party undertakings providing online search engine and other persons that would reasonably be considered to be able to gain access or process the data (including unintended third parties) would reasonably likely use to identify the end user generating the data.147 For information to qualify as personal data, it is not required that all the information enabling the identification of the data subject must be in the hands of one person,148 in particular the requesting third party undertaking providing an online search engine and receiving Article 6(11) DMA data. Moreover, the assessment of anonymity of end users’ shared data should take into account the availability of additional information relating to the end users generating the data via use of the gatekeeper’s search engine.149 186. Second, the anonymisation approach selected by the gatekeeper should be appropriate to achieve effective anonymisation. There are different measures available to achieve anonymisation. Gatekeepers subject to Article 6(11) DMA should carefully assess the most recent developments in the field of anonymisation and identification when selecting such measures. 187. In this context, account should be taken of the specific regulatory framework of the DMA under which data sharing pursuant to Article 6(11) DMA takes place. Moreover, the exercise of the Commission’s legal powers to regulate data sharing under Article 6(11) DMA via an implementing act pursuant to Article 8(2) DMA should be taken into consideration. 188. Through an implementing act under Article 8(2) DMA, the Commission may specify legally binding measures on gatekeepers to ensure effective anonymisation and on the eligibility of third parties to receive data under Article 6(11) DMA.150 Such legally binding measures may prescribe conditions and safeguards under which a gatekeeper must share data with eligible third parties under Article 6(11) DMA. This may include the specification of technical measures that result in the alteration of the data to be provided, as well as administrative, organisational, and contractual measures to be adopted by the gatekeeper before sharing data under Article 6(11) DMA. In relation to measures for the alteration of data, these may include the removal of data liable to be used for the identification of the end user generating the search data (e.g., precise location of the end user, queries with words searched below a specific low number of times, and precise time and sequence of click data).151 189. In relation to other measures to complement the alteration of data by the gatekeeper to mitigate residual likelihood of identification, the implementing act may specify, for example, measures that restrict data usage (including a prohibition to attempt to re- identify end users), access controls, data retention/storage, general and incident reporting, internal monitoring and supervision, and independent auditing."

ragPromptContext: [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[method] Anonymisation — Anonymisation is a fundamental process and set of techniques designed to transform personal data in such a way that the data subject can no longer be identified, either directly or indirectly. This alteration ensures that the data cannot be linked back to an individual, even with reasonable effort. It is employed when personal data is deleted or anonymized following the withdrawal of consent, acting as a crucial safeguard in data processing, particularly for research purposes where the objective can be achieved without handling identifiable data. This process involves carefully processing data, such as location information, to prevent re-identification, a task that is complex and necessitates transparency regarding the methodologies used. The goal of anonymisation extends beyond simply removing identifying information to also preserving the quality and usefulness of the data for its intended purpose. It is a preferred solution and safeguard, recognized by regulations like the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically Article 6(11), and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which require the rendering of personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy. In essence, anonymisation serves as a vital method for making shared personal data suitable for use while upholding the privacy of individuals.
Anonymization is a method by which shared data that constitutes personal data is processed to remove identifying information.

Anonymisation is the process of rendering personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy, as required by DMA and GDPR.

Under GDPR, Data Subject The relation "(Data Subject, Personal Data)" defines a fundamental connection where personal data belongs to, pertains to, or relates to a specific data subject. A data subject is understood as a natural person, an individual, to whom the personal data refers. This relationship is central to data processing, particularly in contexts like connected vehicles, and protects the privacy and data protection rights held by data subjects over their personal information. Personal data is any information that can identify or render identifiable a particular data subject. The data subject is the source of this data, which they may provide through their actions or technical means. When personal data is collected directly from a data subject, they must be informed about its processing. Similarly, the delisting of personal data also directly involves the data subject, who may have personal data in various contexts, such as within their bank account. Data subjects possess significant rights concerning their personal data, including the ability to receive, transmit, reuse, and control it. When personal data is transferred, the interests and fundamental rights of the data subject must be considered. While data subjects have rights over their data, they also bear responsibility for securing their personal data within their own systems. A data subject should not be surprised at the purpose of processing their personal data and it should not be disclosed without their consent. The processing of personal data involves protecting the interests and rights of the data subject.<SEP>Personal data is information that relates to an identified or identifiable natural person (the data subject).<SEP>Personal data relates to a data subject who is not or no longer identifiable after anonymization. Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Data Subject is governed by a framework of rights, obligations, and legal considerations, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Controller is authorized to process a Data Subject's personal data, frequently through contractual agreements, and is obligated to provide essential, timely, and clear information regarding these processing operations, as stipulated in GDPR Article 14(2)(b) and (f). This includes notifying Data Subjects of personal data breaches, especially if they pose a high risk to their rights and freedoms, as mentioned in Article 34 of the GDPR. Controllers are legally mandated to facilitate the easy and full exercise of data protection rights by Data Subjects, ensuring these rights can be exercised without undue hindrance and by providing a simple mechanism for their exercise. This also entails addressing requests for data erasure or objections to processing, and informing Data Subjects about changes and facilitating access to information. For specific activities like processing biometric data, the Controller must obtain explicit, informed, and freely given consent. Transparency from the Controller is also required concerning profiling and automated decision-making processes that impact the Data Subject. In all data processing activities, the Controller must carefully consider the Data Subject's interests, fundamental rights, and freedoms, acknowledging the direct impact of their actions. This assessment varies depending on the specific relationship (e.g., employer-employee, service provider-customer) and the Data Subject's particular situation. In situations involving potential surveillance, the Controller must consider the Data Subject's objection and can only proceed if there is a compelling legitimate interest or for legal claims, also assessing the Data Subject's intention to make data public. When applying the household exemption, key considerations include the Controller’s personal relationship with the Data Subject, the scale and frequency of surveillance, and any potential adverse impact it might have. There must be a balancing exercise between the competing interests of the Controller and the Data Subject's objection, with the burden of proof on the Controller. A significant imbalance, as noted in Recital 47 of the GDPR, can compromise the freedom of consent, and Controllers have been known to attempt to influence Data Subjects for more extensive data collection. It is paramount that the fundamental rights and freedoms of Data Subjects are not overridden by the Controller’s interests, even when a relevant and appropriate relationship exists (e.g., client or in the service of the controller). Controllers must provide clear information to Data Subjects to allow them to correct inaccuracies and select a method for providing information that is appropriate to the manner in which the Data Controller and Data Subject interact. The Controller is responsible for protecting the rights of Data Subjects and responding to their requests for exercising those rights. They are obligated to respond to such requests and make decisions about the processing of personal data for which they are responsible. This includes providing information and taking action on requests from the Data Subject, communicating personal data breaches, and communicating information about data processing and their rights. The Controller enables the Data Subject to monitor data processing and implements pre-contractual measures and data transfers at the Data Subject's request or in their interest. The Controller may offer goods or services to Data Subjects who are in the Union and should compensate any damage a Data Subject may suffer as a result of processing that infringes the Regulation. The Controller can also ask the Data Subject to provide additional information if there are reasonable doubts about their identity, as per Article 12(6) GDPR, and takes into account the reasonable expectations of Data Subjects based on their relationship with the controller when considering legitimate interests. This activity qualifies as 'processing' under Article 4(2) GDPR because it involves consulting and using personal data to determine whether the lecturer’s record exists and is active. The Controller’s obligation to ensure data accuracy (Article 5(1)(d) GDPR) and the right of data subjects to rectification (Article 16 GDPR) further underscore the relevance of this activity.

This operation constitutes processing of personal data under Article 4(2) GDPR because it updates and structures existing records by associating an identifiable natural person (the lecturer) with a course. The CMS annotation linked to this task confirms that the assignment occurs within a system that manages personal data. The Controller’s responsibility to document processing activities (Article 30 GDPR) and ensure lawful bases for processing (Article 6 GDPR) applies here.

The activity 'Lehrveranstaltung erstellen' (Create course/event) involves collecting and recording personal data as part of setting up a new course. The context implies that creating a 'Lehrveranstaltung' requires linking it to at least one lecturer, whose personal data (e.g., name, employee ID, contact details) must be included in the course record. This activity qualifies as GDPR-relevant because it involves the creation of records containing personal data, structuring and storage of personal data within the university’s systems. The Controller’s obligation to ensure data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) and transparency (Article 12 GDPR) applies here.

The activity 'Änderungen vornehmen' (Make changes) involves modifying personal data within course or lecturer records. This task follows the assessment of necessary changes (e.g., updates to lecturer assignments, course details linked to individuals, or corrections to personal information). Under Article 4(2) GDPR, 'altering' personal data is explicitly classified as processing. The Controller’s responsibility to communicate rectifications (Article 19 GDPR) and the Lead Supervisory Authority’s role in enforcing compliance are directly relevant.

The activity 'eingeschränkt Änderungen vornehmen' (Make limited changes) involves modifying personal data within constrained permissions. [organization] Lead Supervisory Authority — The Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) is a central concept within data protection under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), specifically designed for cross-border processing activities. Also recognized as the "one-stop-shop" mechanism, the LSA is the supervisory authority situated in the Member State of a controller's or processor's main establishment. Its primary role is to lead GDPR enforcement for cases that span multiple Member States, acting as the sole point of contact for the controller or processor in such multi-jurisdictional data protection scenarios. The LSA has a leading function in cooperation procedures, explicitly mandated to collaborate with other Concerned Supervisory Authorities (CSAs). Its responsibilities include overseeing data protection operations, conducting investigations, and sharing relevant information with other CSAs. The LSA is also tasked with preparing and submitting draft decisions under Articles 60 and 62, striving for consensus. It plays a crucial role in the Article 60 procedure. Furthermore, the LSA is responsible for handling objections raised by other CSAs. Should a dispute arise where the LSA does not follow a relevant and reasoned objection, or if it deems an objection not relevant or reasoned, it refers the matter to the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) for resolution. The LSA also conducts joint operations, facilitates information exchange, and serves as the primary authority a controller must notify in the event of a cross-border processing breach. As specified in GDPR Article 56, the LSA is a specific supervisory authority for transnational code members, underscoring its integral role in managing cross-border data protection and ensuring compliance, including taking measures intended to produce legal effects like administrative fines.
The Lead Supervisory Authority is the primary interlocutor for the Commission in cases where a gatekeeper has a "main establishment" under the GDPR, responsible for cooperating with concerned supervisory authorities.

[method] Anonymisation — Anonymisation is a fundamental process and set of techniques designed to transform personal data in such a way that the data subject can no longer be identified, either directly or indirectly. This alteration ensures that the data cannot be linked back to an individual, even with reasonable effort. It is employed when personal data is deleted or anonymized following the withdrawal of consent, acting as a crucial safeguard in data processing, particularly for research purposes where the objective can be achieved without handling identifiable data. This process involves carefully processing data, such as location information, to prevent re-identification, a task that is complex and necessitates transparency regarding the methodologies used. The goal of anonymisation extends beyond simply removing identifying information to also preserving the quality and usefulness of the data for its intended purpose. It is a preferred solution and safeguard, recognized by regulations like the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically Article 6(11), and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which require the rendering of personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy. In essence, anonymisation serves as a vital method for making shared personal data suitable for use while upholding the privacy of individuals.
Anonymization is a method by which shared data that constitutes personal data is processed to remove identifying information.
Anonymisation is a method of altering personal data so that the data subject is no longer identifiable, with the goal of preserving data quality and usefulness.
Anonymisation is the process of altering personal data to prevent direct or indirect identification of end users, required for data shared under Article 6(11) DMA.
Anonymisation is the process of rendering personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy, as required by DMA and GDPR.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Lead Supervisory Authority is central to the oversight of cross-border data processing, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Lead Supervisory Authority is identified for a Controller primarily based on its central administration or the location where decisions concerning processing are made. In situations involving both a Controller and a Processor, the Lead Supervisory Authority for the Controller typically assumes the role for both, as outlined in Recital 36. Furthermore, the supervisory authority of a Member State where a Controller's main establishment is located often acts as the competent Lead Supervisory Authority. This authority is competent to supervise cross-border processing activities conducted by a Controller. A key responsibility of the Controller in this relationship is to notify the Lead Supervisory Authority in the event of breaches involving cross-border processing. Beyond notification, the Lead Supervisory Authority serves as the sole interlocutor for the Controller regarding cross-border processing, meaning the Controller interacts exclusively with this authority. The Lead Supervisory Authority is responsible for adopting and notifying decisions to the Controller, who, in turn, is obligated to take measures to ensure compliance with these decisions. Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.
