Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The notion of regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects is not defined in the GDPR, but clearly includes all forms of tracking and profiling on the internet, including for the purposes of behavioural advertising. However, the notion of monitoring is not restricted to the online environment. Examples of activities that may constitute a regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects: operating a telecommunications network; providing telecommunications services; email retargeting; data-driven marketing activities; profiling and scoring for purposes of risk assessment (e.g. for purposes of credit scoring, establishment of insurance premiums, fraud prevention, detection of money-laundering); location tracking, for example, by mobile apps; loyalty programs; behavioural advertising; monitoring of wellness, fitness and health data via wearable devices; closed circuit television; connected devices e.g. smart meters, smart cars, home automation, etc. WP29 interprets ‘regular’ as meaning one or more of the following:  ongoing or occurring at particular intervals for a particular period  recurring or repeated at fixed times  constantly or periodically taking place WP29 interprets ‘systematic’ as meaning one or more of the following:  occurring according to a system 22  pre-arranged, organised or methodical  taking place as part of a general plan for data collection  carried out as part of a strategy Source: Article 37(1)(b) of the GDPR 5 Can organisations appoint a DPO jointly? If so, under what conditions? Yes. A group of undertakings may designate a single DPO provided that he or she is ‘easily accessible from each establishment’. The notion of accessibility refers to the tasks of the DPO as a contact point with respect to data subjects, the supervisory authority and also internally within the organisation. In order to ensure that the DPO is accessible, whether internal or external, it is important to make sure that their contact details are available. The DPO, with the help of a team if necessary, must be in a position to efficiently communicate with data subjects and cooperate with the supervisory authorities concerned. This means that this communication must take place in the language or languages used by the supervisory authorities and the data subjects concerned. The availability of a DPO (whether physically on the same premises as employees, via a hotline or other secure means of communication) is essential to ensure that data subjects will be able to contact the DPO. A single DPO may be designated for several public authorities or bodies, taking account of their organisational structure and size. The same considerations with regard to resources and communication apply. Given that the DPO is in charge of a variety of tasks, the controller or the processor must ensure that a single DPO, with the help of a team if necessary, can perform these efficiently despite being designated for several public authorities and bodies. Source: Article 37(2) and (3) of the GDPR 6 Where should the DPO be located? To ensure that the DPO is accessible, the WP29 recommends that the DPO be located within the European Union, whether or not the controller or the processor is established in the European Union. However, it cannot be excluded that, in some situations where the controller or the processor has no establishment within the European Union, a DPO may be able to carry out his or her activities more effectively if located outside the EU. 7 Is it possible to appoint an external DPO? Yes. The DPO may be a staff member of the controller or the processor (internal DPO) or fulfil the tasks on the basis of a service contract. This means that the DPO can be external, and in this case, his/her function can be exercised based on a service contract concluded with an individual or an organisation. [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

ragPromptContext: [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[organization] Commission — The Commission, most often referring to the European Commission, is a central body within the European Union with extensive responsibilities and powers, particularly in relation to data protection, digital markets, and legal frameworks. It serves as a regulatory authority with the sole power to implement and enforce the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The Commission issues guidelines, such as those in accordance with Article 47 DMA, and is solely responsible for interpreting the DMA provisions covered by these guidelines. It can impose sanctions, conduct proceedings and investigations under the DMA, and is involved in the coherent enforcement of both the DMA and GDPR, cooperating with national authorities and possessing investigatory powers. Under the GDPR, the Commission plays a crucial role in developing a code of icons for standardized information and is empowered to adopt delegated acts to determine the information for these icons. It can also adopt Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to regulate data processing between controllers and processors and lay down such clauses more broadly. A key function includes making adequacy decisions regarding the level of data protection in third countries or international organizations for international data transfers. The Commission monitors these decisions, consults with the European Data Protection Board ("the Board" or EDPB), evaluates their functioning, and reports findings. It can also adopt delegated acts specifying criteria and requirements for certification mechanisms and standardized icons, and implementing acts for specifying technical standards for data protection certification and safeguards. It cooperates with supervisory authorities in third countries to develop international cooperation mechanisms regarding personal data protection, specifying formats and procedures for information exchange relating to Binding Corporate Rules and mutual assistance. Member States must notify the Commission of adopted laws and amendments related to data protection provisions, and the Commission receives Supervisory Authority activity reports. The Commission designates gatekeepers regarding Core Platform Services (CPSs) and recognizes adequacy for data transfers. It has legal powers to regulate data sharing under Article 6(11) DMA via an implementing act pursuant to Article 8(2) DMA. It may specify the ineligibility of potential third-party recipients and consult with other bodies to ensure compliance with DMA obligations. The Commission assesses whether a third country provides an adequate level of protection for personal data and sometimes considers the display of advertisements as part of online advertising CPS and other CPS. It receives audited descriptions of profiling techniques from gatekeepers and transmits them to the EDPB. The Commission participates in the Board's activities without voting rights, can designate a representative, and can request matters to be handled within the consistency mechanism, including requesting opinions from the Board. It is informed of Board decisions and receives communications from the Board Chair. Ultimately, the Commission is granted delegated power to adopt and notify delegated acts, prepare and submit reports, examine the application and functioning of the Regulation, request information, and submit proposals for the overall effectiveness and implementation of data protection regulations, cooperating with the EDPB and supervisory authorities to assess processing operations and consider guidelines for gatekeepers regarding interoperability and geographical limitations.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Vorbereitungs-phase (sid-BF2BB73A-1EC1-4D86-BA99-29D0BD43C5B6)**: The activity 'Vorbereitungs-phase' (Preparation Phase) is part of a university admissions process, as indicated by its association with the document *WiSe2015-16_Leitfaden.pdf* (a guideline for winter semester applications). In an academic admissions context, this phase inherently involves planning, organising, and preparing for the collection and evaluation of personal data from applicants. Typical tasks in this phase include setting up systems or workflows to capture applicant details (e.g., names, addresses, academic records, identification numbers, or contact information), which are explicitly defined as personal data under GDPR (Article 4). Preparing documentation or criteria that will later be used to assess or profile applicants (e.g., eligibility checks, quota allocations, or prioritisation rules) constitutes processing as it structures how personal data will be used. Coordinating with internal or external stakeholders (e.g., *Hochschulstart*) may involve sharing or aligning datasets containing personal identifiers. The context of university admissions (a domain explicitly linked to education and recruitment in the GDPR knowledge graph) inherently requires handling personal data, as applicants are identifiable natural persons whose information (e.g., grades, certificates, or demographic data) is evaluated for selection purposes. Even if this phase does not directly enter data, it enables and organises the subsequent processing of personal data, making it GDPR-relevant. - **Bewerbung durchführen (sid-5BA5FD19-0416-425C-AF53-1EDD7A3BE277)**: The activity 'Bewerbung durchführen' (Submit Application) is performed by the applicant (Bewerber) and involves the active provision of personal data to the university. This task represents the collection and transmission of personal data, as applicants typically submit identifiable information: Name, date of birth, contact details (address, email, phone), and identification numbers (e.g., applicant ID or passport number). Academic/educational data: Transcripts, certificates, or exam results, which are linked to the individual and thus qualify as personal data. Special categories (if applicable): For certain programs, applicants may disclose health data (e.g., disabilities requiring accommodations), ethnic origin, or other sensitive information. Under GDPR, 'processing' explicitly includes collecting and transmitting personal data (Article 4(2)). The act of submitting an application is a deliberate disclosure of personal data to the university (the controller), triggering GDPR obligations. The context of education and recruitment (as highlighted in the GDPR knowledge graph) further confirms that such data is subject to protection. - **Bewerbung bearbeiten (sid-5CCCA870-162C-45A8-88E5-FAF663A44DAB)**: The activity 'Bewerbung bearbeiten' (Process Application) involves the university reviewing, evaluating, and handling the personal data submitted by applicants. This task is a core part of the admissions workflow and inherently processes personal data because it includes consulting and analysing applicant information (e.g., names, academic records, contact details, or special categories like health data for accommodations). Structuring or organising the data for assessment (e.g., sorting applications by criteria, assigning scores, or flagging eligibility). Storing or updating records in the university’s systems, which may involve linking personal data to internal databases. Under GDPR, processing explicitly includes consulting, using, analysing, and structuring personal data (Article 4(2)). The context of education and recruitment (as referenced in the GDPR knowledge graph) confirms that applicant data is protected. Even if the task name does not explicitly mention 'personal data,' the semantics of processing an application in an admissions context necessarily involve personal identifiers. - **Studienplatz vergeben (sid-0728004E-21CC-4D5E-9D26-6FB3182102F5)**: The activity 'Studienplatz vergeben' (Allocate Study Place) involves making admissions decisions based on the processed applicant data. This task is GDPR-relevant because it uses personal data (e.g., applicant names, academic records, or priority criteria) to determine allocations, which constitutes processing under GDPR (Article 4(2)). It may involve profiling or automated decision-making (e.g., ranking applicants by scores or quotas), which is explicitly regulated under GDPR (Articles 22 and 4). It generates outcomes linked to individuals, such as acceptance/rejection letters or waitlist assignments, which require handling personal identifiers. The education and recruitment context (as per the GDPR knowledge graph) confirms that such decisions are based on personal data. Even if the task appears administrative, the underlying data used for allocation (e.g., applicant IDs, grades) is personal and protected. - **Bewerber immatrikulieren (sid-A8E4767C-7AB6-4B9B-8F89-71970FB52A3A)**: The activity 'Bewerber immatrikulieren' (Enroll Applicant) involves registering successful applicants as students, which inherently processes personal data because it requires recording and storing the applicant’s identifiable information (e.g., name, address, date of birth, identification numbers, or payment details for tuition) in the university’s systems. Creating or updating student records, which may include academic history, contact details, or special categories (e.g., disability status). Generating enrollment documents (e.g., student IDs, certificates, or access credentials) linked to the individual. Under GDPR, processing includes recording, storing, and structuring personal data (Article 4(2)). The education context (as per the GDPR knowledge graph) confirms that enrollment data is protected, as it directly relates to identifiable natural persons (students). - **traditionelles Nachrück-verfahren (sid-5767BBF4-4398-4E10-8A08-3BAD565EE85D)**: The activity 'traditionelles Nachrückverfahren' (Traditional Waitlist Procedure) manages the reallocation of study places to applicants on a waitlist. This task is GDPR-relevant because it retrieves and consults personal data of waitlisted applicants (e.g., names, application IDs, priority scores, or contact details) to determine reallocation. Updates or alters the status of applicants (e.g., moving them from waitlist to enrolled), which involves modifying personal records. Communicates decisions to applicants, requiring the use of their contact information (a form of transmission under GDPR). The education and recruitment context (per the GDPR knowledge graph) confirms that waitlist data is personal, as it relates to identifiable individuals. Even if the task is procedural, the underlying data processed (applicant identifiers, rankings) is protected. - **Koordinier-ungsphase 1 mit Entscheidungsphase (sid-24B68543-3A87-4465-B34C-2E97A2B1AD1A)**: The activity 'Koordinierungsphase 1 mit Entscheidungsphase' (Coordination Phase 1 with Decision Phase) involves collaborating with *Hochschulstart* (a centralised admissions service) to align admissions decisions. This task is GDPR-relevant because it shares or transmits personal data (e.g., applicant lists, allocation results, or priority rankings) between the university and *Hochschulstart*, which constitutes processing under GDPR (Article 4(2)). Aligns or combines datasets containing identifiable information (e.g., matching applicant IDs across systems), which falls under structuring or combining data. Enables joint decision-making based on personal data, requiring the exchange of identifiers (e.g., names, application numbers). The education context (per the GDPR knowledge graph) confirms that such coordination involves protected data, as it directly relates to identifiable applicants. The transmission of personal data to a third party (*Hochschulstart*) further triggers GDPR obligations (e.g., ensuring lawful bases for sharing). - **Koordinierungsphase 2 (sid-65665F98-3FDB-4B73-8D2D-A30385D23F6A)**: The activity 'Koordinierungsphase 2' (Coordination Phase 2) continues the collaboration with *Hochschulstart* to finalise admissions decisions. This task is GDPR-relevant because it exchanges or synchronises personal data (e.g., updated applicant statuses, final allocation lists, or rejection notifications) between the university and *Hochschulstart*. Validates or confirms decisions linked to identifiable individuals, requiring the use of personal identifiers (e.g., names, application IDs). May transmit outcomes (e.g., acceptance/rejection data) to other systems or stakeholders, which constitutes dissemination under GDPR. As with the prior coordination phase, the education and recruitment context confirms that the data shared is personal and protected. The cross-organisational transmission of applicant data is a clear GDPR trigger, requiring compliance with Article 4(2) (processing) and Article 6 (lawful basis). - **Clearingphase (sid-248EC068-F0EE-4B10-A7CE-91A2553EE2DF)**: The activity 'Clearingphase' (Clearing Phase) manages the final allocation of remaining study places, often involving direct communication with applicants. This task is GDPR-relevant because it retrieves and evaluates personal data of applicants who were not initially allocated a place (e.g., waitlisted candidates), including names, contact details, and application scores. Updates applicant statuses (e.g., moving them from waitlist to enrolled or rejected), which involves altering personal records. Communicates decisions to applicants (e.g., sending offers or rejections), requiring the use of their email addresses or phone numbers (transmission of personal data). The education and recruitment context (per the GDPR knowledge graph) confirms that clearing phases handle protected data, as they involve identifiable individuals and their application records. The use of contact details for notifications is explicitly a GDPR-relevant processing activity.

result.reason: The activity "Bewerber-account anlegen" (Create applicant account) involves the creation of a user account for an applicant. This inherently requires the collection and storage of personal data such as the applicant’s name, contact details (e.g., email, address), and potentially other identifiers like date of birth or identification numbers. Under GDPR, any operation that collects, records, or structures personal data relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (a Data Subject) is considered processing of personal data. The account creation process is a foundational step in establishing a record tied to the applicant’s identity, making this activity GDPR-relevant.

The activity "vorhandene Qualifikationen eintragen" (Enter existing qualifications) requires the applicant to input personal data related to their educational and professional background. This includes degrees, certifications, grades, and potentially other identifiers like institution names or dates of attendance. Such data are directly linked to the applicant’s identity and professional profile, constituting personal data under GDPR. The act of recording and structuring these qualifications in a system (e.g., CMS) is a clear example of processing personal data, as it involves organizing and storing information that can identify or relate to the applicant as a Data Subject.

The activity "Antrag ausfüllen und Unterlagen hinzufügen" (Fill out application and add documents) involves the applicant providing a wide range of personal data, including but not limited to: Identification data: Name, address, date of birth, contact details (email, phone). Academic/educational data: Transcripts, certificates, qualifications, which are tied to the applicant’s identity. Supporting documents: Potentially CVs, letters of recommendation, or other materials containing personal information. Special categories of data (if applicable): For certain programs, health data, disability information, or ethnic background might be requested. This activity explicitly collects, records, and structures personal data, which is a core processing operation under GDPR. The annotation linked to this task further clarifies that the system dictates which documents are required based on the applicant and chosen program, reinforcing that the data being handled is personalized and directly tied to the Data Subject.

The activity "Angaben vervollständigen" (Complete information) requires the applicant to supplement or correct missing or incomplete personal data in their application. This involves updating, retrieving, and structuring personal information such as contact details, academic history, or other identifiers. Since the data being completed is inherently tied to the applicant’s identity, this activity constitutes processing of personal data under GDPR. The annotation linked to this task specifies the types of documents and details required for different application scenarios (e.g., Bachelor, Master, exchange programs), all of which involve personal data.

The activity "Bewerbung abschließen" (Finalize application) represents the applicant’s submission of their complete application, which includes all previously entered personal data (e.g., name, qualifications, documents). This act of transmitting the application to the university involves the disclosure of personal data to a third party (the admissions office), which is a clear processing operation under GDPR. The submission itself is a form of data transmission, and the application contains comprehensive personal information about the Data Subject.

The activity "Studiengang wählen" (Choose degree program) may appear administrative, but in the context of this process, it involves the applicant selecting a program that will be linked to their personal record. The choice of program is stored in the system (CMS) alongside the applicant’s identity, forming part of their personal data profile. Additionally, the annotation indicates that the system uses this selection to determine which documents are required, implying that the program choice is processed in conjunction with the applicant’s other personal data. Thus, this activity contributes to the structuring and updating of personal data and is GDPR-relevant.

The activity "Unterlagen vervollständigen" (Complete documents) involves the applicant providing additional or missing documents to their application. These documents invariably contain personal data, such as: Identification: Passport copies, ID cards, or birth certificates. Academic records: Transcripts, diplomas, or certificates tied to the applicant’s identity. Other personal documents: Proof of residency, language proficiency certificates, or letters of motivation. The act of submitting these documents is a form of collecting and supplementing personal data, which is explicitly covered under GDPR’s definition of processing. The annotation clarifies that paper-based submissions are handled by the university’s department, further confirming that the documents are part of the applicant’s personal record.

The activity "Qualifikationen (automatisch) prüfen" (Automatically check qualifications) involves an automated processing of the applicant’s submitted qualifications (e.g., grades, degrees, certifications). This activity evaluates personal data to determine eligibility, which falls under GDPR’s definition of profiling and automated decision-making. The system assesses the applicant’s qualifications against predefined criteria, directly impacting their application outcome. The annotation confirms that this is an automated step within the CMS, reinforcing that it processes the applicant’s personal data without human intervention, a scenario explicitly regulated by GDPR (Article 22).

The activity "Bewerbung auf Vollständigkeit prüfen (automatisch)" (Automatically check application for completeness) involves an automated review of the applicant’s submitted documents and data to ensure nothing is missing. This requires accessing, consulting, and evaluating all personal data provided by the applicant (e.g., name, qualifications, supporting documents). The automated nature of this check means the system processes personal data to validate the application, which is a GDPR-relevant operation. The annotation specifies that the system cross-references required documents based on the applicant’s profile, confirming that personalized data is being handled.

The activity "Unterlagen auf Vollständigkeit prüfen und einscannen" (Check documents for completeness and scan) performed by the university’s admissions office involves two key GDPR-relevant actions: Manual review of personal data: The staff examines the applicant’s submitted documents (e.g., IDs, transcripts, certificates), all of which contain personal information. Digitization (scanning): The physical documents are converted into electronic records, which constitutes structuring and storing personal data in a filing system. Both actions are explicit forms of processing personal data under GDPR. The annotation confirms that this task is linked to the CMS, where the scanned documents are stored as part of the applicant’s digital record.

The activity "Bestätigung ggf. mit Hinweis auf nachzureichende Unterlagen erstellen" (Create confirmation with note on missing documents) involves generating a personalized communication to the applicant. This confirmation: Uses the applicant’s contact details (e.g., email) to send the message, which is processing of personal data. References the applicant’s specific application status, including which documents are missing, tying the communication directly to their personal record. May include personalized instructions based on the applicant’s profile (e.g., deadlines, required documents). The creation and sending of this confirmation is a form of transmitting and using personal data to communicate with the Data Subject, making it GDPR-relevant. The annotation links this task to the CMS, where the applicant’s data is managed.

The activity "nachzu-reichende Unterlagen im CMS vermerken" (Note missing documents in CMS) involves updating the applicant’s digital record in the CMS to indicate which documents are still required. This requires: Accessing the applicant’s existing personal data (e.g., name, application ID, current document status). Adding or modifying notes tied to their profile, which constitutes updating and structuring personal data. The CMS is a filing system where the applicant’s information is stored, and any changes to their record are explicit processing operations under GDPR. The annotation confirms the use of the CMS for this purpose.

ragPromptContext: [person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.

Adopted 17 ANNEX: ILLUSTRATIONS OF EXAMPLES 1–12 Adopted 18 Example 1: Controller in a third country collects data directly from a data subject in the EU (under Article 3(2) GDPR) Maria, living in Italy, inserts her name, surname and postal address by filling a form on an online clothing website in order to complete her order and receive the dress she bought online at her residence in Rome. The online clothing website is operated by a third country company that has no presence in the EU, but specifically targets the EU market. In this case, the data subject (Maria) passes her personal data to the third country company. This does not constitute a transfer of personal data since the data are not passed by an exporter (controller or processor), but directly collected from the data subject by the controller under Article 3(2) GDPR. Thus, Chapter V does not apply to this case. Nevertheless, the third country company will be required to apply the GDPR since its processing operations are subject to Article 3(2). Example 2: Controller in a third country collects data directly from a data subject in the EU (under Article 3(2) GDPR) and uses a processor outside the EU for some processing activities Maria, living in Italy, inserts her name, surname and postal address by filling a form on an online clothing website in order to complete her order and receive the dress she bought online at her residence in Rome. The online clothing website is operated by a third country company that has no presence in the EU, but specifically targets the EU market. In order to process the orders received by means of the website, the third country company has engaged a non-EEA processor. In this case, the data subject (Maria) passes her personal data to the third country company and this does not constitute a transfer of personal data since the data are directly collected by the controller under Article 3(2) GDPR. Thus, the controller will have to apply the GDPR to the processing of this personal data. As far as it engages a non-EEA processor, such disclosure from the third country company to its non-EEA processor would amount to a transfer, and it will be required to apply Article 28 and Chapter V obligations so as to ensure that the level of protection afforded by the GDPR would not be undermined when data are processed on its behalf by the non-EEA-processor. ragPromptContext: [data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.
Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction, as defined in Article 2(2) GDPR.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

Staff members that transferred between departments were still able to gain access to the patient files from their “old” departments and the hospital had no procedures in place to match the current position of the staff member with their authorisation. Internal investigation by the hospital showed that at least 150 staff members (out of the 3500) had inaccurate authorisations, affecting at least 20,000 of the 95,000 patient files. The hospital could show that in at least 16 instances staff members had used their authorisations to view patient files. The supervisory authority considers that there has been a breach of Article 32 GDPR. In assessing the seriousness of the case, the supervisory authority first noted that an infringement of Article 32 GDPR is listed among the infringements of Article 83(4) GDPR and therefore falls within the lower tier of Article 83 GDPR. Secondly, the supervisory authority assessed the circumstances of the case. In that regard, the supervisory authority considered that even though the number of data subjects affected by the breach was only 16, this could potentially have been 20,000 in the circumstances of the case and even 95,000 given the systemic nature of the issue. Furthermore, the supervisory authority categorised the infringement as negligent, but to a low degree, which was considered a neutral factor in the circumstances of this particular case due to the fact that the hospital failed to adopt authorisation policies where it surely should have done so but had, otherwise, taken steps to implement strict measures to restrict access. This evaluation was not impacted by the fact that other data protection and security policies were implemented successfully, as the GDPR requires. Lastly, the supervisory authority attributed significant weight to the fact that the patient files include health data, which are special categories of data according to Article 9 GDPR. 23 Adopted Taking all the above into account (nature of the processing and special categories of data vis-à-vis the number of data subjects actually and potentially affected, the supervisory authority concludes that the infringement is considered to be at a medium level of seriousness. The supervisory authority will determine the starting amount for further calculation at a point between 10 and 20% of the legal maximum included in Article 83(4) GDPR. Example 5c – Qualifying the seriousness of an infringement (low level of seriousness) A supervisory authority has received numerous complaints about the way in which an online store handles the right of access of its data subjects. According to the complainants, the handling of their access requests has taken between 4 and 6 months, which is outside the timeframe permitted by the GDPR. The supervisory authority investigates the complaints and finds that the online store responds to access requests a maximum of three months too late in 5% of the cases. In total the store received around 1,000 access requests on an annual basis and confirmed that 950 of these were handled on time. Moreover, the online store had policies in place to safeguard that all access requests were handled correctly and fully. Nevertheless, the supervisory authority concluded that the online store infringed Article 12(3) GDPR and decided to impose a fine. During the calculation of the amount of the fine to be imposed, the supervisory authority was tasked with assessing the seriousness of this case. As a starting point, the supervisory authority noted that an infringement of Article 12 GDPR is listed among the infringements of Article 83(5) GDPR and therefore falls within the higher tier of Article 83 GDPR. Secondly, the supervisory authority assessed the circumstances of the case. In that regard, the supervisory authority carefully analysed the nature of the infringement. Even though the timely right to access to personal data is one of the cornerstones of the data subject rights, the supervisory authority considered that the infringement was of limited seriousness in this respect, given that all requests were handled eventually and with a limited delay. Considering the purpose of the processing, the supervisory authority found that the processing of personal data was not the core activity of the online store, but still an important ancillary in fulfilling its objective of selling goods online. The supervisory authority considered this to increase the seriousness of the infringement. On the other hand, the level of damage suffered by the data subjects was considered minimal, as all access requests were handled within 6 months. Taking all the above into account (nature of the infringement, purpose of the processing and level of damage), the supervisory authority concludes that the infringement is considered to be at a low level of seriousness. The supervisory authority will determine the starting amount for further calculation at a point between 0 and 10% of the legal maximum included in Article 83(5) GDPR. 4.3 - Turnover of the undertaking with a view to imposing an effective, dissuasive and proportionate fine 63. The GDPR requires each supervisory authority to ensure that the imposition of administrative fines is effective, proportionate and dissuasive in each individual case (Article 83(1) GDPR).
