I. PERSONAL DATA BREACH NOTIFICATION UNDER THE GDPR A. Basic security considerations 10. One of the requirements of the GDPR is that, by using appropriate technical and organisational measures, personal data shall be processed in a manner to ensure the appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage13. 11. Accordingly, the GDPR requires both controllers and processors to have in place appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk posed to the personal data being processed. They should take into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation and the nature, the scope, context and purposes of processing, as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons14. Also, the GDPR requires all appropriate technological protection an organisational measures to be in place to establish immediately whether a breach has taken place, which then determines whether the notification obligation is engaged 15. 12. Consequently, a key element of any data security policy is being able, where possible, to prevent a breach and, where it nevertheless occurs, to react to it in a timely manner. B. What is a personal data breach? 1. Definition 13. As part of any attempt to address a breach the controller should first be able to recognise one. The GDPR defines a “personal data breach” in Article 4(12) as: “a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed.” 14. What is meant by “destruction” of personal data should be quite clear: this is where the data no longer exists, or no longer exists in a form that is of any use to the controller. “Damage” should also be relatively clear: this is where personal data has been altered, corrupted, or is no longer complete. In terms of “loss” of personal data, this should be interpreted as the data may still exist, but the controller has lost control or access to it, or no longer has it in its possession. Finally, unauthorised or unlawful processing may include disclosure of personal data to (or access by) recipients who are not authorised to receive (or access) the data, or any other form of processing which violates the GDPR. Example An example of loss of personal data can include where a device containing a copy of a controller’s customer database has been lost or stolen. A further example of loss may be where the only copy of a set of personal data has been encrypted by ransomware, or has been encrypted by the controller using a key that is no longer in its possession. 15. [concept] Binding Corporate Rules — Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) are a set of internal, legally binding provisions adopted by multinational corporations or a group of undertakings, and they serve as an appropriate safeguard and legal framework for the international transfer of personal data. These rules are applied to facilitate data transfers within the same corporate group, particularly when transferring personal data outside the European Economic Area (EEA) or the European Union (EU) to entities located in third countries. BCRs specify requirements for data transfer and processing within the group. They encompass provisions on crucial data protection principles, data subject rights, mechanisms for liability, and compliance, ensuring that adequate protection is maintained for the personal data. An important aspect of BCRs is that they require approval from a supervisory authority, and in specific contexts, they may also require Board approval as defined in Article 47. Additionally, BCRs are subject to specific formats and procedures for electronic information exchange between data controllers, processors, and supervisory authorities. They are also known to include requirements such as the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, as referenced in Articles 47(1) and 47(2)(e) of relevant regulations. BCRs are recognized as a transfer tool for data, sometimes mentioned in relation to derogations from typical data transfer requirements.

[concept] Code of Conduct — A set of rules outlining responsibilities or proper practices for employees, non-compliance with which does not disrupt corporate liability attribution.
A Code of Conduct is a document providing safeguards and mechanisms for data protection in specific sectors. It needs approval and must demonstrate effective application of the GDPR.
A Code of Conduct outlines appropriate review mechanisms, adapts to legal changes, addresses new technological developments, and ensures compliance with the GDPR.
An approved set of guidelines that a processor can adhere to to demonstrate sufficient guarantees for data protection.
A Code of Conduct is a set of provisions for demonstrating compliance with data protection regulations, which can be drafted, amended, approved, registered, and published.
A code of conduct may be subject to review by the Board to determine its compliance with the Regulation, as per Article 40(7).

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Administrative Costs — Administrative costs are expenses incurred by the controller for providing information or taking action on data subject requests.
Administrative Costs are expenses incurred by the controller for activities such as providing copies of personal data.
Administrative Costs are expenses incurred by the Supervisory Authority in handling requests, which may be charged for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests.
[person] Auditor — An auditor, who can be mandated by the controller, conducts inspections/audits to verify compliance.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[person] Data Subject — A Data Subject is defined as an identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates and whose personal data undergoes processing, encompassing operations such as collection, holding, storing, or other manipulations, including biometric and location data. This individual can be identified, directly or indirectly, by reference to an identifier or specific factors of their identity. End users are often considered Data Subjects, and their vital interests may necessitate data processing. Even if a Data Subject's data has been anonymized such that they are no longer identifiable, they are still considered a Data Subject. Their behavior or identity may be monitored, and any personal data relating to them requires either consent or another legitimate basis for lawful processing. Data processing concerning Data Subjects is subject to regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly if goods or services are offered to them within the European Union. Under Article 6 of the GDPR, explicit consent is often required for processing, including profiling and automated decision-making. This consent must be demonstrably obtained through deliberate, informed action. Data Subjects possess fundamental rights to safeguard their human dignity and legitimate interests, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, objection to processing, and data portability. They also have the right to be informed about and challenge automated decision-making and, in some contexts, request delisting from search engines. They can monitor data processing, should be offered format choices for reusing their data, and can transmit their personal data from one controller to another, taking responsibility for securing it in their own system. Data controllers are obligated to provide Data Subjects with specific information, including the identity of their representative, and to communicate efficiently. Their views should be sought during a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) where appropriate. When biometric data is processed, an alternative solution must be offered, and Data Subjects should be consulted during the drafting of codes of conduct when feasible. A Data Subject is also an individual whose personal data may be affected by a data breach, putting their rights and freedoms at risk. In such an event, the controller must inform them, especially if there is a likely high risk of adverse effects or potential damage; communication of the breach is obligatory if their personal data has been compromised and depending on the severity of the consequences. Their vital interests, reasonable expectations (influenced by factors like age, public figure status, and professional position), and personal data require consistent protection, necessitating that their rights and freedoms be safeguarded. They may contact the Data Protection Officer, lodge complaints with supervisory authorities, and seek judicial remedy. A Data Subject has the right to compensation for material or non-material damage suffered due to an infringement of the regulation. Their identity may be scrutinized by a controller if doubts arise.

[method] Administrative Arrangements — Administrative arrangements are provisions that can be inserted between public bodies for data transfers, subject to authorization from the competent SA, including enforceable and effective data subject rights.
A mechanism for personal data transfers between public bodies under Article 46 (3) (b) GDPR, subject to authorization from a competent supervisory authority.
Administrative arrangements are alternative instruments for data transfer, such as Memoranda of Understanding, providing protection through commitments.
Administrative arrangements, such as a memorandum of understanding, provide for enforceable and effective rights for data subjects in the context of data transfers involving public authorities.
Administrative arrangements are provisions inserted between public authorities or bodies, including enforceable data subject rights, used as safeguards.
Administrative Arrangements are agreements related to data protection, which a Supervisory Authority can authorize.
[content] Judgment of the Court of Justice of 12 January 2023 — This refers to a legal judgment, specifically the case RW v Österreichische Post AG, C-154/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:3, paragraph 46.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.
A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
A processor processes personal data on behalf of a controller. An authorized third party may act as a processor for an end user if the end user is a controller.
[organization] Tax and Customs Authorities — Public authorities to which personal data may be disclosed for their official mission.
[concept] Rectification — Rectification refers to the right of data subjects to have inaccurate personal data concerning them rectified.

The first building block relates to the type of entity that can be a controller. Under the GDPR, a controller can be “a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body”. This means that, in principle, there is no limitation as to the type of entity that may assume the role of a controller. ## Test Case 57 - Dienstreiseabrechnung genehmigen - Amount of Correct Activities: 7 - Amount of False Positives: 0 - Amount of False Negatives: 0 - **Expected:** Dienstreiseabrechnung sichten (xtre-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung genehmigen (xttr-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung ablehnen (xu5h-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung an andere Sachbearbeitung weiterleiten (xu3y-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnungsdaten anpassen (xtts-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Kommentar eingeben (xtrf-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung an Antragsteller zurücksenden (xu2f-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e) - **Actual:** Dienstreiseabrechnung sichten (xtre-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Kommentar eingeben (xtrf-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnungsdaten anpassen (xtts-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung genehmigen (xttr-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung an Antragsteller zurücksenden (xu2f-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung an andere Sachbearbeitung weiterleiten (xu3y-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e), Abrechnung ablehnen (xu5h-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e) - **Result:** ✅ Passed - **False Positives:** None - **False Negatives:** None - **Amount of Retries:** 1 ### RAG Metrics (Ragas) - **Faithfulness:** 0.406 - **Context Utilization:** 0.321 - **Samples:** 7 (failed: 0)

Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Dienstreiseabrechnung sichten (xtre-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e)**: The activity 'Dienstreiseabrechnung sichten' (Review travel expense report) processes personal data because it involves examining a travel expense report submitted by an employee (a Data Subject). Such reports inherently contain personal data—including the employee’s name, bank details (for reimbursement), travel dates/locations (which may reveal private movements), and potentially receipts tied to the individual. Under GDPR Article 4(1), any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person qualifies as personal data. Reviewing these details constitutes ‘processing’ as defined in Article 4(2), encompassing operations like consultation, use, and structuring of data. The associated data object annotation further clarifies that the report includes ‘Angaben zur Kostenerstattung’ (reimbursement details), which directly links financial transactions to the employee’s identity. Even if the activity does not modify the data, accessing or reading personal data is explicitly considered processing under GDPR (Recital 30). - **Kommentar eingeben (xtrf-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e)**: The activity 'Kommentar eingeben' (Enter comment) processes personal data because it involves adding notes or annotations to an employee’s travel expense report. Even if the comment itself does not explicitly contain personal identifiers (e.g., names), it is linked to the employee’s record and thus relates to an identified natural person (the employee submitting the report). Under GDPR, any data that can be linked to an individual—including internal comments or administrative notes tied to their file—qualifies as personal data (Article 4(1)). The annotation ‘Dokumente können hochgeladen werden. Notizen können ergänzt werden.’ (Documents can be uploaded. Even internal administrative notes are subject to GDPR if they pertain to an identifiable person (Recital 26). - **Abrechnungsdaten anpassen (xtts-ed2f4ad43858602ad6e00efd76b0f56e)**: The activity 'Abrechnungsdaten anpassen' (Adjust expense report data) processes personal data because it involves modifying an employee’s travel expense report, which contains personally identifiable information. [concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.
Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction, as defined in Article 2(2) GDPR.

[method] Anonymisation — Anonymisation is a fundamental process and set of techniques designed to transform personal data in such a way that the data subject can no longer be identified, either directly or indirectly. This alteration ensures that the data cannot be linked back to an individual, even with reasonable effort. It is employed when personal data is deleted or anonymized following the withdrawal of consent, acting as a crucial safeguard in data processing, particularly for research purposes where the objective can be achieved without handling identifiable data. This process involves carefully processing data, such as location information, to prevent re-identification, a task that is complex and necessitates transparency regarding the methodologies used. The goal of anonymisation extends beyond simply removing identifying information to also preserving the quality and usefulness of the data for its intended purpose. It is a preferred solution and safeguard, recognized by regulations like the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically Article 6(11), and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which require the rendering of personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy. In essence, anonymisation serves as a vital method for making shared personal data suitable for use while upholding the privacy of individuals.
Anonymization is a method by which shared data that constitutes personal data is processed to remove identifying information.
Anonymisation is a method of altering personal data so that the data subject is no longer identifiable, with the goal of preserving data quality and usefulness.
Anonymisation is the process of altering personal data to prevent direct or indirect identification of end users, required for data shared under Article 6(11) DMA.
Anonymisation is the process of rendering personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy, as required by DMA and GDPR.

[concept] Controller Or Processor — Entities or individuals subject to regulations under the GDPR regarding data handling.
A controller or processor is an entity whose conduct is examined for compliance with the GDPR and potentially the DMA.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.
A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
A processor processes personal data on behalf of a controller. An authorized third party may act as a processor for an end user if the end user is a controller.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. The GDPR recognizes that Controllers may not have all information immediately and allows for phased notification.<SEP>Controllers must comply with the provisions of the GDPR, including those related to information provision.<SEP>The controller must comply with GDPR requirements, including those related to transparency and notification.<SEP>A controller's responsibilities are defined under the GDPR. GDPR.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to. These collective requirements define the responsibility and liability of the processor under the GDPR.<SEP>The GDPR, specifically Article 60(10), imposes duties on the processor.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for ensuring data processing adheres to GDPR provisions.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for compliance with the GDPR and must be able to demonstrate it.<SEP>The processing by a processor is governed by a contract or legal act that ensures compliance with GDPR articles. Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Data Subject is governed by a framework of rights, obligations, and legal considerations, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Controller is authorized to process a Data Subject's personal data, frequently through contractual agreements, and is obligated to provide essential, timely, and clear information regarding these processing operations, as stipulated in GDPR Article 14(2)(b) and (f). This includes notifying Data Subjects of personal data breaches, especially if they pose a high risk to their rights and freedoms, as mentioned in Article 34 of the GDPR. Controllers are legally mandated to facilitate the easy and full exercise of data protection rights by Data Subjects, ensuring these rights can be exercised without undue hindrance and by providing a simple mechanism for their exercise. This also entails addressing requests for data erasure or objections to processing, and informing Data Subjects about changes and facilitating access to information. For specific activities like processing biometric data, the Controller must obtain explicit, informed, and freely given consent. Transparency from the Controller is also required concerning profiling and automated decision-making processes that impact the Data Subject. In all data processing activities, the Controller must carefully consider the Data Subject's interests, fundamental rights, and freedoms, acknowledging the direct impact of their actions. This assessment varies depending on the specific relationship (e.g., employer-employee, service provider-customer) and the Data Subject's particular situation. In situations involving potential surveillance, the Controller must consider the Data Subject's objection and can only proceed if there is a compelling legitimate interest or for legal claims, also assessing the Data Subject's intention to make data public. When applying the household exemption, key considerations include the Controller’s personal relationship with the Data Subject, the scale and frequency of surveillance, and any potential adverse impact it might have. There must be a balancing exercise between the competing interests of the Controller and the Data Subject's objection, with the burden of proof on the Controller. A significant imbalance, as noted in Recital 47 of the GDPR, can compromise the freedom of consent, and Controllers have been known to attempt to influence Data Subjects for more extensive data collection. It is paramount that the fundamental rights and freedoms of Data Subjects are not overridden by the Controller’s interests, even when a relevant and appropriate relationship exists (e.g., client or in the service of the controller). Controllers must provide clear information to Data Subjects to allow them to correct inaccuracies and select a method for providing information that is appropriate to the manner in which the Data Controller and Data Subject interact. The Controller is responsible for protecting the rights of Data Subjects and responding to their requests for exercising those rights. They are obligated to respond to such requests and make decisions about the processing of personal data for which they are responsible. This includes providing information and taking action on requests from the Data Subject, communicating personal data breaches, and communicating information about data processing and their rights. The Controller enables the Data Subject to monitor data processing and implements pre-contractual measures and data transfers at the Data Subject's request or in their interest. The Controller may offer goods or services to Data Subjects who are in the Union and should compensate any damage a Data Subject may suffer as a result of processing that infringes the Regulation. The Controller can also ask the Data Subject to provide additional information if there are reasonable doubts about their identity, as per Article 12(6) GDPR, and takes into account the reasonable expectations of Data Subjects based on their relationship with the controller when considering legitimate interests. Data Subject.

Under GDPR, Personal Data The relation "(Personal Data, Processor)" defines the role and responsibilities of a Processor in handling Personal Data. A Processor is an entity that processes personal data strictly on behalf of and under the instructions of a Controller, operating as an agent in managing, extracting, handling, and transferring this data. Key duties include the implementation of robust security measures to protect the personal data entrusted to them. Processors are authorized to perform operations involving personal data, and individuals working under the direct authority of the Processor are also permitted to process such data. Upon the termination of processing activities, the Processor is generally obligated to either delete or return the personal data to the Controller, unless a legal requirement necessitates its storage. Furthermore, a Processor may transfer personal data, and within the context of the EU, they might even make personal data accessible to a third-country authority. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Supervisory Authority is established primarily by data protection regulations, such as the GDPR, and focuses on compliance, breach management, and accountability. A central obligation of the Controller is to notify the Supervisory Authority of personal data breaches, typically within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, especially if it poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, as per Article 33(1) and Article 27(5) GDPR. The Controller is responsible for determining if a breach is notifiable and must ensure the relevant Supervisory Authority is informed, potentially proactively notifying them of infringements or seeking advice. They must also inform the Supervisory Authority about data transfers, documenting assessments and safeguards. Controllers without an EU establishment are required to engage with local supervisory authorities in every Member State where they operate. Furthermore, the Controller must consult the Supervisory Authority if a high risk identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment cannot be mitigated by reasonable means before processing. Controllers are also obligated to cooperate with and make records available to the Supervisory Authority upon request, demonstrating accountability and compliance. The Supervisory Authority plays a significant role in overseeing the Controller's data protection practices. It can advise Controllers on how to inform individuals about breaches and may even order them to do so, particularly for high-risk breaches. The Supervisory Authority verifies the Controller's compliance, handles complaints, and seeks amicable settlements regarding possible infringements. It possesses powers to require the Controller to provide information, carry out investigations, notify infringements, and obtain access to data and premises. The Supervisory Authority can issue warnings and reprimands, order compliance, and impose sanctions, including administrative fines under Article 83 GDPR, especially in cases of unjustified breaches. The level of the Controller's cooperation is considered by the Supervisory Authority when assessing mitigation efforts. The Supervisory Authority also promotes awareness among Controllers regarding their obligations under pertinent regulations and informs Controllers when a received complaint is dismissed or rejected. result.reason: The activity 'QIS-Dienstreiseabrechnung suchen' (Search QIS business trip settlement) involves retrieving a 'Dienstreiseabrechnung' (business trip settlement record). A 'Dienstreiseabrechnung' inherently contains personal data of the employee (e.g., name, employee ID, travel dates, destinations, accommodation details, and potentially bank/payment information for reimbursements). Searching for and accessing such records constitutes 'consulting' or 'retrieving' personal data under GDPR (Article 4(2)), as it enables the clerk to view identifiable information tied to a natural person (the employee).

The activity 'Konten eingeben' (Enter accounts) requires inputting account details linked to the employee’s expense reimbursement. Even if the exact data fields are not specified, account information (e.g., cost center codes, project codes, or internal accounting references) is often tied to an employee’s identity (e.g., via employee ID or payroll system). Entering or updating such data constitutes 'recording' or 'structuring' personal data under GDPR, as it directly or indirectly relates to an identifiable natural person (the employee submitting the expense).

The activity 'Kostenrechnung anpassen' (Adjust cost statement) involves modifying the expense report of an employee. An expense report typically includes personal data such as the employee’s name, travel details (dates, locations), accommodation costs, meal expenses, and potentially payment information. Adjusting these records constitutes 'alteration' or 'updating' of personal data under GDPR, as the changes directly relate to an identifiable individual (the employee).

The activity 'Bankdaten prüfen' (Check bank details) explicitly involves reviewing an employee’s bank account information (as indicated by the associated data object Bank_Registerkarte). Bank details (e.g., IBAN, account holder name) are personal data under GDPR (Article 4(1)), as they directly identify a natural person. Verifying or consulting these details constitutes 'processing' (specifically, 'consultation' or 'use') of personal data.

The activity 'Referenz automatisch anpassen' (Automatically adjust reference) changes the reference code of a 'Dienstreiseabrechnung' from 'Q' (pending) to 'E' (settled), as noted in the annotation. This adjustment is part of the expense settlement workflow, which inherently involves personal data (e.g., employee ID, travel dates, reimbursement amounts). Updating the reference status constitutes 'structuring' or 'alteration' of personal data, as it modifies metadata tied to the employee’s identifiable record.

The activity 'Referenz manuell anpassen' (Manually adjust reference) performs the same function as the automatic adjustment but requires manual intervention. As with the automatic version, this involves updating the reference status of an employee’s expense record, which is linked to their personal data (e.g., travel details, reimbursement status). Manually altering this reference constitutes 'adaptation' or 'organisation' of personal data under GDPR.

The activity 'Abrechnungsdaten einsehen' (View settlement data) involves accessing the settlement data of a business trip, which includes the Übernachtung_Registerkarte (accommodation tab). This data typically contains personal details such as the employee’s name, travel dates, hotel stays, and potentially payment information. Viewing or consulting these records constitutes 'retrieval' or 'consultation' of personal data under GDPR.

The activity 'Buchung durchführen' (Perform booking) executes the accounting/posting of the expense settlement. The annotation clarifies this includes writing data to the HÜL-Tabelle (a financial ledger table), assigning booking types, and generating HÜL numbers—all of which are tied to the employee’s expense record. Posting these entries constitutes 'recording' and 'structuring' of personal data, as the financial transactions are linked to the identifiable employee (e.g., via employee ID or payroll system).

The activity 'Weitere Anpassungen vornehmen' (Make further adjustments) involves additional modifications to the expense settlement, as annotated by the need to 'genehmigen alle Registerkarten aus Dienstreiseabrechnung' (approve all tabs in the business trip settlement). This implies reviewing and potentially editing multiple sections of the employee’s expense record (e.g., travel details, accommodation, payments), all of which contain personal data. Adjusting or approving these records constitutes 'alteration' or 'use' of personal data under GDPR.

The activity 'Bericht erzeugen' (Generate report) creates a report based on the processed expense settlement. Even if the report itself might aggregate data, the underlying source is the employee’s personal expense records (e.g., travel dates, costs, bank details). Generating a report from such data constitutes 'use' or 'disclosure' of personal data, as the report derives from and may still reflect identifiable information (e.g., per-employee breakdowns).

[concept] Administrative Costs — Administrative costs are expenses incurred by the controller for providing information or taking action on data subject requests.
Administrative Costs are expenses incurred by the controller for activities such as providing copies of personal data.
Administrative Costs are expenses incurred by the Supervisory Authority in handling requests, which may be charged for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests.

[content] Article 34 GDPR — Article 34 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) specifies the conditions and requirements for communicating a personal data breach to data subjects. This article outlines the obligations for data controllers regarding such communication, complementing the rights of data subjects. The core of Article 34 GDPR revolves around the notification of data subjects in the event of a data breach. Specifically, it mandates communication to affected individuals when a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. This provision details these additional notification obligations, which may, under certain circumstances, be restricted.
Article 34 of the GDPR outlines the communication of a personal data breach to the data subject.
[concept] Compensation — Compensation is the right for any person who has suffered damage due to an infringement of the Regulation to receive payment from the controller or processor.

[concept] Data Transfers — Data transfers involve the movement of data from one location or entity to another.
Data Transfers refer to the movement of data to third countries or international organizations, which can be based on appropriate safeguards and legal remedies for data subjects.
Data transfers involve the movement of personal data, and possible risks due to absence of adequacy decisions or safeguards (Article 46) must be informed.
Data Transfers involve the movement of personal data from one entity or location to another, especially across borders.

[organization] Board — The Board, generally understood as the European Data Protection Board, is an independent Union body with its own legal personality, established primarily to ensure the consistent application of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It comprises the heads of supervisory authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor, and it adopts decisions through various majority votes of its members, without seeking or taking instructions from external entities. The Board's decisions can be subject to review by the Court of Justice, as outlined in Article 267 TFEU. A central function of the Board involves its supervisory and decision-making responsibilities. It provides essential opinions on draft decisions, especially concerning certification criteria, and these opinions are crucial for the approval of such decisions, potentially leading to common certifications like the European Data Protection Seal. The Board collates and publicly registers all approved certification mechanisms and data protection seals. Supervisory authorities, particularly Lead Supervisory Authorities (LSAs), communicate draft decisions to the Board, especially those relating to objections not followed by the LSA or those not meeting specific thresholds. The LSA is mandated to seek decisions from the Board under conditions specified in Article 60(4) and must inform the Board about its decisions, providing a summary of facts and grounds. Complaint-receiving Supervisory Authorities are also required to inform the Board of their decisions. The Board is instrumental in issuing guidance, including separate guidelines on using codes for international data transfers, and general guidelines on applying the Regulation. These guidelines cover criteria for determining substantial effects on data subjects across Member States and what constitutes a relevant objection. The Board also publishes or endorses opinions and positions pertinent to specific sectors or data processing activities. The Commission consults the Board when assessing the level of protection in third countries or international organizations. Further responsibilities of the Board include issuing opinions on draft codes of conduct, particularly for processing activities across multiple Member States, and collating approved codes into a register. It also issues urgent binding decisions and opinions in cases requiring immediate action, especially regarding provisional measures. The Board receives submissions on various matters, including objections to draft decisions, and is informed of decisions by the LSA. It engages in arrangements for the electronic exchange of information with supervisory authorities, receives activity reports from them, and is the body referred to in Article 68 that receives communications from Supervisory Authorities regarding lists related to Data Protection Impact Assessments. The Board also promotes enhanced cooperation, training, and knowledge exchange among supervisory authorities, draws up annual reports, and adopts its own rules of procedure, with discussions often being confidential.

[person] Employee — An Employee is defined as an individual who is employed by an organization or person, belonging to the legal entity of a data controller or processor. These individuals are typically authorized to process personal data, acting under the authority of the controller. Their access to personal data should be restricted based on their specific duties and role within the company. Employees may interact with personal data in various ways, such as manually deleting personal data after its retention period in accordance with internal procedures. They can also be subjects whose personal data, such as their name, is processed by services (e.g., a taxi service in an illustrative example). Employee actions can also lead to incidents, such as when an employee of a controller makes a mistake resulting in a data breach, or when an employee of a service provider has their electronic notebook stolen, as depicted in CASE No. 11. While employees generally operate under established authority, there can be exceptional cases where they unlawfully exceed this authority. Furthermore, employees may face pressure concerning consent for data processing.
Employees are individuals within an organization who may have concerns or complaints.
An employee is a data subject who has a relevant and appropriate relationship with a controller, often forming the basis for legitimate interest in data processing within a group of undertakings.

[method] Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures — Targeted technical and organisational measures are efforts, possibly jointly with Article 6(4) DMA beneficiaries, to handle personal data breaches and restore data availability.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks.
