[Source: Guidelines_on_Automated_individual_decision_making_and_Profiling_for_the_purposes_of_Regulation_2016679] " greater accountability obligations;  specified legal bases for the processing;  rights for individuals to oppose profiling and specifically profiling for marketing; and  if certain conditions are met, the need to carry out a data protection impact assessment. The GDPR does not just focus on the decisions made as a result of automated processing or profiling. It applies to the collection of data for the creation of profiles, as well as the application of those profiles to individuals. A. Profiling The GDPR defines profiling in Article 4(4) as: any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person’s performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements; Profiling is composed of three elements:  it has to be an automated form of processing; 7  it has to be carried out on personal data; and  the objective of the profiling must be to evaluate personal aspects about a natural person. Article 4(4) refers to ‘any form of automated processing’ rather than ‘solely’ automated processing (referred to in Article 22). Profiling has to involve some form of automated processing – although human involvement does not necessarily take the activity out of the definition. Profiling is a procedure which may involve a series of statistical deductions. It is often used to make predictions about people, using data from various sources to infer something about an individual, based on the qualities of others who appear statistically similar. The GDPR says that profiling is automated processing of personal data for evaluating personal aspects, in particular to analyse or make predictions about individuals. The use of the word ‘evaluating’ suggests that profiling involves some form of assessment or judgement about a person. A simple classification of individuals based on known characteristics such as their age, sex, and height does not necessarily lead to profiling. This will depend on the purpose of the classification. For instance, a business may wish to classify its customers according to their age or gender for statistical purposes and to acquire an aggregated overview of its clients without making any predictions or drawing any conclusion about an individual. In this case, the purpose is not assessing individual characteristics and is therefore not profiling. The GDPR is inspired by but is not identical to the definition of profiling in the Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec (2010)132 (the Recommendation), as the Recommendation excludes processing that does not include inference. Nevertheless the Recommendation usefully explains that profiling may involve three distinct stages:  data collection;  automated analysis to identify correlations;  applying the correlation to an individual to identify characteristics of present or future behaviour. Controllers carrying out profiling will need to ensure they meet the GDPR requirements in respect of all of the above stages. Broadly speaking, profiling means gathering information about an individual (or group of individuals) and evaluating their characteristics or behaviour patterns in order to place them into a certain category or group, in particular to analyse and/or make predictions about, for example, their:  ability to perform a task;  interests; or  likely behaviour. 2 Council of Europe. The protection of individuals with regard to automatic processing of personal data in the context of profiling. Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)13 and explanatory memorandum. Council of Europe 23 November 2010. https://www.coe.int/t/dghl/standardsetting/cdcj/CDCJ%20Recommendations/CMRec(2010)13E_Profiling.pdf . Accessed 24 April 2017 8 Example A data broker collects data from different public and private sources, either on behalf of its clients or for its own purposes. The data broker compiles the data to develop profiles on the individuals and places them into segments. It sells this information to companies who wish to improve the targeting of their goods and services. The data broker carries out profiling by placing a person into a certain category according to their interests. Whether or not there is automated decision-making as defined in Article 22(1) will depend upon the circumstances. B. Automated decision-making Automated decision-making has a different scope and may partially overlap with or result from profiling. Solely automated decision-making is the ability to make decisions by technological means without human involvement. Automated decisions can be based on any type of data, for example:  data provided directly by the individuals concerned (such as responses to a questionnaire);  data observed about the individuals (such as location data collected via an application);  derived or inferred data such as a profile of the individual that has already been created (e.g. a credit score). Automated decisions can be made with or without profiling; profiling can take place without making automated decisions. However, profiling and automated decision-making are not necessarily separate activities. Something that starts off as a simple automated decision-making process could become one based on profiling, depending upon how the data is used. Example Imposing speeding fines purely on the basis of evidence from speed cameras is an automated decision- making process that does not necessarily involve profiling. It would, however, become a decision based on profiling if the driving habits of the individual were monitored over time, and, for example, the amount of fine imposed is the outcome of an assessment involving other factors,"

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[organization] Secretariat — The Secretariat is an administrative body that supports the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and undertakes several key functions, particularly in processing information and managing documentation. This entity reviews and analyzes the completeness of files, often on behalf of the Chair, and may request additional information from the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and/or Concerned Supervisory Authorities (CSAs) to remedy any omissions, especially when a binding decision is sought. The Secretariat is also responsible for evaluating redaction requirements, ensuring the right to be heard is afforded, and being informed of national decision notifications. Its duties further extend to translating documents into English, verifying objections, and referring matters to the EDPB. The Secretariat processes matters submitted to the EDPB, including those received from the LSA, and is involved in the procedure outlined in Article 11(2)(f) of the Rules of Procedure (RoP). Additionally, it performs notifications on behalf of the Chair.
The Secretariat assists the Board in its operations.
The Secretariat provides analytical, administrative, and logistical support to the Board and performs tasks exclusively under the instructions of the Board's Chair. It is provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor.

[concept] Accreditation Criteria — The standards and conditions a body must meet to be accredited to monitor codes of conduct.
Criteria for accreditation of bodies, approval of which requires an opinion from the Board as per Article 41(3) or Article 43(3).

[organization] Commission — The Commission, most often referring to the European Commission, is a central body within the European Union with extensive responsibilities and powers, particularly in relation to data protection, digital markets, and legal frameworks. It serves as a regulatory authority with the sole power to implement and enforce the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The Commission issues guidelines, such as those in accordance with Article 47 DMA, and is solely responsible for interpreting the DMA provisions covered by these guidelines. It can impose sanctions, conduct proceedings and investigations under the DMA, and is involved in the coherent enforcement of both the DMA and GDPR, cooperating with national authorities and possessing investigatory powers. Under the GDPR, the Commission plays a crucial role in developing a code of icons for standardized information and is empowered to adopt delegated acts to determine the information for these icons. It can also adopt Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to regulate data processing between controllers and processors and lay down such clauses more broadly. A key function includes making adequacy decisions regarding the level of data protection in third countries or international organizations for international data transfers. The Commission monitors these decisions, consults with the European Data Protection Board ("the Board" or EDPB), evaluates their functioning, and reports findings. It can also adopt delegated acts specifying criteria and requirements for certification mechanisms and standardized icons, and implementing acts for specifying technical standards for data protection certification and safeguards. It cooperates with supervisory authorities in third countries to develop international cooperation mechanisms regarding personal data protection, specifying formats and procedures for information exchange relating to Binding Corporate Rules and mutual assistance. Member States must notify the Commission of adopted laws and amendments related to data protection provisions, and the Commission receives Supervisory Authority activity reports. The Commission designates gatekeepers regarding Core Platform Services (CPSs) and recognizes adequacy for data transfers. It has legal powers to regulate data sharing under Article 6(11) DMA via an implementing act pursuant to Article 8(2) DMA. It may specify the ineligibility of potential third-party recipients and consult with other bodies to ensure compliance with DMA obligations. The Commission assesses whether a third country provides an adequate level of protection for personal data and sometimes considers the display of advertisements as part of online advertising CPS and other CPS. It receives audited descriptions of profiling techniques from gatekeepers and transmits them to the EDPB. The Commission participates in the Board's activities without voting rights, can designate a representative, and can request matters to be handled within the consistency mechanism, including requesting opinions from the Board. It is informed of Board decisions and receives communications from the Board Chair. Ultimately, the Commission is granted delegated power to adopt and notify delegated acts, prepare and submit reports, examine the application and functioning of the Regulation, request information, and submit proposals for the overall effectiveness and implementation of data protection regulations, cooperating with the EDPB and supervisory authorities to assess processing operations and consider guidelines for gatekeepers regarding interoperability and geographical limitations.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[concept] Processing — Processing, in the context of data management and privacy, encompasses any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or sets of personal data. These operations can be conducted through automated means or otherwise. This broad definition includes, but is not limited to, collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure, or destruction. The concept of processing extends to any act of handling or dealing with data, directly or indirectly, that has the potential to affect the interests and fundamental rights of data subjects. For operations involving personal data, it is crucial to determine specific purposes and means, often requiring consent from the data subject. A fundamental principle dictates that processing should be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. Processing activities can be performed by entities such as a controller or processor. Infringements related to operations involving personal data can lead to liability, damage, and potential legal proceedings.
Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction, as defined in Article 2(2) GDPR.

[method] Processing Operations — Processing Operations refer to any activities or a set of operations performed on data, particularly personal data, by institutions or data brokers. These operations encompass a vast array of actions, including the collection, storage, use, disclosure, further processing, the management of data subject rights, and the handling and manipulation of data. They can also involve linking data, forming different conducts, combining data, or cross-using data. Per Article 4(2) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), these operations are defined as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data or on sets of personal data. These operations are composed of various components, such as data, systems, and processes, all of which should adhere to specific criteria. Activities often include the selection of targeting criteria and the display of advertisements to a specific target audience. Processing operations are a primary object of certification under the GDPR, potentially encompassing governance processes and leading to the creation of a product or service. Both data controllers and processors are obligated to demonstrate compliance when executing these operations. Actions performed on personal data should be limited to what is necessary, contributing to a defined processing purpose, and designed to process only the minimum amount of necessary data. Processing operations are actions carried out by a data controller using collected data, requiring specific information provisions and legal bases. They may also benefit from special regimes under GDPR. Examples include the collection, storage, use, or deletion of data. Some operations may involve the use of CCTV and are subject to the applicability of the household exemption. Records must be maintained for these data handling activities. Furthermore, processing operations that involve personal data may require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR if they pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. When a DPIA is required, these activities necessitate a systematic description, an assessment of necessity, proportionality, and risks, and the implementation of measures to address those risks.
Processing Operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction.
Processing Operations involve any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, etc.
Actions or sets of actions performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, or disclosure.
Actions or sets of actions performed upon personal data, which supervisory authorities are generally competent to oversee, except for courts acting in judicial capacity.
Processing operations refer to any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, as defined in Article 4(2) GDPR.
Processing operations refer to activities involving personal data, such as combining or cross-using data.

[concept] Article 6(4) DMA — Article 6(4) of the DMA requires gatekeepers providing operating system core platform services to allow and technically enable the installation and effective use of third-party software applications or software application stores on their operating system.
This article pertains to the distribution of software application stores and applications, ensuring GDPR compliance.
Article 6(4) DMA outlines requirements for gatekeepers regarding the distribution of software application stores and software applications.
Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) outlines requirements for gatekeepers regarding third-party apps and app stores, including allowing installation, effective use, and enabling default settings, while also allowing for necessary and proportionate protective measures.
Article 6(4) of the DMA allows for certain measures to be put in place by gatekeepers, provided they do not undermine effective compliance.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Operating System — Software that needs to be kept up to date on various machines within a network as a security measure.
An operating system is a platform with which third-party apps or app stores may use or interoperate.
The core software that manages computer hardware and software resources, with which third-party apps and app stores must be allowed to interoperate.
An operating system is a fundamental software platform provided by gatekeepers that facilitates the functioning of hardware and applications.
A software system that manages computer hardware and software resources, within which gatekeepers allow access for apps and app stores.

[organization] Producers — Producers are entities that develop processing solutions (hardware, software, services, systems). They should demonstrate Data Protection by Design and Default (DPbDD) in their development life-cycle and facilitate controllers' needs.
Producers are key enablers for DPbDD, providing solutions to controllers that embed data protection.
Producers are responsible for developing, designing, selecting, and using applications, services, and products with regard to data protection.
[artifact] Optic-Electronic Devices — Optic-Electronic Devices are tools used for monitoring publicly accessible areas on a large scale.

[method] Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures — Targeted technical and organisational measures are efforts, possibly jointly with Article 6(4) DMA beneficiaries, to handle personal data breaches and restore data availability.

[organization] Online Social Network Operator — An online social network operator processes personal data, and such processing is subject to Article 9(1) and 9(2) GDPR.
An online social network operator processes personal data, and such processing is subject to Article 9(1) and 9(2) GDPR.
Under GDPR, Controller The controller must provide a way for human intervention in automated decisions. Human Intervention.

Under GDPR, Processing The processor performs the processing of personal data on behalf of the controller.<SEP>A processor is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>A Processor is involved in Processing and can be liable for damage caused by it. Processor.
Under GDPR, Controller The controller must communicate any rectification of personal data. Rectification of Personal Data.
Under GDPR, Processing Operations Processing Operations Security is concerned with the protection of processing operations. Processing Operations Security.
Under GDPR, Article 6(4) DMA Article 6(4) of the DMA allows measures to impede software that disables or alters operating system functioning. Software.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller may choose to document breaches as part of its Record of Processing Activities.<SEP>Each controller shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility. Record of Processing Activities.

Under GDPR, Optic-Electronic Devices Processing of Personal Data for monitoring publicly accessible areas on a large scale often involves the use of optic-electronic devices. Processing of Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller The Controller should have appropriate technical measures in place to ensure personal data security.<SEP>The controller should have internal processes and technical measures to detect and address breaches.<SEP>The controller should implement technical measures appropriate for data protection. Technical Measures.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. This relationship mandates that the Controller select Processors who offer sufficient guarantees regarding GDPR compliance. This relationship is formalized and governed by a legally binding contract or other legal act, often referred to as a processing agreement. This agreement details how GDPR requirements will be implemented, outlines specific obligations, and defines assistance duties. The Controller must provide documented instructions to the Processor on how to process personal data, and the Processor is obligated to comply. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. This assistance includes deleting or returning personal data at the Controller's choice, providing compliance information, and cooperating with Controller-conducted audits. A critical obligation for the Processor is to notify the Controller "without undue delay" upon becoming aware of a personal data breach it is processing on behalf of the Controller, as mandated by Article 33(2) GDPR. Processors must also notify the Controller of any request from a third-country authority without undue delay and follow the Controller's instructions, unless prohibited by law. The Processor is liable to the Controller for fulfilling these obligations. The Controller can authorize the use of sub-processors, but the Processor must obtain prior written authorization from the Controller for engaging another processor. The Processor is liable to the Controller for the sub-processors' adherence to data protection obligations. In scenarios involving data transfers, such as a third-country company (Controller) engaging a non-EEA processor, the processor acts as a data exporter on behalf of the Controller. The Controller must provide a comprehensive list of all data recipients, including processors. The relationship demands good faith cooperation, involving contract negotiation and management of audit and instruction processes. Controllers also carry out Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) with the processors. In some cases, the lead supervisory authority of the Controller may also become the lead supervisory authority for the Processor. When an end user qualifies as a Controller, an authorized third party may act as a Processor. Processor.
Under GDPR, Delivery Service Identification details may be cross-used by a delivery service without consent, under Article 5(2), point (c) DMA. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>The controller decides on the purposes and means of processing personal data.<SEP>A controller is involved in the same processing concerning data.<SEP>Any Controller involved in Processing shall be liable for damage caused by Processing which infringes this Regulation. Processing.
Under GDPR, Producers Producers should be encouraged to take into account the right to data protection when developing products, services, and applications. Right to Data Protection.
Under GDPR, Processor Each processor shall maintain a record of all categories of processing activities carried out on behalf of a controller. Record of Processing Activities.
Under GDPR, Accredited Monitoring Body An Accredited Monitoring Body monitors Processor compliance and takes action in cases of infringement. Processor.
Under GDPR, Data Processing Equipment The Supervisory Authority can obtain access to data processing equipment. Supervisory Authority.
Under GDPR, Personal Data Breaches Targeted technical and organisational measures are for the effective handling of personal data breaches. Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures.

Under GDPR, Processor Processors must implement technical measures to meet the requirements of the Regulation, including for the security of processing.<SEP>The processor implements appropriate technical and organisational measures and assists the controller in ensuring compliance with security measures. Technical Measures.
Under GDPR, Controller Codes of conduct recommend dispute resolution procedures for resolving disputes between controllers and data subjects. Dispute Resolution Procedures.
Under GDPR, Business User A business user may access performance data for providing customer support. Performance Data.
Under GDPR, Gatekeeper Gatekeepers may need to take measures, alone or jointly with developers, to handle personal data breaches. Personal Data Breaches.

Under GDPR, GDPR The relationship between GDPR and a Processor is characterized by specific obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities directly imposed upon the Processor by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). A processor is subject to the GDPR for any given processing operation, with its role and duties explicitly defined within the regulation. This subjection is set forth in Article 3 of the GDPR, which establishes its territorial scope and applicability, even extending to non-EEA processors when they are engaged by third-country companies. In such cases, these processors must also comply with Article 28 and Chapter V of the GDPR. The GDPR directly imposes various obligations on processors, detailing their responsibilities concerning personal data protection. Processors must ensure compliance with these requirements, particularly by adhering to the instructions provided by controllers. Key responsibilities include compliance with Article 30 (records of processing activities), Article 32 (security of processing), Article 35 (data protection impact assessment), and Article 36 (prior consultation with a supervisory authority) regarding risks. Processors are also subject to GDPR obligations relating to their liability for sub-processors, as outlined in Article 28(4). Furthermore, the GDPR requires processors to implement appropriate security measures and outlines their obligations regarding data breaches and notifications, including the requirement to notify any breach to their controller. Supervisory Authorities (SAs) have the power to take action against a processor for infringing GDPR provisions. The regulation categorizes various infringements that can lead to fines for processors. Certifications under the GDPR are also issued to data processors, further emphasizing their direct accountability and the regulatory oversight they are subject to. These collective requirements define the responsibility and liability of the processor under the GDPR.<SEP>The GDPR, specifically Article 60(10), imposes duties on the processor.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for ensuring data processing adheres to GDPR provisions.<SEP>The Processor is responsible for compliance with the GDPR and must be able to demonstrate it.<SEP>The processing by a processor is governed by a contract or legal act that ensures compliance with GDPR articles. Processor.

Under GDPR, Controller If consent is withdrawn, the controller must stop processing operations based on that consent.<SEP>The controller is responsible for maintaining records of processing operations. Processing Operations.
Under GDPR, Auditor The processor must make information available and contribute to audits conducted by the auditor. Processor.
Under GDPR, Processing Activities The processor should maintain records of processing activities under its responsibility. Processor.
Under GDPR, Article 33 GDPR Targeted technical and organisational measures ensure compliance with Article 33 of the GDPR. Targeted Technical and Organisational Measures.
Under GDPR, Damage Processing that infringes this Regulation can cause Damage to a person. Processing.
Under GDPR, Gatekeeper Gatekeepers may have processors of personal data within their corporate structure. Processor.
Under GDPR, Personal Data Personal data can be processed for the purposes of planning and organisation of work. Planning and Organisation of Work.
Under GDPR, Board The secretariat of the Board provides translations for relevant information to the Board. Secretariat of the Board.
Under GDPR, Online Search Engine The third-party undertaking requesting access is often one providing an online search engine. Third-Party Undertaking Requesting Access.

Gatekeepers’ measures designed to safeguard the integrity of the gatekeeper’s hardware or operating system and/or applied to enable end users to protect their security from being undermined in accordance with Article 6(4) DMA are consistent with the gatekeepers’ obligation under Article 32 of the GDPR to ensure a level of security of personal data appropriate to the risk. 95. result.reason: **Hochschule registrieren** involves the registration of a university ('Hochschule') within a centralized system (likely **DoSV**, the German *Dialogorientiertes Serviceverfahren* for university admissions). Registration processes in an **employment or education context** inherently require the collection, storage, and transmission of **personal data**—such as institutional identifiers, contact details of administrative staff, or credentials for system access. Under **Article 88 GDPR**, member states may provide specific rules for processing employees' or applicants' personal data in contexts like **recruitment, management, or organisation of work**. Since this task is a prerequisite for enabling student application workflows (which involve processing applicants' personal data), it indirectly supports a system where **personal data of students (e.g., names, academic records, identification numbers)** will later be processed. The activity thus enables the **processing of personal data** in a **recruitment/education** context, as defined in the retrieved GDPR knowledge under '[method] Recruitment' and '[data] Personal Data'.

**Hochschule einrichten** involves setting up the university’s operational parameters within the DoSV system. This task likely includes configuring **user accounts, access permissions, or institutional profiles**—all of which require the processing of **personal data** (e.g., names, roles, contact details of administrative staff, or authentication credentials). As part of the **management and organisation of work** in an **employment/education context**, this activity falls under **Article 88 GDPR**, which explicitly covers processing for purposes like **management, planning, and organisation of work**. The task enables the subsequent handling of **applicants' personal data** (e.g., during admissions), making it GDPR-relevant.

**HIS-DoSV Konnektor einrichten** involves setting up a technical connector to the **DoSV system**, which is the centralized platform for university admissions in Germany. This connector will later be used to **transmit, receive, and process applicants' personal data** (e.g., names, addresses, academic records, identification numbers). The activity itself requires configuring **authentication credentials, institutional identifiers, or API keys**, which may include **personal data of administrative staff** (e.g., usernames, roles). As this task directly enables the **transfer of personal data** between systems in an **education/recruitment context**, it is GDPR-relevant under **Article 4(2) GDPR** (definition of processing) and **Article 88 GDPR** (employment context).

**Studienpakete übermitteln** (Transmit study packages) involves sending **study program data** to applicants or other systems. While the name does not explicitly mention personal data, in the context of university admissions, 'Studienpakete' (study packages) typically include **personalized information for applicants**, such as: **Applicant names/IDs** (to address the package), **Academic prerequisites or eligibility status** (linked to the individual), **Contact details** (for delivery or follow-up), **Admission decisions or conditional offers** (directly tied to the applicant’s personal/academic profile). Transmitting such packages constitutes **disclosure of personal data** under **Article 4(2) GDPR**, as it involves **transferring information relating to identified or identifiable natural persons** (applicants). The activity is thus GDPR-relevant.

**Ranglistenköpfe übermitteln** (Transmit ranking headers) refers to sending the **top-ranked applicants' data** (or metadata about rankings) to another system or party. In the context of university admissions, 'Ranglistenköpfe' (ranking headers) inherently include **personal data** such as: **Applicant names/IDs** (to identify ranked individuals), **Academic performance metrics** (grades, test scores—linked to the individual), **Priority or waitlist status** (tied to the applicant’s profile). Transmitting this information constitutes **processing of personal data** under **Article 4(2) GDPR**, as it involves **disclosing identifiable information about natural persons** (applicants). The activity is GDPR-relevant, particularly as it may also involve **profiling or automated decision-making** (ranking applicants).

**Online-Bewerbung konfigurieren** (Configure online application) involves setting up the **digital application portal** for prospective students. This task necessarily includes defining: **Data fields for personal information** (e.g., name, address, date of birth, contact details), **Upload requirements for personal documents** (e.g., CVs, certificates, IDs), **Authentication mechanisms** (e.g., login credentials tied to applicants). Configuring such a portal directly enables the **collection, storage, and processing of applicants' personal data**, as defined under **Article 4(1) and (2) GDPR**. The activity is thus GDPR-relevant, as it prepares the infrastructure for **large-scale processing of personal data** in a **recruitment/education context**.

**Bewerbungs-portal freischalten** (Activate application portal) involves enabling the **online system** where applicants submit their **personal data** (e.g., names, addresses, academic records, IDs). Activating the portal is the final step before **collecting and processing applicants' personal data** at scale. Under **Article 4(2) GDPR**, 'processing' includes **enabling the collection or storage of personal data**, even if the activity itself does not directly handle the data. As this task is a prerequisite for **recruitment processing**, it is GDPR-relevant.

**Studiengangs-informationen anbieten** (Offer study program information) may appear administrative, but in the context of this process, it likely involves **personalized communication** with applicants or prospective students. Offering study information could include: Sending **targeted emails or notifications** to applicants (using their contact details), Providing **individualized program recommendations** based on applicants' profiles (e.g., prior education, interests), Using **tracking mechanisms** (e.g., click behavior on links) to monitor engagement. If the activity involves **using applicants' personal data** (e.g., email addresses, academic history) to tailor or deliver information, it constitutes **processing of personal data** under **Article 4(1) and (2) GDPR**. The context of the surrounding recruitment process strongly suggests this is the case.

**Hochschul-eigene Auswahl definieren** (Define university-specific selection) involves setting the **criteria and rules** for admitting applicants. While this task itself may not directly handle personal data, it defines the **parameters for processing applicants' personal data** during selection (e.g., weighting of grades, quotas, or prioritization rules). The selection criteria will later be applied to **identifiable individuals' records** (e.g., academic transcripts, IDs), making this activity a **preparatory step for profiling or automated decision-making** under **Article 4(4) and Article 22 GDPR**. As such, it is GDPR-relevant because it **enables the subsequent processing of personal data** in a structured manner.

**Vergabeordnung abbilden** (Map allocation regulations) involves implementing the **rules for assigning study places** to applicants. This activity requires processing **applicants' personal and academic data** to apply criteria such as: **Grade-based rankings** (linked to individual applicants), **Quotas or priorities** (e.g., for specific groups, tied to personal attributes like disability status or residency), **Waitlist management** (tracking applicants' positions and identities). The task directly involves **evaluating and structuring personal data** to make admission decisions, which qualifies as **processing** under **Article 4(2) GDPR**. It may also involve **automated decision-making** (Article 22) if rules are applied algorithmically.

**Umfang der Unterstützungs-leistungen festlegen** (Determine scope of support services) likely involves defining **services for applicants or students**, such as: **Counseling or advisory services** (requiring access to applicants' personal/academic data), **Financial aid or scholarships** (processing sensitive data like income, family status, or disabilities), **Accommodations for disabilities** (handling **special categories of personal data** under **Article 9 GDPR**). Even if the task itself does not directly process personal data, it **defines the framework for subsequent processing** of sensitive information tied to identifiable individuals. As such, it is GDPR-relevant, particularly if support services involve **special categories of data** (e.g., health or ethnic origin).

**Studiengänge definieren** (Define study programs) may appear administrative, but in the context of university admissions, it often involves: **Specifying admission requirements** tied to applicants' personal/academic data (e.g., 'applicants with a 2.5 GPA or higher'), **Setting quotas or priorities** based on personal attributes (e.g., residency, gender, or disability status), **Linking programs to applicants' profiles** (e.g., restricting certain programs to specific groups). If the definition of study programs includes **rules that reference or categorize applicants' personal data**, the activity enables **profiling or structured processing** of such data, making it GDPR-relevant under **Article 4(4) GDPR** (profiling) and **Article 6 GDPR** (lawfulness of processing).

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[Source: General_Data_Protection_Regulation_en] "Processing in the context of employment 1. Member States may, by law or by collective agreements, provide for more specific rules to ensure the protection of the rights and freedoms in respect of the processing of employees' personal data in the employment context, in particular for the purposes of the recruitment, the performance of the contract of employment, including discharge of obligations laid down by law or by collective agreements, management, planning and organisation of work, equality and diversity in the workplace, health and safety at work, protection of employer's or customer's property and for the purposes of the exercise and enjoyment, on an individual or collective basis, of rights and benefits related to employment, and for the purpose of the termination of the employment relationship. 2. Those rules shall include suitable and specific measures to safeguard the data subject's human dignity, legitimate interests and fundamental rights, with particular regard to the transparency of processing, the transfer of personal data within a group of undertakings, or a group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity and monitoring systems at the work place. 3. Each Member State shall notify to the Commission those provisions of its law which it adopts pursuant to paragraph 1, by 25 May 2018 and, without delay, any subsequent amendment affecting them. Article 89 Safeguards and derogations relating to processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes 1. Processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes, shall be subject to appropriate safeguards, in accordance with this Regulation, for the rights and freedoms of the data subject. Those safeguards shall ensure that technical and organisational measures are in place in particular in 4.5.2016 L 119/84 Official Journal of the European Union EN order to ensure respect for the principle of data minimisation. Those measures may include pseudonymisation provided that those purposes can be fulfilled in that manner. Identifying a lead supervisory authority is only relevant where a controller or processor is carrying out the cross-border processing of personal data. Article 4(23) of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) defines ‘cross-border processing’ as either the: - processing of personal data which takes place in the context of the activities of establishments in more than one Member State of a controller or processor in the Union where the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State; or the - processing of personal data which takes place in the context of the activities of a single establishment of a controller or processor in the Union but which substantially affects or is likely to substantially affect data subjects in more than one Member State. This means that where an organisation has establishments in France and Romania, for example, and the processing of personal data takes place in the context of their activities, then this will constitute cross-border processing. Alternatively, the organisation may only carry out processing activity in the context of its establishment in France. However, if the activity substantially affects – or is likely to substantially affect - data subjects in France and Romania then this will also constitute cross- border processing. 1.1.1 ‘Substantially affects’. The GDPR does not define ‘substantially’ or ‘affects’. The intention of the wording was to ensure that not all processing activity, with any effect and that takes place within the context of a single establishment, falls within the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. The most relevant ordinary English meanings of ‘substantial’ include; ‘of ample or considerable amount or size; sizeable, fairly large’, or ‘having solid worth or value, of real significance; solid; weighty, important’ (Oxford English Dictionary). The most relevant meaning of the verb ‘affect’ is ‘to influence’ or ‘to make a material impression on’. The related noun -‘effect’- means, amongst other things, ‘a result’ or ‘a consequence’ (Oxford English Dictionary). This suggests that for data processing to affect someone it must have some form of impact on them. Processing that does not have a substantial effect on individuals does not fall within the second part of the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. However, it would fall within the first part of the definition where the processing of personal data takes place in the context of the activities of establishments in more than one Member State of a controller or processor in the Union, where the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State. Processing can be brought within the second part of the definition if there is the likelihood of a substantial effect, not just an actual substantial effect. Note that ‘likely to’ does not mean that there is a remote possibility of a substantial effect. The substantial effect must be more likely than not. ragPromptContext: [organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Accountability — Accountability, as a fundamental principle primarily introduced and explicitly required by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), mandates that data controllers are responsible for ensuring and demonstrating compliance with all data protection principles and measures. This principle extends beyond mere adherence, requiring controllers to actively prove their compliance efforts and justify decisions regarding data processing, potentially to a supervisory authority. Under GDPR, accountability is an overarching principle, intrinsically linked with transparency and fairness, and is considered a key component of data protection by design and default (DPbD). It places the onus on controllers to select and implement necessary technical and organizational measures to protect data. While centrally focused on demonstrating compliance, accountability also encompasses concepts related to documenting breaches and highlights the significant role of the data protection officer in these processes. Data exporters are also explicitly required to demonstrate compliance under this principle.

Under GDPR, Controller The (Controller, Processor) relationship describes an arrangement, primarily defined by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), where a Processor handles personal data on behalf of a Controller. The Controller retains the primary and ultimate responsibility for ensuring overall compliance with data protection principles, including data protection by design and by default (DPbDD), and this accountability extends to any Processor and sub-processors involved. The Processor processes personal data only on these documented instructions. Even without a written agreement, the existence and definition of this relationship hold. The Processor has various duties, including assisting the Controller in fulfilling obligations related to data subject rights and Articles 32 to 36 of the GDPR, ensuring compliance with data protection obligations, and reporting to the Controller. Adopted 23 IV. ASSESSING RISK AND HIGH RISK A. Risk as a trigger for notification 100. Although the GDPR introduces the obligation to notify a breach, it is not a requirement to do so in all circumstances: • Notification to the competent supervisory authority is required unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. • Communication of a breach to the individual is only triggered where it is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. 101. This means that immediately upon becoming aware of a breach, it is vitally important that the controller should not only seek to contain the incident but it should also assess the risk that could result from it. There are two important reasons for this: firstly, knowing the likelihood and the potential severity of the impact on the individual will help the controller to take effective steps to contain and address the breach; secondly, it will help it to determine whether notification is required to the supervisory authority and, if necessary, to the individuals concerned. 102. As explained above, notification of a breach is required unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, and the key trigger requiring communication of a breach to data subjects is where it is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. This risk exists when the breach may lead to physical, material or non-material damage for the individuals whose data have been breached. Examples of such damage are discrimination, identity theft or fraud, financial loss and damage to reputation. When the breach involves personal data that reveals racial or ethnic origin, political opinion, religion or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, or includes genetic data, data concerning health or data concerning sex life, or criminal convictions and offences or related security measures, such damage should be considered likely to occur43. B. Factors to consider when assessing risk 103. Recitals 75 and 76 of the GDPR suggest that generally when assessing risk, consideration should be given to both the likelihood and severity of the risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. It further states that risk should be evaluated on the basis of an objective assessment. 104. It should be noted that assessing the risk to people’s rights and freedoms as a result of a breach has a different focus to the risk considered in a DPIA)44. The DPIA considers both the risks of the data processing being carried out as planned, and the risks in case of a breach. When considering a potential breach, it looks in general terms at the likelihood of this occurring, and the damage to the data subject that might ensue; in other words, it is an assessment of a hypothetical event. With an actual breach, the event has already occurred, and so the focus is wholly about the resulting risk of the impact of the breach on individuals.
