[location] Third Country — A "Third Country" is a nation or geographical region situated outside the jurisdiction of both the European Union (EU) and the European Economic Area (EEA), or more broadly, any country outside the territorial scope of specific data protection regulations. This designation is particularly relevant in the context of international transfers of personal data, especially under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Personal data originating from the EU/EEA may be transferred to and processed within a Third Country. However, such transfers are subject to stringent conditions and safeguards as outlined in Chapter V of the GDPR. This is due to the potential for different, and possibly inadequate, legal frameworks for data protection in these jurisdictions compared to GDPR standards. The European Commission assesses the level of personal data protection in Third Countries to determine if they offer an adequate level of protection. Entities, including public bodies, involved in data transfers to a Third Country must adhere to GDPR regulations, implement appropriate safeguards, and sometimes provide specific information to data subjects before data is transferred. The potential risks associated with data processing in a Third Country can be elevated, including concerns about disproportionate government access to data. Supervisory Authorities may have jurisdiction over these transfers and, in some cases, may even suspend data flows to a Third Country.
A third country is a nation outside the EEA to which personal data may be transferred, subject to adequacy decisions or consent.

Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Lead Supervisory Authority is central to the oversight of cross-border data processing, particularly under regulations such as the GDPR. The Lead Supervisory Authority is identified for a Controller primarily based on its central administration or the location where decisions concerning processing are made. In situations involving both a Controller and a Processor, the Lead Supervisory Authority for the Controller typically assumes the role for both, as outlined in Recital 36. Furthermore, the supervisory authority of a Member State where a Controller's main establishment is located often acts as the competent Lead Supervisory Authority. This authority is competent to supervise cross-border processing activities conducted by a Controller. A key responsibility of the Controller in this relationship is to notify the Lead Supervisory Authority in the event of breaches involving cross-border processing. Beyond notification, the Lead Supervisory Authority serves as the sole interlocutor for the Controller regarding cross-border processing, meaning the Controller interacts exclusively with this authority. The Lead Supervisory Authority is responsible for adopting and notifying decisions to the Controller, who, in turn, is obligated to take measures to ensure compliance with these decisions. Note that ‘likely to’ does not mean that there is a remote possibility of a substantial effect. The substantial effect must be more likely than not. On the other hand, it also means that individuals do not have to be actually 4 affected: the likelihood of a substantial effect is sufficient to bring the processing within the definition of ‘cross-border processing’. The fact that a data processing operation may involve the processing of a number – even a large number – of individuals’ personal data, in a number of Member States, does not necessarily mean that the processing has, or is likely to have, a substantial effect. Processing that does not have a substantial effect does not constitute cross-border processing for the purposes of the second part of the definition, regardless of how many individuals it affects. Supervisory Authorities will interpret ‘substantially affects’ on a case by case basis. We will take into account the context of the processing, the type of data, the purpose of the processing and factors such as whether the processing: o causes, or is likely to cause, damage, loss or distress to individuals; o has, or is likely to have, an actual effect in terms of limiting rights or denying an opportunity; o affects, or is likely to affect individuals’ health, well-being or peace of mind; o affects, or is likely to affect, individuals’ financial or economic status or circumstances; o leaves individuals open to discrimination or unfair treatment; o involves the analysis of the special categories of personal or other intrusive data, particularly the personal data of children; o causes, or is likely to cause individuals to change their behaviour in a significant way; o has unlikely, unanticipated or unwanted consequences for individuals; o creates embarrassment or other negative outcomes, including reputational damage; or o involves the processing of a wide range of personal data. Ultimately, the test of ‘substantial effect’ is intended to ensure that supervisory authorities are only required to co-operate formally through the GDPR’s consistency mechanism "where a supervisory authority intends to adopt a measure intended to produce legal effects as regards processing operations which substantially affect a significant number of data subjects in several Member States”. ragPromptContext: [concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[data] Personal Data — Personal Data is defined as any information related to an identified or identifiable natural person, often referred to as a "data subject." This encompasses a broad range of details, varying in sensitivity, volume, and context, that can be observed, inferred, or collected. Examples include names, identification numbers, online identifiers, age, gender, geographic location, website activity, interests, sociographic information, behavior, and pictorial or audio-visual data. It can be directly or indirectly identifiable and exist in physical forms, such as paper. Additional examples include technical interoperability data, message content, search queries, language, content preferences, topics of interest, ranking, query, click, and view data. Specific health data like fitness and calorie intake, and information from connected vehicles pertaining to drivers and passengers, also fall under this definition. Certain categories of Personal Data, such as medical history, clinical treatment, physiological or biomedical state, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, health status, sexual orientation, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning criminal convictions and offenses, are considered special categories that require specific protection. Personal Data also includes information concerning natural persons collected from or about them, including identifiers and factors specific to their identity. The processing of Personal Data, which includes activities like collection, storage, transfer, and use, is stringently regulated by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). These regulations emphasize potential risks to individual rights and freedoms, mandating that any information capable of identifying an individual falls under their purview. Key principles guiding its use include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, adequacy, necessity, proportionality, and data minimization. Data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and limited to what is necessary, with its processing subject to specific rules and safeguards. Data subjects or end-users have rights over this information, including portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. The processing purposes and legal basis, such as explicit consent, for handling Personal Data, including salaries and medical information, must always be clear, and storage periods vary based on data categories and processing purposes, determined by the data controller. Special protection is afforded to children's Personal Data. Entities such as retailers, social media providers, advertisers, banking services, and "gatekeepers" (as defined by regulations) are subject to these regulations when processing Personal Data about employees, customers, or applicants, or data from public registries. This data is frequently used for creating profiles, defining targeting criteria, targeted and behavioral advertising, campaign reporting, training AI models, and automated decision-making. Such processing often requires a valid legal basis, and many digital services require this data to function, prompting explicit disclosure and authorization when an application collects it. Due to inherent privacy risks, Personal Data necessitates careful handling and may be subject to delisting requests. In connected vehicles, Personal Data collected through in-vehicle applications demands user control and privacy considerations and must be deleted upon vehicle ownership change if no longer needed. Personal Data is subject to stringent transfer requirements, especially when sent by an exporter to an importer in a third country or international organization, or when processed outside the EU, requiring appropriate safeguards. Any further use involves specific information and compatibility obligations under GDPR. Regulations mandate its protection through appropriate technical and organizational measures, privacy-enhancing technologies, and default settings to ensure the highest possible security level, safeguarding against unauthorized processing, loss, destruction, or damage. Its processing is also subject to transparency, storage limitations, and accessibility controls, often employing pseudonymization. It is encouraged to be stored in a structured, machine-readable format to support reuse and portability, with choices and explanations provided to the data subject. When shared by gatekeepers or undergoing processing by automated means, it requires anonymization, as outlined in GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9). Gatekeepers are responsible for protecting it against unauthorized disclosure and ensuring its secure transmission, requiring explicit consent for international transfers or sharing with third parties. Breaches involving Personal Data can lead to significant adverse effects on individuals, including loss of control, identity theft, financial loss, and damage to reputation. This information, which may be encrypted or exfiltrated during a breach, is subject to internal security handling and risk mitigation measures. Its exfiltration, sensitivity, volume, and context are factored into risk assessments and constitute a data breach, triggering notification obligations under regulations like GDPR, though if securely encrypted, notification to an authority may not be required. If disclosed to unauthorized parties, it can lead to a confidentiality breach and potential risk to individuals. Processing of Personal Data about natural persons, especially when on a large scale or involving regular and systematic monitoring, may lead to the need for Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) and can necessitate the designation of a Data Protection Officer (DPO), with processing operations determining the required level of DPO expertise. Personal data is often processed in a cross-border manner, making the identification of a lead supervisory authority relevant. Data subjects have the right to portability over this information, including data provided by them, inferred data, and derived data. Overall, Personal Data requires protection through legislation, investigations, and international cooperation, particularly concerning transfers to third countries and processing activities.

[person] Personnel — Individuals who have permanent or regular access to personal data and require training and education on data protection.
Individuals who have permanent or regular access to personal data and require appropriate periodic training and education.
Personnel involved in a job interview process are data subjects who often expect some of their personal data to be shared with job applicants.

[method] Anonymisation — Anonymisation is a fundamental process and set of techniques designed to transform personal data in such a way that the data subject can no longer be identified, either directly or indirectly. This alteration ensures that the data cannot be linked back to an individual, even with reasonable effort. It is employed when personal data is deleted or anonymized following the withdrawal of consent, acting as a crucial safeguard in data processing, particularly for research purposes where the objective can be achieved without handling identifiable data. This process involves carefully processing data, such as location information, to prevent re-identification, a task that is complex and necessitates transparency regarding the methodologies used. The goal of anonymisation extends beyond simply removing identifying information to also preserving the quality and usefulness of the data for its intended purpose. It is a preferred solution and safeguard, recognized by regulations like the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically Article 6(11), and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which require the rendering of personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy. In essence, anonymisation serves as a vital method for making shared personal data suitable for use while upholding the privacy of individuals.
Anonymization is a method by which shared data that constitutes personal data is processed to remove identifying information.
Anonymisation is a method of altering personal data so that the data subject is no longer identifiable, with the goal of preserving data quality and usefulness.
Anonymisation is the process of altering personal data to prevent direct or indirect identification of end users, required for data shared under Article 6(11) DMA.
Anonymisation is the process of rendering personal data anonymous to protect end-user privacy, as required by DMA and GDPR.

Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Lehrenden- daten aktualisieren (sid-8246F1A1-3540-48CD-AA7D-E982C554A4DF)**: The activity 'Lehrendendaten aktualisieren' (Update lecturer data) processes personal data because it involves updating records related to lecturers, who are identifiable natural persons. Under GDPR, employees' personal data (e.g., names, contact details, employment records, qualifications, or contractual information) is explicitly protected (Article 4(1) GDPR). Updating such records constitutes processing as defined by GDPR (e.g., 'organising, structuring, or altering' data). [organization] Gatekeeper — A Gatekeeper is an entity designated under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), specifically pursuant to Article 3(4) or Article 3(9), indicating its provision of Core Platform Services (CPSs). Prominent examples of such organizations include Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta. These Gatekeepers control access to specific digital services and are subject to extensive legal obligations under the DMA, and in many cases, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Their role is central to the regulatory framework designed to ensure fair and contestable digital markets. Gatekeepers process the personal data of end users, often acting as controllers or processors, and are responsible for ensuring that consent obtained for data processing, particularly for online advertising and data combination, complies with both GDPR and DMA requirements. This includes the meticulous recording of consent refusals or withdrawals. They are obligated to enable continuous and real-time access to data, prevent data accumulation, and ensure robust data security. Their responsibilities extend to providing data upon request by business users or authorized third parties, free of charge, and establishing appropriate authentication and authorization procedures for such access. They must also implement security measures for personal data, comply with portability requests under DMA Article 6(9), and provide comprehensive information to data subjects. Furthermore, Gatekeepers are tasked with selecting and implementing anonymization methods for end-user data shared under Article 6(11) DMA and must implement measures to maintain service integrity and security. They also have duties concerning interoperability, including exchanging message content and personal data with other providers while ensuring security for their end users. This includes protecting metadata, verifying communication authenticity, and ensuring compliance with geographical limitations and data protection regulations for Number-Independent Interpersonal Communication Services (NIICS). Gatekeepers must design online interfaces that do not undermine user autonomy, provide reminders, and ensure fair access to datasets by altering data to mitigate identification risks and imposing contractual measures on third-party undertakings for data access and compliance monitoring. Their conduct is subject to examination for compliance with both the DMA and GDPR, and they may have a "main establishment" under the GDPR. They are also separate controllers under GDPR for their own data processing and have obligations under Article 6(4) and Article 8(1) of the DMA.

[concept] Consent — Consent, as defined by Regulations 2016/679 (GDPR), particularly under Articles 4(11), 6(1)(a), and 7, is a fundamental legal basis for the processing of personal data. It signifies a freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's or end user's wishes, demonstrated by a clear, affirmative action, agreeing to the processing of their personal data for specified purposes. This applies to various data handling scenarios, including direct information retrieval, targeted advertising, processing of location data, or the storing/accessing of information on their devices. It is also an alternative legal basis for direct marketing activities when legitimate interest is not applicable and a legal ground for processing sensitive data, such as health or biometric data, under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. For consent to be valid, it must adhere to strict conditions: it must be given freely, without coercion, intimidation, deception, or negative consequences for withholding it. It must also be specific, informed, and granular, ensuring the data subject fully understands what data will be processed, for what purposes, and by whom. This comprehensiveness is crucial, and it grants data subjects control over their personal data processing. Consent is a reversible decision, easily withdrawable at any time. While essential for various data handling scenarios and mandated by regulations like the ePrivacy Directive and the Digital Markets Act (DMA) for certain operations, such as electronic communications or specific tracking techniques, obtaining valid consent can be particularly challenging in complex contexts, including connected vehicles. Consent also holds significance for data portability and international transfers of personal data, especially to third countries without an adequacy decision. Furthermore, it is a key condition for certain derogations under Article 49(1)(a), requiring explicit agreement for proposed transfers. It is a requirement for gatekeepers to enable data sharing but is generally not legally feasible for silent party data as per Article 6 of the GDPR. Despite its importance, obtaining valid consent does not diminish the controller's obligations under the GDPR. In broader contexts, the overarching obligation of endeavoring to reach consensus places concomitant obligations on both the LSA and other CSAs. Consent is a key requirement under DMA and GDPR, requiring an explicit, clear, and straightforward user experience, particularly for cross-use of personal data, and can be refused or withdrawn.
A clear affirmative act establishing a freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of a data subject's agreement to personal data processing.

[organization] Certification Bodies — Certification Bodies are organizations that play a crucial role in establishing and maintaining certification mechanisms, particularly in the context of data protection. These entities are responsible for drafting, presenting, and revising the criteria used for the approval of various certification mechanisms. They possess appropriate data protection expertise and are tasked with performing certification activities. Furthermore, Certification Bodies are accredited to issue and renew certifications, ensuring that products, services, or systems meet specific requirements. They are often referred to as conformity assessment bodies. Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), specifically Article 42(1) and Article 43, these organizations are subject to accreditation by supervisory authorities or national accreditation bodies. Their functions include determining data protection certification criteria and, in some instances, being responsible for accrediting data protection certification mechanisms and seals.

[person] Natural Person — A Natural Person is fundamentally an individual human being, distinct from a legal entity. This individual's actions can be attributed to an undertaking unless they are acting solely for private or purely personal purposes, or as a separate controller. Activities that are purely personal or household in nature, especially when processed without data transfer to a controller or processor, generally fall outside the scope of the GDPR. Natural persons are subjects whose personal data is protected under regulations such as the GDPR. This means their personal data, including sensitive information like physical or mental health data (considered "data concerning health"), may be processed by a controller. They are also individuals whose personal data can be evaluated through profiling and whose vital interests may necessitate protection through personal data processing. Crucially, a natural person is an individual human being whose rights and freedoms are subject to high risk. To safeguard these rights, individuals have the right to an effective judicial remedy. Specifically, they have an effective judicial remedy before the competent national court against final decisions by supervisory authorities that produce legal effects for them. They may also be concerned by a decision and potentially have had the opportunity to bring an action for annulment.
A natural person is an identifiable individual, as defined by GDPR, whose data is protected.

[organization] Supervisory Authorities — Supervisory Authorities (SAs) are independent national public bodies primarily tasked with overseeing the application and enforcement of data protection law, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), within their respective countries. Their foundational mission involves protecting the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects while also facilitating the free flow of personal data within the European Union. These authorities play a crucial role in monitoring adherence to data protection principles, advising on and documenting proportionality and necessity tests, and ensuring the consistent application of data protection principles and individual rights. They evaluate data processing features and assess compliance, including with Article 25 of the GDPR. They are also responsible for establishing and publicizing lists of processing operations that require a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). SAs are also responsible for monitoring and ensuring compliance with data protection rules, possessing equivalent powers and sanctions across the Union. Supervisory Authorities are endowed with significant enforcement powers under GDPR Article 58, allowing them to issue corrective measures and impose administrative fines for infringements. These fines are expected to be effective, dissuasive, and proportionate, adjusted based on aggravating and mitigating factors. Both data controllers and processors are directly accountable to these authorities for GDPR compliance. Past decisions based on Directive 95/46/EC remain in force until amended or repealed. Beyond enforcement, SAs handle and investigate complaints from data subjects, including those related to search engine providers' refusal to erase search results under Article 17 GDPR, and are responsible for assessing delisting requests. They also encourage the development of codes of conduct and foster certification mechanisms, potentially acting as certification bodies themselves, and approving criteria and issuing certifications, as well as receiving reasons for granting or withdrawing certification from certification bodies and making requirements and criteria for certification public. SAs have powers to obtain access to personal data and premises from data controllers or processors. Their competence does not extend to courts acting in their judicial capacity. Supervisory Authorities have a legal obligation to cooperate, exchange information, and endeavor to reach consensus, especially within the "One Stop Shop" (OSS) model and obligations under Article 60 of the GDPR. This involves coordinating through draft decisions, where other Supervisory Authorities (CSAs) receive relevant information and draft decisions from the Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) and provide feedback. They are considered fully acquainted with notified decisions and take decisions on issues handled in the consistency mechanism, which are registered by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). Instances of conflicting views among Supervisory Authorities can lead to EDPB decisions, demonstrating their cooperative yet authoritative role in ensuring GDPR compliance and consistency across the EU. Supervisory Authorities are stakeholders with whom Data Protection Officers (DPOs) act as intermediaries, and data subjects and DPOs can contact them for data protection matters, with DPO contact details and name communicated to them. They are also involved in the exchange of information with controllers, processors, and the Board regarding binding corporate rules and mutual assistance, and cooperate to ensure the consistent application of the Regulation and communicate with the Board, promoting cooperation, information exchange, and training. They are regulatory bodies responsible for interpreting and enforcing data protection regulations, including assessing "substantial effect" on a case-by-case basis.
Supervisory authorities are responsible for overseeing data protection and cooperate with the Commission and EDPB.

Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relationship between a Controller and a Data Subject is governed by a framework of rights, obligations, and legal considerations, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Controller is authorized to process a Data Subject's personal data, frequently through contractual agreements, and is obligated to provide essential, timely, and clear information regarding these processing operations, as stipulated in GDPR Article 14(2)(b) and (f). This includes notifying Data Subjects of personal data breaches, especially if they pose a high risk to their rights and freedoms, as mentioned in Article 34 of the GDPR. Controllers are legally mandated to facilitate the easy and full exercise of data protection rights by Data Subjects, ensuring these rights can be exercised without undue hindrance and by providing a simple mechanism for their exercise. This also entails addressing requests for data erasure or objections to processing, and informing Data Subjects about changes and facilitating access to information. For specific activities like processing biometric data, the Controller must obtain explicit, informed, and freely given consent. Transparency from the Controller is also required concerning profiling and automated decision-making processes that impact the Data Subject. In all data processing activities, the Controller must carefully consider the Data Subject's interests, fundamental rights, and freedoms, acknowledging the direct impact of their actions. This assessment varies depending on the specific relationship (e.g., employer-employee, service provider-customer) and the Data Subject's particular situation. In situations involving potential surveillance, the Controller must consider the Data Subject's objection and can only proceed if there is a compelling legitimate interest or for legal claims, also assessing the Data Subject's intention to make data public. When applying the household exemption, key considerations include the Controller’s personal relationship with the Data Subject, the scale and frequency of surveillance, and any potential adverse impact it might have. There must be a balancing exercise between the competing interests of the Controller and the Data Subject's objection, with the burden of proof on the Controller. A significant imbalance, as noted in Recital 47 of the GDPR, can compromise the freedom of consent, and Controllers have been known to attempt to influence Data Subjects for more extensive data collection. It is paramount that the fundamental rights and freedoms of Data Subjects are not overridden by the Controller’s interests, even when a relevant and appropriate relationship exists (e.g., client or in the service of the controller). Controllers must provide clear information to Data Subjects to allow them to correct inaccuracies and select a method for providing information that is appropriate to the manner in which the Data Controller and Data Subject interact. The Controller is responsible for protecting the rights of Data Subjects and responding to their requests for exercising those rights. Reasoning of the LLM

 - **Antrag stellen und Unterlagen beilegen (sid-6B858C71-612A-4352-A501-358B0F46C82C)**: **Antrag stellen und Unterlagen beilegen** involves the submission of an application for a change of study program, which inherently requires the collection and provision of **personal data**. Typical application documents include: - **Identification data** (name, date of birth, student ID), - **Academic records** (transcripts, certificates, proof of qualifications), - **Contact details** (address, email, phone number), - Potentially **special categories of data** (e.g., health-related accommodations or disability statements). The activity explicitly references 'Unterlagen beilegen' (attaching documents), which are tied to an identifiable natural person (the student). Under **Article 4(1) GDPR**, this constitutes 'processing' as it involves **collecting, recording, and structuring** personal data for administrative purposes (enrollment management). The **imbalance of power** between the university (a **public authority**) and the student further underscores the GDPR relevance, as consent may not be 'freely given' in this context (Recital 43). - **Genehmigung annehmen (sid-FB90AB1E-1092-49BE-9A6D-19ACE59DFDC4)**: **Genehmigung annehmen** involves the student’s explicit **acceptance of an admission offer**, which is tied to their **personal enrollment data** (e.g., name, student ID, program details). This activity processes personal data by: - **Confirming the student’s identity** (linking the acceptance to their records), - **Updating the enrollment system** with their decision (a form of **structuring/storing** personal data under Article 4(2) GDPR). The university, as a **public authority**, processes this data to fulfill its **legal obligation** (enrollment management) under **Article 6(1)(c) GDPR**. The activity is a critical step in the **performance of a contract** (study agreement) with the data subject. - **Eingang bestätigen und Antrag prüfen, Annahme bei nicht zulassungs-freien Studiengängen verbuchen (sid-7B71A8E2-8B0F-484E-A5E1-102AA86ADAF9)**: **Eingang bestätigen und Antrag prüfen** involves two GDPR-relevant operations: 1. **Confirming receipt of the application**: This requires accessing the student’s **submitted personal data** (e.g., name, contact details, academic history) to send a confirmation. 2. **Prüfen (reviewing) the application**: This includes **consulting, analysing, and evaluating** the personal data provided (e.g., transcripts, qualifications, potential special categories like disability statements) to determine eligibility. The activity also mentions **'Annahme bei nicht zulassungs-freien Studiengängen verbuchen'**, which implies **recording/structuring** the student’s admission status in the university’s systems. As a **public authority**, the university processes this data under **Article 6(1)(e) GDPR** (public task) and must ensure **security and confidentiality** (Recital 40). - **über Antrag entscheiden (Beiträge, HZB) (sid-70181670-FBB0-45CF-9F0B-992E81AB2288)**: **über Antrag entscheiden (Beiträge, HZB)** involves **evaluating the student’s application** based on: - **Hochschulzugangsberechtigung (HZB)**: Academic qualifications tied to the student’s identity. - **Beiträge (fees/tuition status)**: Financial data linked to the student’s enrollment (e.g., exemptions, scholarships). This activity **processes personal data** by: - **Analysing** the student’s eligibility (profiling under Article 4(4) GDPR), - **Recording the decision** in the university’s systems (structuring/storing), - Potentially **disclosing** the decision to other departments (transmission). The university acts as a **public authority** with a **legal obligation** to manage enrollments, making this processing necessary under **Article 6(1)(c/e) GDPR**. - **Annahme löschen (nicht zulassungsfreie Studiengänge) (sid-497E9C09-3EE9-4D70-BB00-FA96493C2FB4)**: **Annahme löschen (nicht zulassungsfreie Studiengänge)** involves **erasing personal data** related to the student’s application (e.g., name, qualifications, contact details) from the university’s systems. Even though the goal is deletion, this activity **processes personal data** by: - **Retrieving** the student’s records (accessing personal data), - **Erasing** the data (a form of processing under Article 4(2) GDPR). The university, as a **public authority**, must ensure the deletion complies with **Article 17 GDPR** (right to erasure) and **Article 5(1)(e)** (storage limitation). The activity is explicitly tied to **non-admission programs**, implying selective handling of personal data based on program rules. - **Studiengangswechsel durchführen (sid-8630B3E4-2878-4D73-B48C-A7899171070C)**: **Studiengangswechsel durchführen** involves **updating the student’s enrollment records** in the university’s systems, which requires processing: - **Identification data** (name, student ID), - **Academic data** (current/new program, credits, semester), - Potentially **financial data** (tuition adjustments). This activity **modifies, structures, and stores** personal data to reflect the change, acting under the university’s **public authority mandate** (Article 6(1)(e) GDPR). The process may also involve **transmitting** updated records to other departments (e.g., exam offices, financial aid). - **Antrag aus 3. FS oder höher (sid-D5554C4D-0281-4108-97F5-5183E29A69A2)**: **Antrag aus 3. FS oder höher** involves **reviewing and processing applications from students in advanced semesters**, which requires accessing and evaluating: - **Academic history** (transcripts, credits, previous semesters), - **Personal identification data** (student ID, name), - Potentially **special categories** (e.g., health-related leaves of absence). [concept] Inquiries — Inquiries are specific requests for information, which are part of the mutual assistance provided between supervisory authorities.

[concept] Controller — A Controller is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that, either alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes ("why") and means ("how") of processing personal data. This entity acts as the primary decision-maker in data processing activities, bearing overall responsibility for personal data protection under frameworks like the GDPR. Examples include banks, social media providers, and insurance companies. Gatekeepers, particularly under DMA Article 6(9), are also likely considered Controllers for data porting, especially when their legitimate interests involve indicating criminal acts or threats to public security. Controllers are subject to Union or Member State law and must be able to justify any doubts about a data subject's identity, including when processing pseudonymized data while retaining the ability to identify the data subject. Controllers have extensive responsibilities under GDPR, encompassing ensuring data accuracy, complying with data protection principles, and implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard personal data. They must identify and mitigate risks to data subjects' rights, establish necessary safeguards, and guarantee data integrity and confidentiality. Key obligations also include managing in-company data processing, restricting access to sensitive data, informing data subjects about processing purposes, obtaining valid consent, and providing mechanisms for individuals to exercise their data rights. Controllers are required to demonstrate valid processing grounds, define data retention periods, implement data deletion procedures, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs). They must assess datasets for bias, develop measures to prevent errors, and comply with national laws regarding the age of digital consent by obtaining parental authorization when necessary. Furthermore, Controllers are responsible for assessing and verifying the sufficiency of guarantees provided by a processor, authorizing the use of sub-processors, deploying electronic means for transparency information, and adhering to principles when communicating privacy statements and subsequent changes to data subjects. They are also responsible for demonstrating compliance with GDPR, including having a valid lawful ground for processing personal data and demonstrating legitimate interests when applicable. The Controller supports and involves the Data Protection Officer (DPO), determining the necessary level of expert knowledge for data processing, and their primary activities are related to core tasks and do not involve personal data processing as ancillary activities. Regarding personal data breaches, the Controller is responsible for recognizing, addressing, and notifying personal data breaches. They must act on initial alerts, establish if a breach occurred, gather evidence, and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if conditions are met. This includes assessing the specific circumstances of a breach, the affected data, and the potential impact on individuals. Controllers determine whether to notify individuals and supervisory authorities, and must record all data breaches—whether non-notifiable or notifiable—to comply with Article 24 of the GDPR. They are required to establish an internal register of breaches, determining the method and structure for documentation and recording specific details as per Article 33(5). Controllers must also consider encryption quality and implementation to comply with data protection regulations and assess which supervisory authority is the lead for breach notification, responding promptly to breaches and meeting their obligations under Article 33. For cross-border processing, a Controller typically requires a main or single establishment within an EU Member State. Their main establishment in the Union is generally its central administration, unless processing decisions are made elsewhere. They are ultimately accountable, even if tasks are delegated, such as to a DPO, and must ensure DPO autonomy while publishing their contact details. If established in the EU, a Controller falls under the GDPR's cooperation mechanism and may have a lead supervisory authority, which is generally the main one when both controller and processor are involved. Controllers are the entities upon whom administrative fines may be imposed for GDPR infringements and are subject to GDPR under Article 3 for international data transfers, acting as exporters or importers of personal data. Their activities are assessed for GDPR compliance and may lead to infringement claims. They are often targets of draft and final decisions from Supervisory Authorities, retaining a right to be heard. They are obligated to comply with these decisions and notify the authorities of any adopted measures. They may also transfer personal data to third countries or international organizations. A Controller is an entity responsibly liable for any processing of personal data carried out by them or on their behalf, and must implement appropriate and effective measures to demonstrate compliance with this Regulation. They are liable for damages caused by infringements of the Regulation, and a data subject can seek judicial remedies against them. A Controller is also a natural or legal person directly and individually concerned by decisions of the Board and may bring an action for annulment.

[concept] Controller Or Processor — Entities or individuals subject to regulations under the GDPR regarding data handling.
A controller or processor is an entity whose conduct is examined for compliance with the GDPR and potentially the DMA.

[method] Administrative Arrangements — Administrative arrangements are provisions that can be inserted between public bodies for data transfers, subject to authorization from the competent SA, including enforceable and effective data subject rights.
A mechanism for personal data transfers between public bodies under Article 46 (3) (b) GDPR, subject to authorization from a competent supervisory authority.
Administrative arrangements are alternative instruments for data transfer, such as Memoranda of Understanding, providing protection through commitments.
Administrative arrangements, such as a memorandum of understanding, provide for enforceable and effective rights for data subjects in the context of data transfers involving public authorities.
Administrative arrangements are provisions inserted between public authorities or bodies, including enforceable data subject rights, used as safeguards.
Administrative Arrangements are agreements related to data protection, which a Supervisory Authority can authorize.

[organization] Supervisory Authority — A Supervisory Authority (SA) is an independent public authority established by a European Union Member State, as mandated by Article 51 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its core responsibility is to monitor and enforce the application of data protection law, primarily the GDPR, within its specific national jurisdiction. The overarching goal of an SA is to safeguard the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals regarding the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the European Union. SAs act as competent national bodies under Articles 55 or 56 of the GDPR, endowed with a broad spectrum of powers, including investigation, corrective actions, authorization, and advisory functions. Their decisions, which carry legal effects, are subject to judicial remedies, and they are obligated to respect the right to be heard. Supervisory Authorities are responsible for handling complaints lodged by data subjects, especially when controllers fail to address their requests. They are also the competent national authority to which personal data breaches must be notified without undue delay, typically within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals. For cross-border breaches, an SA can act as the lead authority, request further details, advise on informing individuals, and order controllers to do so. They also receive information about the Data Protection Officer's (DPO) name and contact details. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to determine the nature and gravity of infringements, ensure compliance, and order appropriate measures against data controllers or processors. This includes the ability to impose effective, proportionate, and dissuasive administrative fines for GDPR infringements, considering factors such as circumstances, economic viability, and proportionality. They may hold parent companies liable and impose fines for non-compliance with Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) requirements. Additionally, a supervisory authority must be consulted if a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, and it possesses the power to prohibit such processing operations. They can also require documentation of a DPO designation analysis and request access to records of processing operations. Beyond enforcement, Supervisory Authorities play a crucial role in GDPR accreditation and certification mechanisms. This involves approving criteria, reviewing existing certifications, accrediting certification bodies, and potentially acting as a certification body themselves. They can establish additional accreditation requirements, sometimes in cooperation with a National Accreditation Body. SAs are authorized to oversee and approve administrative arrangements for data transfers under Article 46(3)(b) GDPR, adopt standard contractual clauses for data processing matters, approve safeguards, and apply consistency mechanisms. They are also responsible for publishing lists of processing operations subject to mandatory DPIAs and for conducting prior consultations if DPIA results indicate a high risk or if existing operations have been pre-checked. While typically one lead supervisory authority exists for cross-border processing, some Member States may have more than one SA, all of whom are bound by the content of a draft decision once consensus is reached. They are also responsible for verifying compliance with data protection regulations and may require a controller to communicate a personal data breach to the data subject.

[organization] Gatekeepers — Gatekeepers are undertakings, primarily digital platforms, designated by the European Commission. These entities provide core platform services, acting as essential gateways between business users and end users, and possess significant data-driven advantages. They may also be entities offering number-independent interpersonal communications services. Gatekeepers are explicitly addressed by the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and its Guidelines, with harmonized rules applying to them to ensure contestable and fair markets. They may fall under the notion of large online platforms and function as either controllers or processors of personal data, specifically identified as controllers under the GDPR in certain scenarios. Gatekeepers face extensive obligations concerning data processing and user consent. They must enable end users to freely choose to opt-in to data processing and sign-in practices covered by Article 5(2) DMA. This requires providing a user-friendly solution for users to provide, modify, or withdraw consent, including offering granular choices regarding the combination or cross-use of personal data. When seeking consent, Gatekeepers must specify the intended purpose of personal data processing. They are also obliged to adopt technical and organizational measures to comply with the GDPR and facilitate compliance for DMA beneficiaries, while ensuring valid and user-friendly consent mechanisms that respect data protection principles. Additionally, Gatekeepers are required to offer interoperability and comply with data minimization principles. They must enable data portability under Article 6(9) DMA, maintaining an internal list of porting data categories. Data sharing obligations under Article 6(11) DMA also apply, including the requirement to ensure data anonymization. Gatekeepers must submit independently audited descriptions of their consumer profiling techniques to the European Commission within six months of their designation under DMA Article 15. While incentivized to innovate, they must not undermine other DMA obligations and have specific responsibilities regarding third-party apps and app stores.

Under GDPR, Controller In the context of the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a Controller is defined as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This role is fundamental to the GDPR framework, outlining significant obligations and responsibilities for any party involved in deciding how personal data is processed. Controllers are accountable for ensuring compliance with all GDPR provisions, particularly as detailed in Article 3. The Controller has legal obligations to ensure compliance with the GDPR and is responsible and liable under its provisions, with these obligations often referred to as "GDPR controller obligations." The responsibilities of a Controller include applying GDPR rules to data processing, adhering to foundational principles like lawfulness and fairness (Article 5(1)), and fulfilling transparency obligations. Specific duties extend to maintaining records of processing activities (Article 30), ensuring the security of processing (Article 32), conducting data protection impact assessments (Article 35), and engaging in prior consultation (Article 36) for managing risks. Controllers must also comply with regulations regarding data storage periods, implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, and adhere to specific legal bases, such as legitimate interest, for processing data. The GDPR places a significant burden of proof on the Controller, requiring them to demonstrate "compelling legitimate grounds for the processing" when applicable. They must ensure consent mechanisms meet GDPR standards and act upon withdrawal requests. Compliance with obligations related to accountability, engaging processors, and maintaining data security is paramount. Regarding data breaches, the GDPR mandates that controllers implement appropriate security measures, ensure compliance with processing principles, and adhere to relevant provisions for breach notification, as specified in Article 60(10). Unless a breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the Controller is required to notify the competent supervisory authority and, in certain cases, the affected individuals. The GDPR further defines notification and communication requirements for Controllers regarding breaches, and they must retain documentation in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. The GDPR also places the burden of proof regarding objections on the Controller. Supervisory Authorities are empowered to take enforcement action, including imposing fines, for any infringement of GDPR provisions resulting from a Controller's actions. The ability for data controllers to obtain GDPR certifications further underscores their pivotal role and accountability within the regulatory framework, though some Controllers currently face broad and systemic issues in compliance with the GDPR. Under GDPR, Controller The relation "(Controller, Personal Data)" signifies that the Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. This involves significant authority and responsibility over the entire lifecycle of personal data, encompassing decisions related to its processing, protection, management, and transference. The Controller is explicitly responsible for establishing the retention period for documentation containing personal data and makes choices regarding its deletion or return. A core obligation of the Controller is to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and to uphold data subject rights, including guaranteeing data accuracy and facilitating the exercise of those rights. The Controller is always required to have an appropriate lawful ground for the processing of personal data, and while explicit consent may be obtained, it is not always the sole lawful basis, especially when processing is essential for a contract. The Controller is also responsible for the overall protection and security of personal data, which includes managing and responding to any data breaches, and applying appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard it. This responsibility extends to implementing measures to minimize the processing of personal data. In addition to determining purposes and means, the Controller collects, processes, and stores personal data. The Controller may also determine its identification requirements and, in the EU, has the capability to make personal data accessible to a third-country authority, and may specifically process data indicating criminal acts when considered within their legitimate interest. Persons under the direct authority of the Controller are authorized to process personal data. The Controller is ultimately responsible and liable for any processing of personal data, including its transferring. Personal Data.

[organization] Gatekeepers — Gatekeepers are undertakings, primarily digital platforms, designated by the European Commission. These entities provide core platform services, acting as essential gateways between business users and end users, and possess significant data-driven advantages. They may also be entities offering number-independent interpersonal communications services. Gatekeepers are explicitly addressed by the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and its Guidelines, with harmonized rules applying to them to ensure contestable and fair markets. They may fall under the notion of large online platforms and function as either controllers or processors of personal data, specifically identified as controllers under the GDPR in certain scenarios. Gatekeepers face extensive obligations concerning data processing and user consent. They must enable end users to freely choose to opt-in to data processing and sign-in practices covered by Article 5(2) DMA. This requires providing a user-friendly solution for users to provide, modify, or withdraw consent, including offering granular choices regarding the combination or cross-use of personal data. When seeking consent, Gatekeepers must specify the intended purpose of personal data processing. They are also obliged to adopt technical and organizational measures to comply with the GDPR and facilitate compliance for DMA beneficiaries, while ensuring valid and user-friendly consent mechanisms that respect data protection principles. Additionally, Gatekeepers are required to offer interoperability and comply with data minimization principles. They must enable data portability under Article 6(9) DMA, maintaining an internal list of porting data categories. Data sharing obligations under Article 6(11) DMA also apply, including the requirement to ensure data anonymization. Gatekeepers must submit independently audited descriptions of their consumer profiling techniques to the European Commission within six months of their designation under DMA Article 15. While incentivized to innovate, they must not undermine other DMA obligations and have specific responsibilities regarding third-party apps and app stores.

[concept] Processor — A Processor, as defined by Article 4(8) of the GDPR, is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. This entity's primary function is to handle personal data strictly according to the controller's documented instructions, without independently determining the purposes or means of the processing activity, and thus, processors do not pursue independent objectives for data processing. A website hosting company is an example of a Processor. Processors are responsible for protecting personal data and are involved in the processing of personal data, with specific legal obligations under the GDPR, including adherence to its principles, ensuring confidentiality, and implementing robust security measures. They must provide sufficient guarantees, such as compliance with codes of conduct or certification mechanisms, and are required to operate under a binding contract or legal act with the controller. This contract typically details their responsibilities, including assisting with Data Protection by Design and by Default (DPbDD), implementing technical and organizational measures, conducting data protection impact assessments (DPIA), and providing compliance information. The processor assists the controller in carrying out a DPIA, and its roles and responsibilities in a DPIA must be contractually defined. Processors are also obligated to notify the controller of any data breach without undue delay, inform the controller of any infringing instructions, and are subject to audits. Upon termination of processing activities, they must delete or return personal data. They have specific obligations regarding personal data breaches, as mentioned in Article 33 requirements, particularly Article 33(2). Processors can also act as exporters or importers of personal data, transferring data to third countries or international organizations under specific conditions, always on behalf of the controller and must implement appropriate safeguards for data transfers. While their name may not be explicitly included in consent forms, they are listed as recipients of data. They are held liable to the controller for the performance of their sub-processors' obligations, necessitating that sub-processors also provide sufficient guarantees. Processors' activities and processing operations are assessed for GDPR compliance, and they can be the direct cause of a data breach. They may be the subject of infringement claims, addressed by the final decision of a competent supervisory authority, and can be directly and individually concerned by an EDPB binding decision, against which they may bring an action for annulment. For Processors located in the EU, they must identify an applicable ground for transfer before responding to requests from third-country authorities, as stipulated under Article 48. The designation of a representative does not affect their liability under GDPR, and they may be subject to legal actions for damages if they infringe the regulation or act outside of controller instructions. A data subject can seek judicial remedies against a processor. A Processor may be required to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO), especially if their core activities involve key operations to achieve their goals, or if their core activities require such a designation under GDPR. When a DPO is designated, the processor is required to publish and communicate the DPO's contact details according to Article 37(7) of the GDPR. The DPO advises the processor on GDPR obligations and assists in monitoring internal compliance with the GDPR. The processor may assign the task of maintaining records of processing operations to the DPO, and the processor supports and involves the Data Protection Officer. For the cooperation procedure to apply, a Processor involved in cross-border processing must have a main or single establishment in an EU Member State. This main establishment oversees such cross-border processing. The main establishment is where its central administration is located in the Union, or where its main processing activities take place if no central administration exists in the Union. Processors are subject to the authority of a Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) or Concerned Supervisory Authority (CSA), and LSAs may interact with Processors to gather relevant information, such as investigation findings, reports, and meeting records. Processors involved in cross-border processing are subject to procedures and potential enforcement action and may be directly targeted by decisions from the LSA. As parties targeted by a draft decision, their right to be heard must comply with national law, and their rights may be affected by changes in a revised draft decision. A Processor's actions can lead to complaints and prompt action by an LSA. Processors have obligations under Article 60(10), are informed of decisions by the LSA, and are obliged to notify the LSA of any measures adopted to comply with a decision entailing corrective measures. A processor can benefit from the one-stop-shop system if established in multiple Member States, and its establishment in multiple Member States can trigger the lead authority mechanism. Guidance can be provided on their implementation of appropriate measures and demonstration of compliance.

While their personal data may be cross-used with or without explicit consent depending on the specific legal basis, they generally have choices concerning data access. Their data is also subject to re-identification attempts by gatekeepers. A crucial aspect of the End User's rights is data portability, as outlined in DMA Article 6(9) and GDPR Article 20. Explicit and specific consent is required from the End User for personal data transfers to third countries that do not have an adequacy decision. Furthermore, the End User's consent is essential for sharing their personal data when business users request access to it in the context of a Core Platform Service.

[Source: EDPB_guidelines_202007_controllerprocessor_final_en] "Adopted - After public consultation 1 Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR Version 2.1 Adopted on 07 July 2021 Adopted - After public consultation 2 Version history Version 2.1 20 September 2022 Minor corrections Version 2.0 7 July 2021 Adoption of the Guidelines after public consultation Version 1.0 2 September 2020 Adoption of the Guidelines for public consultation Adopted - After public consultation 3 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The concepts of controller, joint controller and processor play a crucial role in the application of the General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), since they determine who shall be responsible for compliance with different data protection rules, and how data subjects can exercise their rights in practice. The precise meaning of these concepts and the criteria for their correct interpretation must be sufficiently clear and consistent throughout the European Economic Area (EEA). The concepts of controller, joint controller and processor are functional concepts in that they aim to allocate responsibilities according to the actual roles of the parties and autonomous concepts in the sense that they should be interpreted mainly according to EU data protection law. Controller In principle, there is no limitation as to the type of entity that may assume the role of a controller but in practice it is usually the organisation as such, and not an individual within the organisation (such as the CEO, an employee or a member of the board), that acts as a controller. A controller is a body that decides certain key elements of the processing. Controllership may be defined by law or may stem from an analysis of the factual elements or circumstances of the case. Certain processing activities can be seen as naturally attached to the role of an entity (an employer to employees, a publisher to subscribers or an association to its members). In many cases, the terms of a contract can help identify the controller, although they are not decisive in all circumstances. A controller determines the purposes and means of the processing, i.e. the why and how of the processing. The controller must decide on both purposes and means. However, some more practical aspects of implementation (“non-essential means”) can be left to the processor. It is not necessary that the controller actually has access to the data that is being processed to be qualified as a controller. Joint controllers The qualification as joint controllers may arise where more than one actor is involved in the processing. The GDPR introduces specific rules for joint controllers and sets a framework to govern their relationship. The overarching criterion for joint controllership to exist is the joint participation of two or more entities in the determination of the purposes and means of a processing operation. Joint participation can take the form of a common decision taken by two or more entities or result from converging decisions by two or more entities, where the decisions complement each other and are necessary for the processing to take place in such a manner that they have a tangible impact on the determination of the purposes and means of the processing. An important criterion is that the processing would not be possible without both parties’ participation in the sense that the processing by each party is inseparable, i.e. inextricably linked. The joint participation needs to include the determination of purposes on the one hand and the determination of means on the other hand. Processor A processor is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or another body, which processes personal data on behalf of the controller. Two basic conditions for qualifying as processor exist: that it is a separate entity in relation to the controller and that it processes personal data on the controller’s behalf. The processor must not process the data otherwise than according to the controller’s instructions. The controller’s instructions may still leave a certain degree of discretion about how to best serve the Adopted - After public consultation 4 controller’s interests, allowing the processor to choose the most suitable technical and organisational means. A processor infringes the GDPR, however, if it goes beyond the controller’s instructions and starts to determine its own purposes and means of the processing. The processor will then be considered a controller in respect of that processing and may be subject to sanctions for going beyond the controller’s instructions. Relationship between controller and processor A controller must only use processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures so that the processing meets the requirements of the GDPR. Elements to be taken into account could be the processor’s expert knowledge (e.g. technical expertise with regard to security measures and data breaches); the processor’s reliability; the processor’s resources and the processor’s adherence to an approved code of conduct or certification mechanism. Any processing of personal data by a processor must be governed by a contract or other legal act which shall be in writing, including in electronic form, and be binding. The controller and the processor may choose to negotiate their own contract including all the compulsory elements or to rely, in whole or in part, on standard contractual clauses. The GDPR lists the elements that have to be set out in the processing agreement. The processing agreement should not, however, merely restate the provisions of the GDPR; rather, it should include more specific, concrete information as to how the requirements will be met and which level of security is required for the personal data processing that is the object of the processing agreement. Relationship among joint controllers Joint controllers shall in a transparent manner determine and agree on their respective responsibilities for compliance with the obligations under the GDPR."
